as mapped above, and unit eval-1 (`compute_eval`, `_eval_report`).

## The ranker

`search::Corpus::new` tokenizes and indexes the records once (the
reference's token cache); `Corpus::search` ranks one query with
`search::Options` (mode, `max_results` with Python's slice semantics, half
life, `rrf_k`, the lane and rescue switches, `allow_empty_query`, scope and
excluded-scope filters, a corpus-stats provider callback). The reference's
admission, actor filters, claim anchoring, `hydrate`, `matched_leg_out` and
each hit's snippet and path-drift report need the store or the filesystem
and are not here: the store unit adds them around `Corpus::search`.

Scores are bit-identical to the reference: the same operations in the same
order, `f64` throughout, sums accumulated in the reference's order. Three
operations are not one IEEE-754 operation and are written out in
`search/num.rs`: `int / int` (CPython's correctly rounded true division,
which `timedelta.total_seconds`, `avgdl` and the coverage fractions use),
`round(x, 4)` (decimal rounding, half to even, of the exact binary value)
and `math.log`'s domain errors. The scores depend on the platform's libm
through three functions, the same ones CPython's `math` calls: `log` (the
Okapi IDF), `exp` (the recency decay) and `log1p` (the keyword scorer's
term-frequency residual). Rust's `f64::ln`, `exp` and `ln_1p` call the
platform's `log`, `exp` and `log1p`, so on one machine both read the same
libm; on another libm either may round differently in the last place, and
the golden files pin macOS's. `search_ranker.jsonl` is built so that no
input it hands those functions (662: 150 `log`, 507 `exp`, 5 `log1p`) lies
within 0.05 ULP of a rounding midpoint (the smallest margin is 0.0515,
recorded in its header and asserted by its generator), so any libm that
rounds correctly or nearly gives the same bits; `search.jsonl` has no such
check. The selector arm of the lane multiplies by
`0.0 * 0.7**k`, which is exactly zero for any `pow`, so `pow` is not read.

Where the port refuses what the reference might answer, it returns
`SearchError::InvalidInput`, a name the reference never raises: a NaN
half-life, a timestamp whose fields name no datetime, and candidates that
mix naive and aware `created` (or, browsing, `updated`). On that last one
an in-memory caller outside the store diverges from the reference: there
CPython raises TypeError only where its sort happens to compare a naive
with an aware value (two tied scores), and otherwise answers. A store
cannot produce such a set (`store_rows._dt` reads a naive timestamp as
UTC). Everything else, including the reference's own ValueError,
OverflowError and TypeError (a naive `now`; a record naive in one of
`created` and `updated` and aware in the other, once it scores), is
reproduced as an error of that name.

Accidents of the reference the port copies (and `gen_search_ranker.py`'s
docstring lists): a record's anchor day is the date of `created` in its own
UTC offset while the query's window is read in `now`'s; a month name's
year is `\s+\d{4}` with no word boundary after it ("may 20245" reads May
2024); the order ask `which ... (first|last)\b` has no word boundary
before first/last ("which atlast"); `\d` and `int()` read any Unicode
decimal digit; "last year" at year 1 is ValueError and the relative
periods at the ends of the calendar OverflowError, out of `search` itself;
`_scaffold_floor_stats` drops a provider's `avgdl`, so a temporal query
with a provider prices length against the pool's mean.

Timing the ranker against the reference: every query of
`search_ranker.jsonl` in its four core modes, records prepared before the
clock in both, the query's text in and the ranked hits out:

```sh
cargo test --offline --release --test bench_search -- --ignored --nocapture
../.venv/bin/python tools/bench_search.py 5
```

On an Apple M-series laptop at 10 repetitions (324 records, 208 queries in
four modes, 832 searches a pass), three runs each: the reference 918.5,
915.5 and 915.2 ms per pass, native 24.65, 25.00 and 24.56 ms (37x). The
reference's hits also carry their snippet, which native does not build.

A query's cost grows with its distinct terms times the records they
touch, with no cap, in the reference and here alike: neither bounds the
terms. Measured on 3,000 records of 30 words, a query of 74 corpus words
and N terms no record holds: the reference (Python 3.13) takes 0.70, 6.93
and 75.4 s in keyword mode and 1.19, 11.5 and 112 s in bm25 mode for N =
1,000, 10,000 and 100,000 and 1.91, 18.4 and 188 s in hybrid mode; native release 0.01, 0.06 and 0.53 s (keyword), 0.01,
0.05 and 0.46 s (bm25), 0.02, 0.11 and 1.02 s (hybrid). Upstream nothing
bounds the terms either: `memory_search` takes the query as a plain
string, and the only limit before it is the MCP SDK's 4 MiB request body
(about 400,000 such terms). What upstream does bound is the records: the
handler ranks a pool it draws from FTS5 (`handlers/search.py`,
`POOL_SIZE` 200), not the whole store. No cap is added here.

## Snippets and the token cache (`search.py`)

`search::snippet` and `search::token_cache` reproduce the snippet path and
the per-candidate token cache of `search.py`. They need nothing from the
machine but the tokenizer; each memo is a value the caller holds, as
`search_dedup::RawTokenCache` is.

### Map, by function

| function | reference lines | needs from the machine | status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `TOKEN_CACHE_ENTRIES`, `_TOKEN_CACHE`, `clear_token_cache` | 522-534 | a process-wide cache and its lock | built (`TokenCache`, `TokenCache::clear`) |
| `_memory_tokens` | 538-563 | the cache | built (`TokenCache::memory_tokens`, a memory as its body and scopes) |
| `seed_memory_tokens` | 567-600 | the cache | built (`TokenCache::seed_memory_tokens`) |
| `search_bm25.term_counts`, `_scope_tokens` | bm25 119-123, 167-172 | nothing | built (`token_cache::term_counts`, `search::scope_tokens`, `search::body_stream`, which `Corpus::new` now calls) |
| `EXPAND_TOP_SCORE_MARGIN`, `top_hit_leads_runner_up` | 646, 649-667 | nothing | built (`snippet`) |
| `_SNIPPET_SCAN_CHARS`, `_SnippetTokens` | 819-858 | nothing | built (`SNIPPET_SCAN_CHARS`, `SnippetTokens`) |
| `SNIPPET_TOKEN_ENTRIES`, `TOKEN_SURFACE_ENTRIES`, `clear_snippet_caches` | 859-878 | two process-wide memos and their locks | built (`SnippetMemo`, `SnippetMemo::clear`) |
| `_token_surfaces`, `_snippet_tokens` | 880-917 | the memos | built |
| `_query_biased_snippet` | 918-1040 | the memos | built |
| `_build_hit`, `_claim_anchors` | 1041-1118, 1964-1979 | the store | not built (unit search-1b) |

### What each part reproduces, and the decisions

- **The LRUs.** `token_cache::Lru` is an `OrderedDict` used as the
  reference uses it: a hit moves the key to the end, a new key goes at the
  end, a held key keeps its place and takes the new value (`d[k] = v`),
  and past the bound the front goes. The three memos share it. Each
  look-up-and-touch and each insert-and-evict holds a lock; the
  tokenizing runs outside it, as in the reference. The bounds are the
  reference's (5,000, 5,000 and 20,000); `with_entries` takes another
  bound as a `usize`, the golden file's eviction cases run at bounds of 0
  to 3 (the generator sets the module constants for those rows). A bound
  the reference could be patched to below zero (where `popitem` of an
  empty dict raises KeyError) has no counterpart. The
  `_caches.register` calls are left to the unit that wires `_caches`.
- **The token cache.** The key is `(body, tuple(scopes))`: scopes in
  another order are another key. `MemoryTokens.body_tf` keeps the dict's
  order, first occurrence first. `seed_memory_tokens` splits the index
  text on single spaces, so two spaces give an empty token, and an empty
  text gives no tokens; a held entry stands and is touched.
- **The scan.** `lexicon::token_spans` is `_TOKEN_RE.finditer` over the
  existing hand matcher `find_tokens`, giving each match's offsets. The
  surfaces of a raw token are interned by its text, in scan order, so the
  surface memo's eviction order is the reference's.
- **The alias anchors.** `_ALIAS_ANCHOR_PATTERNS` are the four
  `_SYMBOL_ALIASES` literals under IGNORECASE (flags 34).
  `lexicon::alias_anchor_starts` extends the existing hand matcher of
  those literals with an ASCII case fold: under `re`'s IGNORECASE no code
  point but the ASCII pair matches `c`, `f`, `n`, `e` or `t` (checked over
  every code point on 3.13.13). Under the regex decision this is rule 3
  (a matcher already built, the search tokenizer); no new pattern is
  written, and the four patterns are in the engine's inventory through
  the `ast` scan of `search_lexicon.py`.
- **The window.** Anchors keep duplicates (a token and an alias at one
  offset count twice), the window arithmetic is signed (`max_chars` may
  be zero or negative), and a tie keeps the earliest window.
- **The matched terms** are Rust strings: a search's `matched` holds
  tokens, which never hold a surrogate. Bodies are code points.

### Fixtures

`gen_search_snippet.py` writes `search_snippet.jsonl` (ungated) and
`search_snippet_unicode.jsonl` (UNICODE_GATED: `\w`, `str.strip`, NFKC and
the fold past ASCII). Each snippet row is written for the terms as given
and again for each term's first token (the stemmed form a search
matches), so both a miss and a hit of an unstemmed spelling are pinned.
Long bodies are spelled as repeated pieces, a memo key past 200
characters as its length and a SHA-256 prefix, and a seeded sweep (1,500
ASCII bodies, 300 past ASCII, from a 64-bit LCG the Rust test runs too)
as a digest.

Tests: `golden_search_snippet`, `search_snippet_kills`,
`search_snippet_robustness` (the scan's time does not grow with the body
past `_SNIPPET_SCAN_CHARS`).

## Write-time dedup (`search_dedup.py`)

`search_dedup` reproduces the whole reference module (559 lines), built
as one unit: it needs nothing from the machine but the tokenizer, and
its store half reads a store only through methods the caller supplies.

### Map, by function

| function | reference lines | needs from the machine | status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `HIGH_SIMILARITY`, `MEDIUM_SIMILARITY`, `_CONTAINMENT_MIN_TOKENS`, `_CONTAINMENT_CEILING` | 47-66 | nothing | built (constants) |
| `_content_token_set` | 69-85 | the tokenizer | built (`content_token_set`) |
| `_raw_content_token_set` | 88-93 | the tokenizer | built (`raw_content_token_set`) |
| `RAW_TOKEN_SET_ENTRIES`, `_RAW_TOKEN_SETS`, `clear_raw_token_set_cache`, `raw_content_tokens` | 117-148 | a process-wide cache and its lock | built (`RawTokenCache`, a value the caller holds; `_caches.register` has no counterpart) |
| `_pairwise_content_jaccard` | 151-229 | nothing | built |
| `similarity_bound` | 232-253 | nothing | built (counts as `i64`) |
| `find_similar`, `_find_similar_jaccard` | 256-287, 415-431 | the cache | built |
| `_score_similar_jaccard`, `_build_active_hit`, `_build_tombstone_hit`, `_active_sort_key`, `_tombstone_sort_key` | 314-412 | the cache | built (private; `Pass` picks the builder, labels and key) |
| `find_similar_tombstones`, `_find_similar_tombstones_jaccard` | 454-499 | the cache | built |
| `_similar_in`, `find_similar_in`, `find_similar_tombstones_in` | 513-559 | a store's digest | built (`DigestStore`) |
| `models.snippet_for`, `_truncate_at_word` (default 200) | models 1057-1068, 1111-1127 | nothing | built (`snippet_for`, which calls `models_text::snippet_for`) |

### What each part reproduces, and the decisions

- **The cache.** `RawTokenCache` is the reference's `OrderedDict` LRU
  keyed on the text: a hit moves the key to the end, a miss tokenizes
  outside the lock and inserts at the end (a key another thread inserted
  meanwhile keeps its place and takes the new value, as `d[k] = v` does),
  then the oldest keys go while more than `entries` are held. `entries`
  is the reference's `RAW_TOKEN_SET_ENTRIES`, a Python int its tests
  patch; under a negative bound the loop empties the cache and then
  `popitem` raises `KeyError` (`DedupError::EmptyCache`), which the port
  reproduces. The process-wide cache becomes a value every entry point
  takes, so no state is ambient; `keys()` shows the order for the tests.
  Only the order and the bound are observable: a held set equals a
  recomputed one.
- **The score.** `pairwise_content_jaccard` expands a compound only where
  the other side lacks it, drops stopword parts, and divides two counts
  (each exact in an `f64`, so one correctly rounded division, as Python's
  `int / int`). `max` and `min` pick as Python's do between equal values.
  `similarity_bound` takes its counts as `i64` and divides them with
  `search::num::int_true_div` (exact for magnitudes under 2**72, so
  `n + m - shared` is computed in `i128`).
- **The sort.** The reference sorts hits on `(similarity, datetime)`
  tuples with `reverse=True` (the rounded similarity, so two raw scores
  that round alike tie). A tie compares the datetimes, and Python raises
  `TypeError` for a naive against an aware one. Which pairs CPython's
  `list.sort` compares depends on its algorithm, but within a group of
  equal similarity holding both kinds it must compare one of each: if it
  never did, every comparison it made would answer the same whether every
  naive value lay before every aware one or after, so it would order the
  group alike in two orders that need different answers. So the port
  raises (`DedupError::NaiveAware`) exactly when such a group exists, and
  otherwise answers the stable descending order. Aware values order by
  their instant; naive by their wall clock. `records::Memory` can hold a
  naive datetime (pydantic keeps one), so the case is reachable.
- **The hits.** `SimilarHit` carries the fields the model does;
  `confidence` is the enum, `relevance` one of the four labels, and the
  tombstone pass alone fills `removed_at` and `removed_reason`. Records
  reach the scorer through `Candidate`, implemented for `Memory` and
  `Tombstone`; a store's `LightRecord` is the store's own type.
- **Order of effects.** `find_similar_tombstones` of an empty list answers
  before the body is tokenized (the cache is untouched); `find_similar`
  of an empty list tokenizes the body. A record with no tokens is skipped
  before scoring, a score of zero is dropped whatever the medium
  threshold, and a threshold is reached at equality (NaN reaches none).
- **The store.** `DigestStore` names the five methods `_similar_in` calls:
  `digest_candidates`, `light_records`, `digest_memo` (given the
  computation as a closure over the store), `load_all` and
  `load_tombstones`. The scoring dict keeps an id's first place and its
  last tokens, so `light_records` is handed the ids in that order; a
  record the light reader returns whose id was not scored raises
  `KeyError` (`DedupError::MissingKey`), as `scoring[record.id]` does. A
  memo answer of `None` falls back to the full scan. Wiring the trait to
  `store::digest` is left for the unit that ports `store_digest`'s
  `digest_candidates`, `light_records` and `digest_memo`.
- **`snippet_for`.** `search_dedup::snippet_for(body)` is
  `models_text::snippet_for(body, 200)`; the helper and
  `_truncate_at_word` live in `models_text` (see "The text helpers of
  `models.py`").

No regular expression is used by this module; the tokenizer's are the
`lexicon` module's.

### Fixtures and tests

`tests/contract/gen_search_dedup.py` writes `search_dedup.jsonl` (120
cases, ASCII text only, class i) and `search_dedup_unicode.jsonl` (18
cases, text past ASCII and lone surrogates, gated on Unicode: the
tokenizer and `str.strip` read it). Each case starts from an empty cache;
the scripted store logs every call. `golden_search_dedup` compares each
case whole; `search_dedup_kills` (12) pins inputs a plausible wrong port
answers otherwise (symmetric expansion, a kept stopword part, the
containment gate at 7, sorting the unrounded score, wall-clock order of
aware values, a tie of naive and aware, the cache's touch and negative
bound, the snippet's back-off at 159, a dict's first place and last
value); `search_dedup_robustness` (6) feeds a body of 100,000 words, 6,000
records past the cache bound, compounds of 50,000 parts and 100,000
dashes, 3,000 tied records, the `i64` and float extremes and a million
ideographic spaces. The reference takes 1.76 s, 1.22 s, 0.49 s and 0.10 s
on the first four (Apple M-series); the whole robustness file runs in
2.7 s in a debug build.

## Write-time supersession (`supersession.py`)

`supersession` reproduces `supersession.py` (816 lines), whose detector
decides at write time whether a claim-sized body replaces or conflicts
with a stored one. It needs nothing from the machine but the tokenizer,
the regular expression engine and a process-wide cache; the detector
reads stored bodies through the store. The module is cut in two units,
leaves first: supersession-1a (built) holds the tables, the patterns,
the two models and the per-body features (reference 145-518, in
`src/supersession/mod.rs` and `src/supersession/features.rs`);
supersession-1b (built) holds the detector (520-797) in
`src/supersession/detect.rs`. `_strip_provenance`, `_PROVENANCE_RE` and
`claim_sized` were ported earlier in `store::digest` and are re-exported
here.

### Map, by function

| function | reference lines | needs from the machine | status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `_PROVENANCE_RE`, `_strip_provenance` | 133-143 | nothing | built in `store::digest` (`strip_provenance`, hand-written), re-exported |
| `_NUMERIC_TOKEN_RE`, `_ASCII_DIGIT_RE`, `_numeric_token_set` | 145-165 | nothing | built (`numeric_token_set`, a sorted set) |
| `MAX_CLAIM_TOKENS`, `MAX_CLAIM_SENTENCES`, `MIN_JACCARD`, `MIN_CONFLICT_JACCARD`, `MIN_CONFLICT_KIN_JACCARD`, `CONTEXT_WIDTH`, `MIN_CONTEXT_SHARED`, `MAX_LINKS_PER_WRITE` | 167-183 | nothing | built (constants) |
| `CHANGE_CUES`, `_CUE_RE`, `_VALUE_PREPS`, `_WORD_RE`, `_CLAUSE_RE`, `_PROPER_NOUN_RE`, `_INTEGER_RE`, `_DOTTED_RE`, `_CUE_TOKENS` | 185-265 | nothing | built (`CHANGE_CUES` in insertion order, `cue_pattern`, `VALUE_PREPS`, the pattern texts, `cue_tokens`) |
| `_SENTENCE_RE`, `claim_sized` | 251, 325-333 | the tokenizer | built in `store::digest` (hand-written sentence count), re-exported |
| `SupersessionMatch` (`note`, `detector`), `SupersessionReport` | 268-317 | nothing | built |
| `change_cues` | 336-338 | nothing | built |
| `_WORD_TOKEN_ENTRIES`, `_WORD_TOKENS`, `clear_word_token_cache`, `_word_tokens`, `_first_content_token` | 341-370 | a process-wide cache and its lock | built (`WORD_TOKEN_ENTRIES`, `word_tokens`, `first_content_token`, `clear_word_token_cache`, `word_token_cache_len` for the tests) |
| `anchored_values` | 373-404 | the cache | built |
| `_proper_nouns` | 407-418 | the cache | built (`proper_nouns`) |
| `value_tokens`, `anchor_tokens` | 421-447 | the cache | built |
| `_numeric_shape`, `values_are_kin` | 450-475 | nothing | built (`numeric_shape`) |
| `_content_stream`, `_context` | 478-492 | the tokenizer | built (`content_stream`, `context`) |
| `_surface_forms`, `_surface_form` | 495-512 | the cache | built (`surface_forms`, a list in first-seen order; `surface_form`) |
| `_one_claim_replaced`, `_Old`, `_held`, `_stored`, `_claims_among`, `detect_supersession`, `_floor`, `detect_supersession_in`, `_SCORE_BATCH`, `_best_first`, `_detect`, `_rule` | 520-797 | the store's bodies and digest | built, unit supersession-1b (`one_claim_replaced`, `floor`, `SCORE_BATCH`, `detect_supersession`, `detect_supersession_in` over `SupersessionStore`; `_Old`, `_held`, `_stored`, `_claims_among`, `_best_first`, `_detect` and `_rule` private) |

### What each part reproduces, and the decisions

- **Patterns.** Every pattern the unit calls is the engine's `Regex`,
  built once (a `LazyLock` per pattern) from the reference's own text
  with no flags, and called with the reference's method:
  `_NUMERIC_TOKEN_RE.findall`, `_ASCII_DIGIT_RE.search`,
  `_CUE_RE.finditer`, `_WORD_RE.findall`, `_CLAUSE_RE.split` (with
  `maxsplit` 1 in `anchored_values`, none in `_proper_nouns`),
  `_PROPER_NOUN_RE.match`, `_INTEGER_RE.fullmatch` and
  `_DOTTED_RE.fullmatch`. All eight are already in the engine's
  inventory (`pyre_inventory.jsonl`) under the engine, so the inventory
  is unchanged. `_SENTENCE_RE` and `_PROVENANCE_RE` stay the hand-written
  matchers of `store::digest`. A pattern the engine does not build is
  `SupersessionError::Pattern`, a failed call `SupersessionError::Call`,
  so no public function panics on them.
- **`_CUE_RE`** is built at run time as the reference builds it: the
  cues sorted by length, longest first, with a stable sort (cues of one
  length keep `CHANGE_CUES`' order), each through `re.escape`
  (`pyre::atom::escape`), joined by `|` between `\b(` and `)\b`. The
  golden file's header holds the reference's pattern text and the test
  compares it. No cue is a prefix of another, so with `\b` on both sides
  another order of the alternation finds the same matches; only the
  pattern's text tells the order apart. `\b` reads Unicode word
  characters over `body.lower()` (`unicode::lower`, final sigma and
  growing lowerings included), so `émoved` holds no cue.
- **Strings.** `str.split()` splits on runs of `str.isspace`
  (`unicode::is_space`: `\x1c` to `\x1f`, NBSP, U+2028 and the rest);
  the three `str.strip` sets are the reference's; `str.isdigit` is
  `unicode::is_digit` (Unicode digits, so `build-٣` anchors); `len` counts
  code points; `math.ceil(0.5 * min(...))` is the float ceiling, exact at
  these sizes.
- **Stopwords.** `search._STOPWORDS` is `search_lexicon._STOPWORDS`,
  which the crate holds as `lexicon::is_stopword`; `search_dedup` uses the
  same set. `attribution::STOPWORDS` is a different constant and is not
  read.
- **Sets and order.** `anchored_values`, `_proper_nouns`, `value_tokens`,
  `anchor_tokens`, `_numeric_token_set` and `_context` are sets in the
  reference and `BTreeSet<String>` here (order free). `_surface_forms`
  is a dict in first-seen order and a `Vec<(token, form)>` here.
  `anchored_values` keeps the first content token per cue and goes on to
  the next cue.
- **The word-token cache.** `_WORD_TOKENS` is a process-wide map from
  the word as given (not lowered) to its content tokens, behind a lock
  held for the whole lookup, emptied whole when it holds 65,536 words
  before a new one is kept. It changes no answer. Its clearer is
  registered with `caches::register` under
  `supersession.clear_word_token_cache` on the cache's first use, the
  counterpart of the reference's `@_caches.register` at import.
- **`SupersessionMatch`.** Its text fields are code points. `note()`
  writes `repr` of the cue (`None` when absent) and of both values
  through `pyvalue::repr_str`; `detector()` is `numeric` when both values,
  lowered, have a numeric shape (`\d` is Unicode, so `٨٤٤٣` is
  `int:4`).
- **`MAX_CLAIM_TOKENS`, `MAX_CLAIM_SENTENCES`** are public here and
  private copies in `store::digest`, which is not edited by this unit;
  the golden header holds both values.

### Reference findings

- **`_PROPER_NOUN_RE` is quadratic** on a long capitalised word that
  fails at its end (`A` repeated then `+`, `Aa` repeated then `+`, `A`
  then `a` repeated then `+`): the repeats of both
  alternatives backtrack over the whole word. CPython 3.13.13 takes
  0.047 s at 5,000 characters, 0.19 s at 10,000 and 0.76 s at 20,000.
  On the engine the memo (pyre-9) holds `match` to at most 75 steps per
  character (70.3 measured) and steps at 2n within 2.2 times steps at n.
- **`anchored_values` is quadratic in a clause holding many cues**:
  each cue splits and reads the words of the whole rest of its clause.
  The reference takes 0.077 s at 10,000 characters of
  `moved to port 9443 then ` and 7.6 s at 100,000; the port keeps the
  reference's calls and so its family (`anchored_values`,
  `anchor_tokens` and `_surface_forms` together take 15.7 s at 100,000
  in a release build), held to ten times the clause within 200 times
  the time.

### Fixtures and tests

`tests/contract/gen_supersession_features.py` writes
`supersession_features.jsonl` (176 cases, ASCII bodies only, not gated)
and `supersession_features_unicode.jsonl` (26 cases, bodies past ASCII,
gated on Unicode). A body row holds every feature of the body; a `kin`
row a pair's kinship and shapes; a `note` row a match's note and
detector; the `sweep` row 20,000 bodies drawn from a word list by a
seeded generator, pinned by count and SHA-256. `golden_supersession_features`
checks every row whole and regenerates the sweep;
`supersession_features_kills` (13) pins the cue pattern's order, `\b`,
`str.isdigit` and `str.split` past ASCII, the strip sets, the skipped
first word, the slot rules, the numeric cap and lowering, the kinship
floor, the context's exclusions, the compound's length floor, the note
and detector, and the cache keyed on the word as given;
`supersession_features_robustness` (7)
pins the steps of `_PROPER_NOUN_RE` and `_CUE_RE` on hostile words and
bodies of 10,000 to 200,000 characters, linear time of the features,
the quadratic family of `anchored_values`, a megabyte body, lone
surrogates and 70,000 distinct words through the cache (emptied once).

### Unit supersession-1b, built (`supersession::detect`)

Reference lines 520-797 (at the fold of supersession-1a, as at
`86fc4b76`), in `src/supersession/detect.rs` (617 lines, 511 of them
code). The module's `mod.rs` gains the module line and its `pub use`.

- **The two entry points.** `detect_supersession(cache, new_body,
  existing, exclude_ids)` takes the records as `search_dedup::Candidate`
  (`Memory` implements it; only `id` and `body` are read).
  `detect_supersession_in(cache, store, new_body, exclude_ids)` reads a
  store through `SupersessionStore`, whose five methods carry the
  reference's names: `digest_shares` (answering `DigestShare`, the
  native shape `store::digest_query` already holds), `digest_tokens_of`
  (called with its default `removed=False`, so the trait has no such
  argument), `bodies_of`, `digest_memo` (handed the computation as a
  closure over the store, as `search_dedup::DigestStore` is) and
  `load_all`. The memo key `("supersession", new_body,
  frozenset(exclude_ids))` is `SupersessionMemoKey` (the body unstripped,
  the ids a set). A memo answer of None falls back to
  `detect_supersession` over `load_all()`. Ids reach the store in the
  order the reference's generators yield them (the unstamped records of
  a batch, then its stamped ones), repeats kept; a map leaves out an id
  it does not hold. `exclude_ids` is a slice: the reference iterates its
  argument twice when the digest is not there (`frozenset(exclude_ids)`,
  then the scan's `set(exclude_ids)`), which only a one-shot iterator
  would tell apart, and both callers pass a list.
- **The token cache.** Every `raw_content_tokens` the reference makes
  goes through the caller's `RawTokenCache`, `claim_sized`'s included
  (its answer comes from `store::digest::claim_sized`, which tokenizes
  without the cache; the port reads the stripped body through the cache
  beside it), so the cache's keys end in the reference's order: the new
  body, then each record twice (claim size, tokens), then the new body
  again for the rule. The golden rows record the keys.
- **`_detect` and `_claims_among`** are one loop here (the generator is
  consumed by the one caller in order). The scored records are sorted by
  `(-round(score, 4), id)` with a stable sort: ids compare by code point
  (`PyStr` order), and one id twice keeps its order, as Python's key
  sort does (the key tuples are equal, never compared further).
- **`_best_first`** is a pull-driven state machine (`next_scored`), so
  its reads interleave with the rule's exactly as the generator's do:
  the bounds are computed and sorted on the first pull; each pull
  computes the ceiling (`round(bound, 4)` of the next unscored share, or
  -1.0) and hands on the heap's top only when its rounded score is
  strictly above it; otherwise it reads the next batch of 64. A batch is
  `bounded[position:position + 64]`, which may reach past `total` (the
  first share whose bound is under the floor): those shares are scored
  and pushed too, as the reference does. `similarity_bound` takes `i64`
  counts: a claim that is a `PyValue::Int` within `i64` is read exactly,
  a bool as 0 or 1, and anything else (an int past `i64`, None, a float,
  a string) is declined (`DetectError::Claim`, class `NotPorted`). The
  reference's `DigestShare.claim` is always `int(row[2])`, a token count
  of at most `MAX_CLAIM_TOKENS`, so the decline is unreachable from the
  store; on a share a caller scripts, the reference raises `TypeError`
  for None and a string and answers for a float.
- **The heap.** `heapq` is ported as CPython's `_heapq` runs it:
  `heappush` appends and sifts down, `heappop` moves the last entry to
  the root and sifts up (the smaller child up to a leaf, then down),
  every comparison Python's `<` on `(-round(score, 4), id, score, _Old)`
  tuples, the first unequal item deciding. Past an equal key, id and
  score, `_Old` compares its id, then its token sets (`<` is the proper
  subset) and then its body readers, two distinct functions, which
  raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'function'
  and 'function'` (`DetectError::Unorderable`). That is reachable only
  through one id repeated among the shares, which one `SELECT` keyed by
  record never yields; the port reproduces it rather than calling it
  unreachable, and the golden rows pin the raise (one id twice in a
  batch), the subset order (a stamped and an unstamped share of one
  id, both at the containment ceiling of 0.575: the subset pops first
  whichever was pushed first), the raw score deciding two scores that
  round alike (the lower pops first), two token sets of one size,
  neither a subset of the other, kept in the order pushed, and
  `_siftup` moving up the right child of such an unordered pair.
- **`_Old.body`** is `Held` (a body in hand: the scan's records and the
  stamped shares, stripped) or `Stored` (read through `bodies_of([id])`
  when the rule first asks; None skips the record). A stored body is
  not stripped: an unstamped share whose stored body carries a stamp is
  read with the stamp, as the reference reads it (a golden row's
  summary of a short claim holds the stamp).
- **`_rule`** reads records until a list holds `MAX_LINKS_PER_WRITE`
  and then stops pulling, so records past that point are never scored
  and their tokens and bodies never read. Set differences and
  intersections are on token strings; `sorted` of strings and of
  `(str, str)` pairs is code point order (`String` order, UTF-8 byte
  order being code point order). The replaced value is compared through
  `unicode::lower` (`str.lower`, final sigma included). The summary is
  `models_text::snippet_for(old_body, 100)`; the similarity
  `search::num::round4`.
- **`_one_claim_replaced`** is ported (`one_claim_replaced`) though the
  rule inlines it, and is pinned on its own.

No pattern is compiled in this unit; the features' patterns are
supersession-1a's.

Left for later units: wiring `SupersessionStore` to the store's digest
(`digest_tokens_of`, `bodies_of` and `digest_memo` are not yet in
`store::digest*`; the unit that wires `search_dedup::DigestStore` can
implement both traits), the write path that stores the links (the
`h_write` units) and durability's `_anchored_new_reference`.

#### Fixtures and tests

`tests/contract/gen_supersession_detect.py` writes
`supersession_detect.jsonl` (94 cases, ASCII bodies only, not gated) and
`supersession_detect_unicode.jsonl` (12 cases, bodies past ASCII, gated
on Unicode: the tokenizer, `str.lower` and the features' patterns read
the Unicode data). A `scan` row is `detect_supersession` over its
records; an `in` row is `detect_supersession_in` over a scripted store
that answers shares, tokens and bodies from the row and logs every call
with its arguments; both record the report (every match field, the
similarity's bits) and the token cache's keys after. The rows cover
every outcome (supersedes by kin and by context; conflict by kin, by
context and by overlap with the fallback pair), a cue with no pair, the
replaced value kept and not kept (lowered), the floors at equality with
and without a cue, claim size on either side, exclude_ids, both caps,
ties broken by id (and a tie of two raw scores, 0.112150 and 0.112069,
that round alike), stamped bodies on either side, tokens or a body
gone, the digest absent and a memo of None (each with and without
exclude_ids, which the fallback scan honours), a memo hit, a share under
the floor read in a batch over it, the ceiling at a bound equal to the
score and under its rounding, 65 and 129 shares of tied bounds, the cap
reached before the second batch, and a repeated id in each order the
heap reads it. The
`sweep` row draws 5,000 stores of 20 records and a new body from a word
list by a seeded generator and pins, per store, the scan's report, the
digest path's report and its call log, by count and SHA-256 (the two
reports agree on every store). Generating the ASCII file takes about
27 s under CPython 3.13.13.

`golden_supersession_detect` checks every row whole and regenerates the
sweep (23 s in a debug build). `supersession_detect_kills` (17) pins
the ceiling rounded and strict (an unrounded ceiling or `>=` hands a
record on before the next batch is read), the read order of a rounded
tie by id in both paths, the stable bound sort (which shares make the
first batch), the walk stopped by a full list (one batch's tokens and
five bodies read), a cue match kept only with the replaced value
(lowered), a cue never conflicting, the sorted fallback pair, the
100-character summary, the floors at equality, a share under the floor
scored in its batch, a repeated id raising or ordered by token sets,
by raw score, in the order pushed and by `_siftup`'s right child, an
unstamped share's stored body read with its stamp, and the fallback
scan's exclude_ids; each of sixteen such mutants of the port fails it.
`supersession_detect_robustness` (4) feeds 20,000 shares with the list
full after the first batch (one batch's tokens read; 2,000 against
20,000 within ten times), bodies of 100,000 words (10,000 against
100,000), 1,000 records tied in score (100 against 1,000, both paths)
and integer extremes and other types in a share's claim and shared
count. The reference takes 0.49 s on the bodies of 100,000 words,
0.012 s on the 20,000 shares and 0.021 s on the 1,000 tied records
(Apple M-series); the robustness file runs in 23 s in a debug build,
most of it the timing rounds.

## The store, read only

`store::StoreFile::open` reads a store file as the reference's read-only
commands do (`store_schema.connect_read_only`):

- a rollback-journal file with no `-wal` is read in place with `mode=ro`;
- a file whose `-wal` and `-shm` are both there (a daemon has it open, or
  one died with it open) is read in place with `mode=ro` through the
  `-shm`: the committed frames of the `-wal` are read and nothing is
  checkpointed;
- a WAL-mode file without both, or a `-wal` without its `-shm`, is copied
  (with its `-wal`) into an owner-only directory
  `bettermemory-native-read-<pid>-...` under the temp dir, taken again when
  either file changed during the copy (three tries), and read
  `immutable=1` (or `mode=ro` with a `-wal`).

Then the file is admitted (`store::admission`, `store_admission.admit_store`
in full) before any table is read: under a 2 s deadline (a progress handler
every 100 virtual-machine steps) and with no value over 16 KiB, its
`sqlite_master` is held to the reference's own schema (built in memory from
`store/reference_schema.json`, the reference's schema texts, pinned to the
golden `store_admission.json`): a view, a trigger the reference never
writes, a virtual table, an index on an expression or with a WHERE, a
unique index on a table it writes, one of its own objects with another
text, a generated column, a default that is not a literal, a check or a
foreign key, and a table of its own not shaped as it shapes it are refused
with the reference's `StoreRefusedError` text (`LaterStoreError`, with its
key and needed revision, when meta names a later revision). Meta is then
read under the same deadline. The reference's regular expressions are
written out by hand over Python's own `\w`, `\s`, `\d` and `re.I`
equivalences. SQLite's limits after admission are its defaults, as the
reference leaves them: an admitted file's tables compute nothing, so a read
costs what the rows hold. No deadline is put on reads after admission (the
reference has none, and one would refuse a large store the reference
reads); the progress handler stays installed and idle.

What a read can change on disk: nothing, byte for byte, in the four
situations above (`store_read_only` hashes every file of the store and
keys directories before and after a full read). One recorded exception,
shared with the reference's `mode=ro` read of the same file: a `-wal` and a
stale `-shm` left by a writer that died. Both are there, so the file is
read in place, and SQLite rebuilds the wal-index in the `-shm`; the store
file and the `-wal` are unchanged (`stale_shm_is_rewritten_and_nothing_else`).

The private copy. Its directory is made 0700 under another prefix
(`bettermemory-native-new-*`), its `.lock` created 0600 and locked
(`File::lock`) there, and only then renamed to `bettermemory-native-read-*`,
so a sweeper never sees a live reader's directory unlocked
(`sweepers_never_remove_a_live_readers_directory`: 400 opens against
concurrent sweeps). A store with no `-wal` (the usual closed WAL store) is
read through a copy SQLite opens immutable (no lock, no `-shm`). On macOS
and FreeBSD the copy's name is removed before a byte of the store is
written to it and SQLite reads it as `/dev/fd/N`, so no signal at any
moment leaves the store's bytes under a name
(`a_copy_without_wal_never_has_a_name`). Not on Linux: `/dev/fd/N` there is
a symlink to `/proc/self/fd/N`, whose link text is the removed name plus
" (deleted)", and SQLite's unix VFS resolves the link before opening and
fails ("unable to open database file"; the first CI run). Linux copies the
store under a name, as the `-wal` case below and the reference do, and
removes the name after the admitted connection's first read
(`a_store_without_wal_is_read_through_a_copy`). With a `-wal` (a writer died
before checkpointing), SQLite needs both files by name (it finds the
`-wal` beside the path it opens and builds a `-shm` there), so the copy
and its `-wal` carry names from the start of the copy until the admitted
connection's first read, then both are removed and reads go on from the
open descriptors (`read_only_wal_store_with_orphan_wal`). That window is
the copy's duration plus admission (a 960 MB file copies in 0.51 s here
from the page cache, so a 200 MB store with its `-wal` is named for about
0.1 s, plus the few milliseconds admission takes). What remains after
SIGTERM, SIGINT or SIGKILL (the reader installs no handler; the drop does
not run on any of them): the directory and its empty 0600 `.lock`, and, if
the signal lands in that window, the named 0600 copy (and its `-wal` in the
`-wal` case). On macOS and FreeBSD that window exists only with a `-wal`;
on Linux it exists for every copy. Only a later native open sweeps them: it removes this user's
`bettermemory-native-read-*` directories whose lock can be taken (the
kernel releases a dead reader's lock) or that have no lock and are over an
hour old, and `bettermemory-native-new-*` directories over an hour old. The
sweep's uid is read from a directory it just made with `mkdir`, never a
name another user could take first. The reference's own `bettermemory-read-*`
directories are never touched. On Windows a directory that holds an open
file cannot be renamed (the first CI run's "Access is denied"), so the
directory is made under its swept name and locked in place, and a sweeper
counts it dead only when its lock can be taken and its lock file is over a
minute old;
names cannot be removed while open, so the named copy (and `-wal`) stays
for the reader's whole life, and a killed reader leaves the directory with
the copy until the next open sweeps it. An I/O failure on this path names
its step ("create the private directory's lock file: ...", "rename the
locked private directory: ...", "copy the store: ..."), never a path. The reference removes its copy on close, on
garbage collection and at interpreter exit (`weakref.finalize`), so Ctrl-C
cleans it; SIGTERM (no handler in the CLI) and SIGKILL leave it, and
nothing sweeps it.

Consistency. `verify_chain` runs all its statements in one read
transaction, so the rows come from one snapshot, as the reference's single
`SELECT` gives them; `read_transaction` groups more (bm-verify reads meta,
the counts and the chain in one). The head and origin files are outside
SQLite and are read as the reference reads them, so while a writer appends,
the head can be behind the snapshot (`stale`) or ahead of it
(`tail_deleted`) in both builds; no MAC, link or seq problem appears
(`verify_while_a_writer_appends`: 40 native verifies during 7,738 writes
gave 10 `ok` and 30 `stale`; the reference, 40 verifies during about 180
writes of its own GIL-bound writer, gave 35 `ok`, 2 `stale` and 3
`tail_deleted`). One order differs: the native verify reads the origin file
before the rows, the reference after; only a rekey moves that file.

The cost of that snapshot to a writer, and the batches. On a
rollback-journal store read in place, a read transaction holds SQLite's
SHARED lock, and a writer must wait for it. When this arises: every
reference writing open switches the store to WAL (`store._connect`), so
with the reference's own writers a rollback-journal store exists only
until the first writer opens it: a restored or backed-up file (`backup`
writes DELETE mode), or a store a foreign writer keeps in that mode. The
real case is that first open: it switches the file to WAL and waits for
the reader's lock to do it. Measured (`rotation_race`'s
`a_reference_writers_first_open_under_a_native_verify`, release, the intact
base in DELETE mode with 300,000 rows appended, the reference's
`Store.open` started 0.1 to 0.4 s into a native verify, 10 runs each): under
a one-snapshot verify the open took median 723 ms, worst 853 ms; under the
batched verify median 11.2 ms, worst 12.4 ms (the open's own work
included). `writer_stall` measures the other case with a native writer
held in DELETE mode, standing in for a foreign writer: one small commit
every 5 ms while verifies ran back to back for 20 s, three runs; N1b's
one-snapshot verify let it wait up to 966 ms, the batched verify median
0.32 to 0.34 ms, p99 1.9 to 2.0 ms, worst 4.6, 6.8 and 9.7 ms, longest
single read-lock hold 2.0 to 5.0 ms.

How the batches work. `verify_chain` on such a file (no private copy, not
WAL, no transaction open: `reads_in_batches`) reads the log in batches of
1,024 rows by seq, each its own statement, the chain state carried across
them (`Batched`). The first row, the highest seq (`cap`) and the rekey rows
through `cap` are read in one short transaction. The rows are then read
through `cap` and on to the log's end as it stands when a batch comes back
short, at most `EXTRA_BATCHES` (8) batches past `cap`, so a writer
appending as fast as batches are read cannot keep a pass going
(`a_fast_writer_cannot_keep_a_pass_going`: one row a batch, two rows
appended after every batch, the pass stops after the rows there were and
8 more). A `rekey` row past `cap` is a segment the pass has no key for: it
stops with `StoreError::Changed`. `StoreFile::verify_loading` is what a
command calls (`bm-verify` does): it loads meta's fingerprint and the key
ring through the caller's loader, verifies, and on `Changed` loads them
again (waiting 50 ms at a time while the ring's current key is not yet
the one meta names: a rotation renames its new key in after its commit),
and also verifies again when the head reads `tail_deleted` while the log
now holds the head's row with the head's MAC (a writer appended between
the last batch and the head read). A report that names a row, segment or
origin problem is returned at once: another pass cannot heal it
(`a_tampered_store_under_a_writer_ends_tampered`). At most 20 tries, then
`StoreError::KeptChanging`: "the store kept changing while it was checked;
nothing was found wrong; run the check again", never `tampered`;
`bm-verify` prints it as chain status `kept_changing` and exits 3 (0 ok, 1
a log that does not verify, 2 a failure). The time bound: one pass over
300,000 rows measured 0.83 to 0.90 s, so 20 tries with their 50 ms waits
come to about 18 s on that size in the worst case, with the restore lock
held throughout (a restore is held off that long). A quiet store takes one
pass.
WAL files, copies and a caller's transaction keep one snapshot and run
once, as the reference.

What the batches guarantee, and what not. Every row read is the row the
log held when its batch was read. Under writers that only append (every
writer this package runs), the rows read are a prefix of the log as of the
end of the pass, so a MAC, link or seq problem is named only where one
snapshot at the end of the pass would name it, and on a quiescent store
the report is the one-snapshot report (`golden_store_files` verifies every
case both ways at 1, 2, 3, 7 and 1,024 rows a batch and compares). Not
guaranteed: the rows are not one snapshot. A row changed or deleted in
place, by a writer that is not this package's, after its batch was read is
not seen; one changed before is reported as it is read. The end of a pass
does not read `cap` or the rows behind it again: that would be a second
pass, and only the head-row check above is cheap enough to make.

A rotation during a batched verify (`rotation_race`, release, 300,000
rows, the reference's `rotate_key(apply=True)` started 0 to 1 s into the
verify, 30 runs each): retried with the same ring, as N1b did, 23 of 30
were `tampered` (`foreign_segment`, `final_key_mismatch`); through
`verify_loading`, 30 of 30 `ok`.

A finding about the reference, not changed here: its `log verify` reads
the head file after the rows, so under a concurrent rotation or a writer
on a DELETE-mode store it reports `tampered` with head `tail_deleted` (an
independent review measured 6 of 20 under rotation and 20 of 20 under a
5 ms writer).

The restore lock (`store::restore_lock`, `restore_lock.reading`). An open
takes it before SQLite opens the file and holds it until the `StoreFile`
drops: on POSIX the parent of the store path as given (not resolved)
locked shared with `flock` (`File::try_lock_shared`), tried every 50 ms
for 2 s; held exclusively past that (a restore), the open is refused with
`StoreError::RestoreRunning` (`RestoreRunningError`, "<store> is not
opened: a restore is running; try again when it has finished", exit 75
from the reference's read-only commands). A restore's marker with no lock
held refuses no read. Nothing is created. A directory `flock` cannot lock
falls to the record file `<store>.restore-lock` (checked, never created,
never held). The path as given decides the lock, as in the reference: a
relative path, one through `..` and a linked directory reach the store's
directory, but a link to the store file from another directory locks that
other directory, so a restore of the real store does not see the read
(pinned as the reference does it). Windows: the record file locked and
let go, then the store file held open without delete sharing and the
record checked again behind it; compiled only under `cfg(windows)` and
untested. Known open item: std's `try_lock` on Windows locks the whole
record file (a mandatory `LockFileEx` lock), where the reference locks one
byte at 1 MiB so the marker stays readable; while a native read checks,
a reference restore's marker read or write can fail with a lock
violation. A byte-range lock is out of reach without `unsafe` or a crate
outside `Cargo.lock` (no `windows-sys` there); the hold is kept as short
as the reference's (taken, then let go at once). Not ported: the
reference's pass for the thread that holds the lock itself (no native
restore exists), its one-time log line and process-wide memory of
record-mode directories. Pinned by `store_restore_lock.json`: 4 plain
cases, 3 record-mode cases, 4 path cases, a restore meeting a read, the
wait, poll and exit status. The fixture is POSIX only: on Windows its generator is
not run (`POSIX_ONLY` in `tests/contract/generate.py`, named in the
manifest), `golden_restore_lock.rs` is not compiled, and
`restore_lock_not_posix.rs` records the gap as a class (os) case. The
Windows lock is exercised there only by the tests that open a store.

A finding about the reference, shared by both builds (to be filed): a
read through a symbolic link to the store file from another directory
locks the link's directory, not the store's, so a restore of the real
store does not see that read.

The native verify reads the origin file before the rows, the reference
after (only a rekey moves that file). The native key ring reader reads a
key file over 1 MiB as unreadable.

"Not found" instead of waiting: `StoreFile::open` canonicalizes the path
and checks `is_file` before it takes the restore lock, so a read that lands
in the gap of a restore's swap fails with io NotFound instead of waiting or
being refused (seen once in 23,095 native reads). Left as is: the
reference has the same order (`store.py`: `is_file` before `reading`).

The record file is opened read-write without creating it, as the
reference opens it `O_RDWR`: where it is readable but not writable both
builds read that as nothing to hold. (Opened read-only, as the first
version of this port did, the native build would still check the lock
there: stricter than the reference.)

The fold check is ported (N1e, below); validated records are N1d's.

Readers. `meta`, every table's rows (`each_row`), `store_rows`' memory,
tombstone and episode readers (`MemoryRow`, `EpisodeRow`), the log walked
in seq order, `verify_chain`, `history_replaced` (the `log verify --json`
field), and `query_candidates` with its scope, client, model and cap
filters, and `ranked_rows`. What the reader accepts that the reference's
models would reject (pydantic validation is not ported): an `id` that is
not a ULID; an empty scope list or scopes the scope rules refuse; more
than 64 entries in `verified_paths`, `verified_commits`,
`verified_versions`, `verified_absent_paths` or `claims`, or entries that
are not strings (the reference also turns each into `str`); a
`confidence` or `source` outside its enum; a `category` outside its enum;
`corroborations` below 0; list columns holding JSON that is not a list (an
error here, a ValidationError there); and it does not read `links`,
`origin`, `actor`, the path targets or `last_corroborated`'s model.

`store::keys::load_key_ring` reads the fixed names only, into buffers sized
from the file's length and wiped on drop. Two differences, neither able to
change a report: a file over 1 MiB is read as unreadable, and retired keys
are ordered by the part of the name between the id and `.key` rather than
by whole file name (`ab` and `ab.c` order differently); the ring's order is
only read to find the one key a row verifies under, and two distinct keys
never verify one MAC (`retired_key_order_cannot_change_a_report`).

The fixtures. `store_bases.json` holds five base stores (intact; rekeyed;
restored, with a `store_restored` row; accepted, with a `history_accepted`
row; both rows appended directly through `log.append_history_replaced` with
neutral `/fixture/...` paths, since a real restore or accept-history signs
the host's resolved paths into the row, and the rewind, the moved-aside file
and the head and origin rewrites are not reproduced;
the FTS corpus) as the SQL that rebuilds each and its keys directory's
files, written once through the reference by `python -m
tests.contract.gen_store_files --bases`, which also proves each rebuilt
store answers as its original. `store_files.jsonl` holds 40 cases (a base
and a recipe: SQL, a key file removed or written, a truncation) with the
reference's answers: in full for the five bases, by sha256 digest of the
rows, meta, `sqlite_master` and records for the tamper and version
variants, the exact refusal for the 18 admission cases, and what the
reference raises for the four schema-text cases; the counts are literals in
the test, so a line removed fails it. The Rust tests
rebuild each case and compare with no Python; each read runs under a 10 s
bound on its own thread. `tests/test_contract_golden.py` regenerates the
answers from the committed bases through the reference, so a change in how
the reference reads a store shows there. Not pinned by the bases: how the
reference writes a store (the bases are written once).

The SQLite version: the reference runs 3.50.4; the crate bundles 3.54.1.
`sqlite_spike` rebuilds `search.jsonl`'s FTS5 table: all 27 queries give
the same rows, order and `bm25()` bits. Every case of `store_files.jsonl`
(rebuilt by 3.54.1 here, by 3.50.4 for the reference) reads the same. And
one file is kept as bytes: `store_real.sqlite` (95,744 bytes, page size 512,
VACUUMed, WAL mode, the intact records and the FTS corpus), written by the
reference's SQLite 3.50.4 (`--real`; the header's writer version is checked)
and read as it is by `the_reference_written_file_reads_the_same`: all 1,793
answers equal, the 32 FTS prefilter queries' rows and `bm25()` bits and the
FTS shadow tables' schema rows included. Its bytes are not reproducible, so
`generate` compares a logical dump of it, clock-minted values masked, with a
fresh build.

Schema text that is not text. A `sqlite_master` value that is not UTF-8 is
never decoded lossily (a replaced name would match no table, and the
per-table checks would see nothing, a generated column included): the
reader refuses the file, carrying the `OperationalError` the reference's
fetch raises out of `connect_read_only` (`Could not decode to UTF-8 column
'name' with text ...`). A type, name or tbl_name that is not TEXT, or a sql
that is neither TEXT nor NULL, is refused with its own wording. An accident
of the reference the port does not copy: a BLOB sql makes `_blanked`
(`src/bettermemory/store_admission.py:113-115`) raise `TypeError: cannot
use a string pattern on a bytes-like object`; `store_files.jsonl`'s header
lists it under `deliberate_differences`. Four cases pin these: a name not
UTF-8, one hiding a generated column, a comment not UTF-8, a BLOB sql.

An accident of the reference the port copies: `query_candidates` orders
by `bm25()` alone (`ORDER BY score ASC LIMIT ?`), so equal scores come in
whatever order the plan gives; `ranked_rows` breaks ties by rowid.

`examples/bm-verify.rs`: `bm-verify <store file> <keys dir>` prints one JSON
object: the admission's refusal (its reason names schema objects only) or
the version contract's outcome, each table's row count, the key ring's
shape, the chain report and each phase's milliseconds, from one snapshot.
No record content, payload text or key byte is printed.

`bm-verify --fold <store file> <keys dir>` runs `log verify` instead of
the chain alone and prints its merged report under `log_verify` in the
reference's full shape less `path` (`status`, `store_id`,
`key_fingerprint`, `rows`, `segments`, `head`, `origin`, `problems` sorted
by seq, `fold`, `unaccounted_ids`) and its milliseconds under
`ms.log_verify`; its exit status is then the merged report's, or 3 with
status `kept_changing` when key rotations kept the log moving (below). A chain
problem without a `seq` raises KeyError in the merge, as in the reference.
The fold's labels are record ids and table keys, and a `payload_invalid`
detail is the reference's exception text, which can quote a payload value.

Timing the chain verification: 50,001 log rows of about 650 signed bytes,
written by the reference, three runs each, Apple M-series: the reference's
`verify_chain` 205.8, 205.3 and 203.1 ms (about 244,000 rows a second);
native release (sha2 0.11.1, which uses the aarch64 SHA instructions) 142.8,
148.6 and 141.6 ms (about 347,000 rows a second), 1.4 times the reference.
The prediction of at least ten times is missed: both are bound by
HMAC-SHA256 on the CPU's SHA instructions (the reference's `hmac` is
OpenSSL's), and walking the rows costs about 29 ms of the native time.

## The document frequency memo (`store_index.py`, unit store_index-1)

`store::docfreq` reproduces the memo `Store.ranking_statistics` and
`Store.document_frequencies(..., memoised=True)` price a search's BM25
legs with. `store_index.py` as it is now holds it at these lines:

| function | lines | needs from the machine | status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `_ADMISSION_INPUTS` | 68-74 | SQLite (the store's side) | the statement, run by the trait's implementation |
| `_DocFreqInputs` | 77-118 | nothing | built: `DocFreqInputs`, its terms held by `Entry` |
| `DOC_FREQ_STORES`, `DOC_FREQ_TERMS` | 149-150 | nothing | built |
| `_row_mask` | 153-159 | nothing | built: `row_mask` |
| `_DOC_FREQS`, its lock, `_clear_doc_freqs` | 162-169 | a process-wide lock | built: `memo()`, `DocFreqMemo::clear` |
| `_memoised_document_frequencies` | 388-433 | the store's side | built: `DocFreqMemo::document_frequencies` |
| `_current_inputs` | 436-456 | the store's side | built |
| `_HEAD_KINDS`, `_ADVANCE_ROWS` | 459-464 | nothing | built: `HEAD_KINDS`, `ADVANCE_ROWS` in `docfreq_store::advance` (store_index-advance) |
| `_PATCH_ROWS`, `_PATCH_WINDOW` | 467-471 | nothing | built |
| `_advanced_inputs` | 474-602 | the log and the digest | built: `StoreDocFreq`'s `advanced_inputs` (`docfreq_store::advance`, store_index-advance); the trait's default stays None |
| `_patched_masks` | 605-661 | the FTS table | built: `patched_masks` |
| `_admitted_mask` | 664-677 | nothing | built: `admitted_mask` |
| `admitted_rows` | 680-701 | the store's side, SQLite | built: `docfreq_store::admitted_rows` (poolmemo) |
| `_admitter` | 704-733 | the store's side | built: `docfreq_store::Admitter` (`new`, `decide`), its head `DocFreqMemo::admitted_inputs` (poolmemo) |
| `ranked_admitted_rows` | 736-760 | the FTS table | built: `docfreq_store::ranked_admitted_rows` over `index_reads::RankedQuery` (poolmemo) |
| `admitted_share` | 763-777 | the store's side | built: `docfreq_store::admitted_share` (poolmemo) |
| `_admitted_rows_read` | 780-811 | SQLite | built: in `docfreq_store::admitted` (poolmemo) |
| `_keep_doc_freqs` | 814-839 | the lock | built: `DocFreqMemo::keep` |
| `Store._read_doc_freq_inputs` | store.py 1766-1830 | the digest or the memory rows | built: the grouping `DocFreqInputs::from_rows`, the reads `StoreDocFreq::admission_rows` (store-2) |
| `_memory_head` | 369-385 | SQLite | built: `StoreDocFreq::memory_head` (store-2) |
| `digest_mark(build=False)`, `digest_admission_rows` | store_digest.py 476-509, 780-802 | SQLite, a write transaction | built: `StoreDocFreq::digest_mark`, `digest_admission_rows`, their warnings as data (store-2) |
| `Store.document_frequencies` | store.py 1681-1742 | a transaction's state | built: `docfreq_store::document_frequencies` (store-2) |
| `Store._term_masks` | store.py 1832-1851 | the FTS table | built: `StoreDocFreq::term_masks` over `reads::term_masks` (store-2) |
| `Store.ranking_statistics` | store.py 1744-1764 | a transaction's state | built: `DocFreqMemo::ranking_statistics` and `docfreq_store::ranking_statistics`, the uncached read inside a transaction (store-2) |

The store's side is the trait `DocFreqSource`: `memory_head`,
`store_key` (the store's path text and id), `in_transaction`,
`admission_rows` (the rows and whether the digest answered),
`read_inputs` (by default the grouping of those rows), `advanced_inputs`
(by default None, so a source that does not override it reads the inputs
again at every changed head; the store's source overrides it, unit
store_index-advance below), `term_masks` and `fts_rowids` (the patch's
statement).
The store's implementation is `store::docfreq_store::StoreDocFreq`
(unit store-2, below). The test double
`tests/common/docfreq_source.rs` runs the reference's statements over an
in-memory SQLite database and writes out `_advanced_inputs` for the
test; its SQL carries no parity weight.

Decisions:

- A mask is a bit set of `u64` words (`Mask`), of any width, as the
  reference's Python `int`; counts are popcounts of the intersection.
- The memo is a value (`DocFreqMemo`) with one process-wide instance
  (`memo()`), so the tests run their own. One mutex guards the stores
  and each entry's terms, taken as the reference takes its lock; the
  reads of the store's side and the admit predicate run outside it. An
  entry is compared by identity (`Arc::ptr_eq`), as the reference's `is`.
- A row's scopes text is parsed with `json::loads` and kept as
  `PyValue` items: a list of any items is a group's scopes, a value that
  is not a list skips the row, and a text that is not JSON raises
  (`DocFreqError::Py`), as `_load_json` raises there: the docstring's
  "whose scopes parse" holds only for texts that parse to something
  other than a list.
- `_row_mask` raises IndexError for a position at or past its width
  rounded up to whole bytes; `row_mask` answers `DocFreqError::IndexError`
  there (the bound taken in `u128`, so a width near `usize::MAX` does not
  overflow, where the reference would fail to allocate) and sets bits below that bound past the width, as the bytearray.
  A row number read twice keeps the later position and leaves the count
  of positions as it was (`index[rid] = position`).
- The BM25 lengths are summed in `i128` where the reference's are
  unbounded ints; the average is `int_div`, Python's correctly rounded
  `int / int`, rounded once at any size (a sum past 2^53 included).
- A term named twice in a direct call is read twice, the second answer
  kept, as the reference's `found` dict; `ranking_statistics` makes the
  terms sorted and unique first.

Fixtures: `tests/contract/gen_store_docfreq.py` drives the reference's
own memo over a stand-in store (`_Fake`, the reference's
`_memory_head`, `_advanced_inputs`, `_read_doc_freq_inputs` and
`_term_masks` over the same five tables), through write sequences, a
term past the patch window, more than eight changed rows, more than 256
rows since a head, no digest, a log of another history, scopes texts
that are not lists or not JSON, a transaction, a write between the two
head reads, nine stores and 4097 terms. Each query records the answer,
the calls made to the store's side with every admit call, the stores
kept and the queried store's terms. No row depends on the platform or
the Python release, so the file is not gated. Tests:
`golden_store_docfreq`, `store_docfreq_kills` and
`store_docfreq_robustness` (scopes nested 100,000 deep, row numbers at
the ends of `i64`, lengths whose sum passes `i64`, eight threads on one
memo, a query over ten times the rows within `TENFOLD`).

No regular expression is used.

### The store's side (unit store-2, first part)

`store::docfreq_store` implements `DocFreqSource` over a real store
connection (`StoreDocFreq`) and puts the two entry points over it.
Reference lines as they are now: `store_index._memory_head` 369-385,
`_ADMISSION_INPUTS` 68-74, the patch's statement 635-637;
`store_digest.digest_mark` 476-509 (with `build=False`) and
`digest_admission_rows` 780-802; `Store.document_frequencies` 1681-1742,
`Store.ranking_statistics` 1744-1764, `Store._read_doc_freq_inputs`
1766-1830 and `Store._term_masks` 1832-1851 of `store.py`.

- Constructors: `StoreDocFreq::of_store` over a `WritableStore` outside
  any transaction, `of_transaction` over a `Transaction` (with the
  store's path and id, which the transaction does not expose), and
  `over` for any connection to a store at a path (a read-only
  connection among them). `in_transaction` is `self._tx_depth or
  self._conn.in_transaction`: the transaction form answers true always,
  also after its connection rolled back (the reference's depth stays 1
  until the block ends); the others answer `!is_autocommit()`.
- `store_key` is `(str(self._path), self._store_id)`: the path as
  `versions::path_text` spells it (PurePath's spelling: `.` and doubled
  separators dropped, `..` kept, nothing resolved). Two spellings of one
  file are two memo keys, as in the reference (`Store._bind` keeps the
  path `store_path` made).
- `memory_head` runs `_memory_head`'s statement (a copy of the one in
  `store/pool.rs`, which is left as it is) with its typing: a `seq` that
  is not an integer is TypeError.
- `admission_rows`: `digest_admission_rows` where it answers, with
  lengths; else `_ADMISSION_INPUTS` with length 0 and no lengths. The
  grouping stays `DocFreqInputs::from_rows`.
- `digest_mark` (`build=False`) is composed from `digest_query::mark`,
  `digest::{state, built, ingest}` and `open::require_current_writer`:
  the mark when the digest is current; None with nothing done when it
  has to be built; else `Store._transaction`'s work on the store's
  connection, which appends no log row, so the head does not move. Outside
  a transaction: one `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction (the writer check,
  `_built` again, `_ingest`, `_mark`, `COMMIT`; rolled back on failure),
  a connection left inside a transaction no call owns rolled back first
  (`_clear_residue`: `reads::note_residue`'s line once per process, then
  `ROLLBACK`). Inside one (`of_transaction`) it joins as `_joined` does:
  `_require_open` (a transaction SQLite rolled back is OperationalError,
  the store's own wording), the savepoint `nested_1` (the reference's
  `nested_<depth>`; the name is not observable), `_built`, `_ingest`,
  `_mark`, `RELEASE`; on failure `ROLLBACK TO` and `RELEASE`, and where
  that fails the third warning and the whole transaction rolled back. What
  it applied commits or rolls back with the caller's transaction. Every
  failure but an overflow is caught, as the
  reference catches `sqlite3.Error`, `OSError`, `ValueError`, `KeyError`
  and `TypeError`: a busy writer, a read-only connection and
  `query_only` all fall back to the memory rows. An overflow of the
  digest's seq is `DocFreqError::Py(OverflowError)`, uncaught as there.
- The warnings (`the digest could not be brought current`, `the digest
  could not be read`, `_joined`'s `a nested write could not be taken
  back` and `note_residue`'s line) are data: `DigestWarning`s with the
  kind, the path text, the class, SQLite's extended result code and the
  text, read with `StoreDocFreq::warnings`, with `message()` as
  `record.getMessage()`; nothing is printed. The class is the one the
  reference raises: SQLite's by its code; `StoreVersionError` for the
  writer check's versions; OperationalError for a rolled-back
  transaction, a later writer and a text that is not UTF-8. The shared
  `DigestError::Unreadable` keeps no class, so it is named by what
  failed, and where the label alone cannot tell, by reading again after
  the rollback what failed: a record that does not load is named by the
  loader's own class (`RecordError::class`: ValidationError,
  JSONDecodeError, ...); the first log payload after the digest's seq
  that does not read by `json.loads`' class (UnicodeDecodeError for bytes
  that do not decode, JSONDecodeError) or the indexing's (TypeError for
  a value that is not a dict, KeyError for a key it lacks); an id that
  is a text holding a lone surrogate, which reads and which binding
  refuses after every payload is read, by the class of a record named
  before it that does not load, else UnicodeEncodeError; any other lone
  surrogate UnicodeEncodeError; an `int()` that fails ValueError; a
  record column missing is sqlite3.Row's IndexError, which `digest_mark`
  does not catch, so it is raised. The fixture pins class, code and the
  message, the root spelled `<root>` and the exception's text `<exc>`
  where it is SQLite's or a library's wording.
- Inherited from `store::digest::mutated_ids` (the gap the pool's
  section states, not this unit's code): a log payload past the
  digest's seq whose id is a list or an object, or a payload in UTF-16
  or UTF-32 bytes, which the reference reads (the id through `str()`,
  the bytes by `json.detect_encoding`) and applies, does not read here:
  `digest_mark` warns (KeyError for the id, JSONDecodeError for the
  bytes) and answers None, so `digest_admission_rows` is None, the memo
  reads the memory rows and `ranking_statistics` gives no average where
  the reference answers from the digest. No writer writes either.
- `digest_admission_rows` answers the rows as the reference hands them
  on (`DigestRow`: `int()` of the row number, `str()` of the scopes, the
  home, client and model columns as they are, `int()` of the length);
  the typing below is the grouping's (`admission_rows`). sqlite3
  converts a row's columns, steps to the next row and only then hands
  the row on, and the port reads in that order: a step that fails is the
  second warning and None before the row ahead of it is converted, a
  conversion that fails (a text that is not UTF-8) is the second warning
  and None, and `int()` of a row number or length that does not read
  raises and is not caught. `int()` is a Python int: a number past 64
  bits (a REAL past 2**63 or a numeral text with underscores, planted in
  an INTEGER column; no writer writes one) is read whole as
  `docfreq::PyInt` and handed on as it is. It is refused only where the
  reference refuses it: the grouping's `array('q')` takes a length
  past 64 bits on a row whose scopes are a list as OverflowError (in row
  order, after that row's refused actor; a row whose scopes are not a
  list is skipped and its length never read), and the patch's statement
  binds the lowest changed row number, OverflowError past 64 bits. A
  row number past 64 bits is an index key of its own, which no FTS row
  matches (`digest_big_numbers` in the fixture). `_read_doc_freq_inputs`' fallback is a
  generator over the same steps: a row is grouped once the step to the
  next one succeeded, so a step that fails raises after the rows before
  the one ahead of it were grouped (their scopes parsed, their `Actor`
  built), and a conversion that fails after every earlier row was.
- Typing at the seam. Scopes are `str()` of the column (`SqlValue::py_str`:
  NULL is `"None"`, which `json.loads` refuses, as there). A client or
  model that is NULL or TEXT is taken as it is, bytes are decoded as
  UTF-8 (pydantic's `str` does), anything else is ValidationError
  (`DocFreqError::Source("ValidationError")`), raised at the first row
  whose scopes are a list (where the reference builds the group's
  `Actor`), after the earlier rows were grouped. A home project is
  handed to `admit` as it is: a text as `Home::Text`, a BLOB (which TEXT
  affinity keeps; only a planted row holds one) as `Home::Bytes`, on
  both paths. The memo's rows carry the home as text (`AdmissionRow`), so
  a BLOB's bytes and a text that starts with U+F8FF are spelled after
  that mark there (`with_home` reads it back), and no two homes the
  reference keeps apart are one group key. A scopes text that is not
  JSON is JSONDecodeError on every path (the shared `load_scopes` names
  it ValueError; the class is named at this seam). A bytes client and
  the same text as one group key are one
  group here and two in the reference: `admit` is asked once more there,
  and the answer is the same.
- `term_masks` is `reads::term_masks` turned into masks (`row_mask` over
  the set positions, width the index's length); body or scopes is the
  OR of two reads of `memories_fts` alone. A row number the digest holds
  twice (planted: no constraint forbids it) gives the later row the
  index's length as its position, so the read spans every position the
  index holds, and `row_mask` answers as `_row_mask` does: inside the
  last byte the memo answers, past it IndexError (`digest_rid_twice`,
  `digest_rid_past_bytes`). `fts_rowids` runs the
  patch's statement; a limit past `i64` binds as `i64::MAX`.
- `advanced_inputs` is `_advanced_inputs`, built by unit
  store_index-advance (below): an entry kept at an older head is carried
  over by the log's record rows, its terms kept, as the reference does.
  The differences the store-2 part listed from not porting it (the terms
  started again, one `could not be brought current` warning where the
  reference logs two, a digest row changed without a log row read again)
  are gone; the last is the reference's own behaviour and is reproduced.
- A difference this unit keeps: on a read-only connection, a log
  payload id holding a lone surrogate that comes after an existing
  record's id is named UnicodeEncodeError (or a later unloadable
  record's class) in the warning, where the reference logs
  OperationalError (code 8: the earlier record's write fails before the
  surrogate is bound). Answers are equal; only the warning's class
  differs (smallest input `ro_valid_then_sur` in the verifier's notes).
  On a writable or `query_only` connection, and with the surrogate id
  first, the classes agree.
- The entry points take one admit shape, `StoreAdmit`: `(scopes, home
  project as Option<Home>, Option<&DocActor>)`. The memo's path calls it
  per group; the uncached path (`reads::document_frequencies`) per row,
  through an adapter that turns the home column and `identity::Actor`
  into the same shape. `document_frequencies` goes through the memo when
  `memoised` and not in a transaction, else uncached;
  `ranking_statistics` is the memo's four items outside a transaction
  and the uncached three with no average inside one. The memo is the
  caller's: `docfreq::memo()` for the process, a `DocFreqMemo` of its own
  in a test.
- A difference the reference has with itself, reproduced: the uncached
  read builds every row's `Actor` before it looks at the scopes, the
  memo only for rows whose scopes are a list, so a row with an
  unreadable actor and scopes that are not a list raises on one path
  only; and the memo reads the digest's copy of a row's scopes, the
  uncached read the memory row's, so a memory row whose scopes were
  changed under the digest answers differently on the two
  (`scopes_not_list` in the fixture).

Not in this part, with owners: `Store.reopen` (store.py 1965-2002) is
unit store-2b, built as `WritableStore::reopen` ("Opening a store for
writing", "Another connection"); the unaccounted-id set it shares is the
caller's `store::provenance::Provenance`. `_advanced_inputs` is unit store_index-advance's
(below). `store_orphans` is store-1's. The read-only search pool (`store/pool.rs`)
reads its rows' admission and its statistics through `DocFreqMemo` over
a source of its own that is `StoreDocFreq` for every read but the
digest's rows (unit poolmemo, below). A `StoreFile` has no constructor of
its own: `over` takes its connection where a caller has one.

Fixture: `tests/contract/gen_store_docfreq_store.py` makes each case's
store with `Store.create` under `store_create.json`'s fixed values,
opens it as the owner and writes through the reference's own writers
(`_mutate` in `_transaction`, clocks fixed). Steps: a store with no
memory, a digest behind by one and by several, no digest state, another
fingerprint, scopes that are not lists under the digest, an unreadable
actor, a write between two calls, a home put and delete, a tombstone,
terms with quotes and FTS operators, scope-only hits, admit by scope,
project and actor and none, inside a batch, after a failed nested write
in one, after the connection's own ROLLBACK in one, `query_only`, a
second connection holding the write lock (busy timeout 0), a read-only
open and a second spelling of the path; the digest asked directly
(`mark`, `rows`, `head`) inside a batch that commits, inside one that
raises, after the connection's ROLLBACK and on a connection left inside a
transaction no call owns; a home stored as a BLOB; a log with no memory
row and a planted `index_rebuilt` row; memory rows whose scopes are not
JSON read under a new memo key; a digest seq past 64 bits; a digest
client planted as bytes (UTF-8 and not); digest row numbers and lengths
past 64 bits (`digest_big_numbers`); the memory rows read past a
step that fails at the second and at the third row (a view in place of
`homes` whose project overflows there); log payloads planted past the
digest's seq that do not read (a list, a dict without the key, a text
where a dict is indexed, bytes that do not decode, text that is not
JSON); a record a planted log row names that does not load (a links
column that is not JSON, then bytes that do not decode); a length that
does not read on the digest's row ahead of a step that fails; a digest
table without its NOT NULL holding a NULL length; the digest's
join over a view of nothing (the second warning, code 1); a writer check
that fails on `meta`; an entry carried over a moved head under a busy
writer. A step's `sql` holds what the tables do not carry, run by the
replay before it lays them. Recorded per step: the tables the step
changed (the log as the rows appended), every answer, the memo's keys
(`<root>` for the case's directory) and terms kept, the digest's state,
admission columns and token count after, whether the head checkpoint
moved, each memo entry's inputs (`entries`), and each warning's format,

(`digest_rid_twice` to `read_only`) and `store_docfreq_advance.jsonl`

`store_tx.jsonl`'s (Unicode, pydantic-core, POSIX only). Tests:
`golden_store_docfreq_store` (with `golden_store_docfreq_store_not_posix`
recording the Windows gap), `store_docfreq_store_kills` and
`store_docfreq_store_robustness` (20,000 rows and 4,097 terms within
