## The fold check

`store::fold` (`StoreFile::refold`, `StoreFile::log_verify_loading`, `fold::merge`)
reproduces `store_events.refold` and `log_verify`, read only. The mutation
rows of the log (`MUTATION_KINDS`) are replayed into a SQLite database in
memory built from the reference's own `SCHEMA` and `MEMBERSHIP_SCHEMA`
(the texts `store/reference_schema.json` pins), less the FTS5 table and
its three triggers, which the fold never compares; the
`memory_links_cleanup` trigger, the keys and the unique index on
verifications stay, so SQLite's affinities, conflicts and cascades act as
in the reference. Each kind is applied as `store_rows._apply_mutation`
applies it: the same statements, the values Python would bind in the same
order (a `str()` of a payload value, `int()`, `list()`, `payload.get`'s raw
value), so a binding error is the one Python's sqlite3 raises at the same
parameter. What the reference catches (ValueError and its subclasses
JSONDecodeError and UnicodeEncodeError, KeyError, TypeError,
ValidationError) is a `payload_invalid` problem with the first line of
`str(exc)` cut to 200 characters: `json`'s decode messages
(`json::decode_failure`, CPython 3.13's C scanner, trailing-comma messages
included), the int digit limit, `int()`'s and `list()`'s messages, the
UnicodeEncodeError of a lone surrogate bound as text, pydantic's
`N validation error(s) for <Model>` line, the messages of
`_membership_values`, `_membership_key` and `validate_path_targets`. What
is applied before a row raises stays applied (the reference has no
savepoint per row). Anything else is `FoldError::Raised` with the class
the reference lets out of `refold` (AttributeError, ProgrammingError,
OverflowError, IntegrityError, RecursionError, OperationalError for text
that is not UTF-8 in a live table ...).

The comparison reads each folded and membership table on both sides over
the columns the reference's schema gives it, keyed by `_TABLE_KEYS`, as a
Python dict holds them: an int equals a float of the same value, text never
equals a blob, two rows with one key keep the first key's spelling and the
last row's values (`rows` counts keys, not rows). `unaccounted` and
`missing` are sorted by `str()` of the label, stably. The index text
columns are compared only while the signed log names the reference's
tokenizer (`python_tokenizer_fingerprint`), and are spelled once per row
the replay leaves rather than once per put (the same text: nothing else
reads them).

Not ported: `_unaccounted_memory_ids`, the in-process memo the reference's
`Store` keeps of the last fold's unaccounted ids; nothing native keeps
state between calls. `native_text.mutation_payload` is not needed: it
shapes a payload before it is signed, and the fold reads what was signed.

Deep JSON: the reference parses a payload inside `refold`, several frames
below the top of its stack, so a payload nested 9,996 to 9,999 deep raises
RecursionError out of `refold` there (macOS arm64, CPython 3.13; the window
is lower on Windows, whose default stack is smaller, and moves with the
caller's depth), while native parses up to 9,998 and applies the row. At
20,000 both sides agree: the reference's C scanner hits its own recursion
guard and raises RecursionError, and native's JSON load stops at its
depth limit with `LoadError::Recursion`, which the fold lets out as
`FoldError::Raised("RecursionError")`: the same class out of `refold`. No case pins the window; it is a
platform fact, not a contract.

Memory: the log is read and applied in batches of `FOLD_BATCH` (4,096) rows,
parsed on up to 8 threads, and a payload's text is not kept beside its
parsed value (it is read again only to spell a decode error). The live and
folded tables are compared by a SHA-256 of each row's values in their key
form, so neither side's rows are held twice. A single payload is still held
whole while it is parsed: a single 50 MB payload still peaks at about 1.8
GB (the reviewer's measurement).

### A writer during the fold

`log verify` must describe one state of the log: the chain report and the
fold read the same rows, and an honest writer (one that appends signed
rows and applies them in the same transaction, as the reference's writers
do) never makes it read anything but `ok`.

One read, two consumers. Each log row is read once and the same row is
fed to the chain verifier and to the fold's replay (`fold::OneRead`, a
`LogSource` whose `each` hands every row to `verify_chain_from`'s visit and
then to the replay).

- A rollback-journal store read in place, where a read transaction holds
  the shared lock that blocks every commit: `first`, the rekey rows and the
  log's last seq are read in one short read, then the rows in batches of
  1,024, each its own statement, on to that seq. There the batched phase
  follows a writer: it reads the log's last seq again and goes on in
  batches to it while more than a batch was appended, at most
  `FOLLOW_ROUNDS` (4) times. Then one read transaction is begun and held
  for the rest: the rows after the last batch, the head file (read after
  the rows, as in the reference), the log's row count and first seq, the
  live tables. The tables' shape (`sqlite_master`, each
  table's `PRAGMA table_info`) is read just before it and read again in it
  only if `PRAGMA schema_version` moved. The rows read in it are applied
  after it ends. The hold is bounded by reading the live tables and the
  row count plus the rows appended since the last follow (fewer than a
  batch unless the writer outruns the reader four times). `bm-verify
  --fold` prints the longest hold under `ms.longest_hold`.
- A WAL store, a private copy or a caller's transaction: the same pass,
  the load included, in one read transaction. The head file is outside
  SQLite: if it names a row past the snapshot that the log now holds and
  the report is otherwise clean, the pass runs again.
- A private copy cannot be read forward. A closed WAL store is read as a
  copy; when a writer opens the store after the copy was taken and moves
  the head file, the head names a row the copy lacks. That is no
  tampering: when the report's only complaint is that head, and the store
  or its `-wal` is no longer what was copied (or a writer's `-shm` is
  there now), the check ends "kept changing" (`StoreError::KeptChanging`,
  `bm-verify` exit 3) and the store opened again reads the writer's rows
  in place. A copy whose source nobody wrote keeps its report: a tail
  removed from a closed store reads `tampered`. (Found on the Linux
  runner, CI run 43797351206: one verify in eight read `tampered` when it
  copied the closed store just before the test's writer made its first
  commit. The reference's read-only commands copy a closed store the same
  way and read the head file later, so they can report this as tampered.)

What the report describes, in plain words:

- WAL (and a copy, or a caller's transaction): the store as it was when
  the pass began. An edit made during the pass, of any kind, is not seen
  by this pass and is seen by the next.
- Rollback journal: the log as it was read, batch by batch, and the tables
  as they are at the end. A row appended during the pass is read in its
  batch or in the snapshot and needs no second pass. An edit that touches
  a table row, edits a log row not yet read, or removes or inserts log rows
  (anywhere: the row count and first seq read in the snapshot must be the
  rows the pass visited) reads `tampered` in that pass. A log payload
  edited behind the read position, with the tables left alone, is not seen
  by this pass (its MAC was checked on the bytes read before the edit, and
  the replay used the same bytes): this pass reads `ok`, the next reads
  `tampered`. `fold_writer::an_edit_during_a_pass` pins each case. A key rotation met during the pass (a
rekey row past the rekey read) loads the ring again, at most `LOAD_TRIES`
times, then `StoreError::KeptChanging` (`bm-verify` exit 3); nothing else
reruns a pass.

A not-ok report is a one-snapshot fact. The batches assume the log only
grows. Before a report that is not `ok`, or a raise (from loading the
ring, from `reads_in_batches` or from the pass), is returned,
`PRAGMA data_version` is compared with its value before the pass; if
another connection committed meanwhile, or the snapshot's row count or
first seq is not what the pass visited (whatever the report), the whole
pass runs once more inside one read transaction and that report is
returned. The count costs about 46 ms under the lock on the 310,008-row
store. That costs a
writer one stall, and only when something looks wrong. What may rewrite rows under a read: a restore
replaces the file, and a native read holds the restore lock for the life of
its `StoreFile`, so none can run mid-pass; `log.append_history_replaced`
only appends (one signed control row in its own write transaction); nothing
in `src/bettermemory` updates or deletes a log row. So no honest operation
rewrites a log row under a read.

Finding about the reference: `log_verify` reads the chain (`verify_chain`)
and then the fold (`refold`, which reads the log and each live table) in
separate statements with no transaction around them, so a commit between
them can make it report a row the chain has not seen, or a table row whose
log row it did not replay, as unaccounted. Not changed.

Measured (`fold_writer.rs`, the populated case): 8 verifies per test under
a writer committing every 2 ms (1 row, and 20 rows a transaction), in WAL
and rollback-journal mode, every one `ok`; a planted row under the same
writer, 5 of 5 `tampered` in both modes; 7 edits made from the pass's hook
after its first batch, in both modes (`an_edit_during_a_pass`, above). The
file (5 tests) runs in 6.5 to 7.8 s in a debug build, and no assertion
depends on the machine's speed.
Ignored timings: with 20 rows a transaction back to back, 8 verifies all
`ok` (WAL 0.6 s while 12,340 rows were written; rollback journal 1.6 s,
20,000 rows; release). A writer's commit latency on a rollback-journal
store while verifies run back to back
(`writer_latency_under_native_log_verify`, release), on a 310,008-row store
of the first shape below: one commit every 5 ms, 3 verifies (all `ok`) in
23.9 s while 2,747 commits ran, median 0.50 ms, p99 5.3 ms, worst 621 ms;
commits back to back, 3 verifies (all `ok`) in 37.0 s while 48,816 commits
ran, median 0.40 ms, p99 3.0 ms, worst 715 ms, longest hold 695 ms. With no
writer the longest hold is 392 to 396 ms, nearly all of it the live tables
(310,000 memories) read in the snapshot.

The differential (`native/tools/fold_differential.py`, a tool, not a
test): seeded random stores built by the reference from the three bases
(populated, plus every kind, plus drift), edited behind the log or given a
fuzzed signed payload, each run by the reference's `log_verify()` and the
release `bm-verify --fold` on the same file and compared field for field.
Edits that would put a REAL into a TEXT-affinity column are skipped (the two
SQLites spell it differently). Seed 1, 600 stores: 244 edited, 341 fuzzed,
48 edits skipped, 600 the same, 0 different.

Findings about the reference, reproduced and pinned in `fold.jsonl`, not
changed: (1) a row planted as an exact copy of a `memory_links` row whose
`note` is NULL is not reported (SQLite lets the key repeat since NULLs are
distinct; the dict collapses the two), case `duplicate_null_note_link`;
(2) a store whose `checkouts` lacks the optional `unresolved_json` column
(one an earlier build created, read before its owner's open adds it) reads
every checkout row as unaccounted, since the live tuples are one column
shorter than the replay's, case `optional_column_absent`; (3) payloads the
reference does not catch (a `conflict_put` whose `conflict` is not an
object, a list bound as a column, an int past 64 bits, a NULL in a NOT NULL
column, `int()` of infinity) make `refold` and `log verify` raise instead of
reporting `payload_invalid`, cases `raised_*`; (4) a planted row whose key
is NULL or a blob is labelled by that value (`null_key_planted`,
`blob_key`), and labels that print alike sort in the order the rows were
read (`keys_that_print_alike`).

`fold.jsonl` (`tests/contract/gen_fold.py`): 162 cases (the 163rd,
`raised_recursion`, a payload opened 20,000 times, is in
`fold_python.jsonl`, gated on the Python release: whether `json.loads`
raises RecursionError there is the interpreter's and the system's), each the
reference's `refold()` and `log_verify()` (`path` left out) on a store the
native test rebuilds: the 40 cases of `store_files.jsonl` (17 refused at
open, compared as a refusal), `store_real.sqlite`, and the intact base
with a prelude from the header (signed rows appended with the base's key,
the table rows the reference's `_apply_mutation` writes for them, the head
file) and a recipe: `populated` (every folded and membership table filled),
66 planted, edited and deleted rows (three per table), 18 hostile or odd
live tables (index text alone, text not UTF-8, a blob, NUL, a huge value,
a blob key, a NULL key, a duplicated row, keys that print alike, one and
two membership tables absent, the optional column absent, an extra
column, a missing column, memories emptied), 4 tokenizer-drift cases, 41
signed rows the fold reports as `payload_invalid` in one case, 6 cases a
payload makes the reference raise, an empty log after `store_created` and
no log at all; and `every_kind`, a prelude that applies every kind in
`MUTATION_KINDS` at least once (the generator asserts it): every delete
kind, membership deletes and membership re-puts over their own key, a re-put
replacing a memory's links, a delete then tombstone then restore of one id,
a verification with a NULL machine replaced, a checkout without
`unresolved_json`, an int standing probability, a tombstone whose
corroborations are a string and links null, a memory with a filename,
verification lists given as a dict and as a string, and re-puts over the
same key in conflicts, imports and quarantine; 22 cases edit one table each
on it, and one adds drift. The generator asserts that every `*_edited`
case reports something its unedited base does not, except the blind spot
`drift_index_text_edited` (the index text is not compared under drift), and
that no recipe's SQL can make a float (a REAL literal, a division, a
function that gives a REAL), since SQLite spells a REAL in a TEXT column by
its own version's rules; `real_for_integer` is exempt (an INTEGER column
keeps 1.5 a REAL). Preludes are shared by name in the header, long ASCII
runs are built from a count, and a table with nothing unaccounted or missing
is written as its row count alone. `golden_fold.rs` compares every case field for field
(`fold_every_case`) and feeds hostile payloads (deep JSON, 2 MB strings,
NUL, lone surrogates, numbers past every range, NaN and infinities) and
tables (text not UTF-8, blobs, NULL and blob keys, extra and dropped
columns, a dropped table, an emptied or altered log) to `refold`, which
must give a report or a typed error (`hostile_inputs_never_panic`).

Timing and memory, `/usr/bin/time -l`, Apple M-series, release, reference
`log_verify()` on `connect_read_only` against native `bm-verify --fold`
(two runs each, WAL and rollback-journal mode alike), on two stores built
through the reference's `_apply_mutation`:

| store | rows | mutation rows | payload bytes | reference | native | ratio | peak RSS reference | native |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| puts | 310,008 | 310,007 (memory puts; a third re-put an earlier id) | 264,011,832 | 31.1 s | 7.46 to 7.54 s | 0.24 | 1.82 GB | 0.96 GB |
| mixed | 46,008 | 9,207 (the rest telemetry `search` rows) | 16,211,432 | 1,103 ms | 327 to 332 ms | 0.30 | 164 MB | 80 MB |

Before batching, native peaked at 4.1 to 4.6 GB on a store of the first
shape. The reviewer's measurements on other stores gave ratios of 0.42 and
0.10 (the owner's snapshot). The fold parses the payloads on up to 8 cores
and spells the index text on every core; replaying them is one transaction
on prepared statements, in seq order.

## The event reads (`store_events.py`, `store::event_reads`)

`store_events.py` holds the telemetry writes, the event reads and the log.
By function, with the reference's lines and status:

| function | lines | needs from the machine | status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `record_event`, `_primary_code`, `_busy`, `_time_left`, `_waiting_until` | 69-175 | the monotonic clock, a sleep | `store::record_event` (storeev1) |
| `import_event`, `imported_event_keys` | 178-225 | none | `store::record_event` (storeev1) |
| `_named_payload` | 228-239 | none | `store::record_event` (storeev1) |
| `iter_events` | 242-263 | none | built here |
| `record_migration`, `record_capture` | 266-309 | the clock | `store::record_event` (storeev1) |
| `capture_rows` | 312-336 | none | built here |
| `NAMING_BOUND`, `events_of_kinds` | 339-392 | local time for a naive `since` | built here |
| `session_events_of_kinds` | 395-424 | none | built here |
| `events_since` | 429-456 | local time for a naive `since` | built here |
| `_window_floor` | 459-485 | none | built here |
| `iter_events_backward` | 488-497 | none | built here |
| `log_rows`, `refold`, `log_verify` | 502-632 | none | `store::fold` (read only) |

`store::event_reads` reproduces the read side, each function over a
`&Connection` (the reference's `self._conn`), so the writing store
(`store::open`) and the read-only one both serve. It also holds
`CAPTURE_KINDS` (`log.py:169`, the five `capture_*` kinds), which
`record_capture` checks against.

- The reference's readers are generators: a read that raises partway has
  yielded the rows before the raise. Each function answers a `Read`, the
  items and the raise that stopped it (None when the rows ran out), with
  the raise's Python class from `EventReadError::class`.
- `iter_events` is `log.iter_rows` after `since_seq`: every column is
  `str()`, so a blob payload is read as its `b'...'` spelling and skipped,
  and a payload SQLite stored as text from a number is read as that
  number and skipped. The other readers pass the fetched value to
  `Store._event_from_raw`, which `json.loads` a blob. Both shape the event
  through `store::rows::event_from_columns`.
- `sqlite3` decodes every selected column when it fetches a row, so a text
  that is not UTF-8 in any of the seven columns (the `mac` too) stops the
  read with OperationalError at that row.
- The cut is `_iso(since.astimezone(utc)).replace("+00:00", "Z")`, and
  both `events_since` and `events_of_kinds` compare its first nineteen
  characters against the stamp. A `since` out of range once in UTC raises
  OverflowError. A naive `since` is the machine's local time in the
  reference: the caller gives its offset (`local_offset`, seconds east,
  which a later machine binding answers over `localtime`); without one the
  read declines (`native:not_ported`).
- `events_of_kinds` checks its kinds before anything else (no kinds is no
  read, and no raise from the cut), then spells each of `naming` as
  `json.dumps(str(n), ensure_ascii=False)[1:-1]`, deduplicated: an empty
  naming reads nothing, more than `NAMING_BOUND` (200) narrows nothing.
  A kind or needle holding a surrogate raises UnicodeEncodeError when it is
  bound, after the floor: a window with no floor answers nothing.
- `_window_floor` and `session_events_of_kinds` name their index with
  `INDEXED BY`; when SQLite refuses the hint with an OperationalError (the
  index is gone) the query is asked again without it, as the reference
  does. The refusal comes at prepare time in both.
- No regular expression is used.

Fixtures (`gen_store_event_reads`): `store_event_reads.jsonl` builds small
stores in memory from the `log` table's DDL (mixed kinds, both stamp
spellings, rows out of order, `log_by_ts` or `log_by_session` dropped,
payloads that are not objects, a blob payload, integer columns, a `mac`
that is not UTF-8) and runs every reader over them: since bounds, aware
offsets with seconds, the year 1 and 9999 overflows, namings under, at and
over the bound, surrogates in kinds, needles and sessions. Every read is
ordered by `seq` or asks `MIN(seq)`, so no row depends on the SQLite
release and the file is not gated. `store_event_reads_naive.jsonl` holds
the naive `since` reads under `TZ=XST-05:30` (19,800 seconds east), set
with `time.tzset` and given back inside the generator: POSIX only, with
`store_event_reads_not_posix.rs` recording the gap; the kills test checks
the naive path everywhere.

Reference finding (CPython `sqlite3`, seen under 3.13.13): when
`session_events_of_kinds` is given a session holding a surrogate on a
store without `log_by_session`, on a connection whose statement cache
already holds the unhinted query, the failed bind reports the hint's stale
error and the read raises OperationalError ("no such index:
log_by_session") with the UnicodeEncodeError as its context; on a fresh
connection it raises UnicodeEncodeError. Repro: build the `mixed` store
with `log_by_session` dropped, read session `s1`, then session
`"s\ud800"`. The port answers UnicodeEncodeError (the cold-cache answer):
the cache is connection state outside the function's arguments. The
fixture reads surrogate sessions on a fresh connection.

### The event writes (`store::record_event`, unit storeev1)

`store::record_event` reproduces lines 69-309 on the writable store
(`WritableStore`), with the row stamped through a crate entry of the
transaction, `Transaction::append_at`, which takes the reference's
`ts=` (`ts or _utcnow_iso()`: an empty text is stamped now) without
changing `append`'s callers.

- `record_event` refuses a kind of `_NOT_TELEMETRY` with the reference's
  ValueError. Its payload is `event_payload`: the fields through
  `event_redact::redact_event_fields` (with `secret_spans` as that lane's
  `spans` argument), then the actor's record set when it is not empty and
  the fields hold no `actor`. Tries are `max(1, attempts)`; a try is
  retried only when its error is busy (`busy`: the OperationalError's
  primary code 5 or 6, through `event_hook::is_busy` and `primary_code`),
  tries remain, and `_time_left` holds (`deadline - monotonic() > 0.05`,
  the clock read only then). The pause is `Provider::pause`
  (`EVENT_RETRY_PAUSE_SECONDS`). A failure the reference's `except
  (sqlite3.Error, OSError, RuntimeError)` catches (`caught`: SQLite, the
  clock, a rolled-back transaction, a later writer, a RecursionError) is
  swallowed with one warning when `best_effort` is on or its primary code
  is SQLITE_READONLY, and raised otherwise; any other error is raised.
- Once SQLite commits, the log row is durable. If updating the keyring
  checkpoint raises an OS error, the event logger receives the SQLite
  file path and the typed error in a warning. A handler exception then
  follows the same catch and retry rules as the rest of that try. A busy
  handler can therefore cause a second signed row when a retry succeeds.
  A joined event leaves this warning to its outer transaction's provider.
- Each outer write rereads `min_writer_revision` under the write lock.
  A missing value means zero. A malformed value raises `StoreVersionError`
  with its key and the store path. A higher revision sets `query_only`
  and raises an uncoded `OperationalError` naming both revisions. A failed
  SQLite query keeps its SQLite error code. The writing open's digest
  catches the same refusals and leaves the digest as it stood.
- `_waiting_until` reads the store's busy timeout and the monotonic clock
  once per try when a deadline is given, lowers the timeout to what is
  left (through `store::reads::set_busy_timeout`) only when less than the
  timeout is left, and gives the timeout back after the try.
  Inside an open transaction (`EventTransaction::Joined`), the writer
  makes one try under a savepoint (`Transaction::scope`).
- The clocks and the sleep are the crate's `Provider` (`now`,
  `monotonic`, `pause`), which every writer already takes: no second
  clock trait. The deadline is an argument (`EventCall::deadline`), which
  a caller reads from its `HookScope`.
- `WritableStore` implements the hook's `BusyTimeout`. It keeps the
  seconds from the last successful setter, including fractional
  milliseconds. SQLite receives its integer milliseconds. A deadline
  gives the connection back its original setting even when a write fails.
- A keyless connection supplies its `key_state.refusal` text to
  `record_event`. The writer checks the kind first, logs one warning for
  a valid event and returns before redaction, the clock or a transaction.
  Event and capture columns keep their Python code points until the MAC
  needs UTF-8. A lone surrogate raises after the timestamp and payload
  are ready. A capture checks its kind before the lock and its guard
  before encoding the columns. A guard refusal retains its exception class
  and the code points of its message.
  If a clock or guard unwinds, the writer restores the held timeout,
  rolls back the interrupted scope, and propagates the interruption.
- `import_event` takes the row from `rows::event_import_payload` under the
  event's own `ts` and `session`. `imported_event_keys` matches `payload
  LIKE '%<needle>%'` with the needle `canonical_payload({"imported_from":
  x})[1:-1]`, so `%` and `_` in `x` match as wildcards, as in the
  reference; each column is `str()` of the fetched value, and the payload
  goes through `_named_payload` (`named_payload`: the stored text unless
  the naming changes a field of a JSON object).
- `record_migration` takes `engine_version` from
  `Provider::engine_version`, as `store::create` does. `record_capture`
  checks `CAPTURE_KINDS` (`store::event_reads`) and runs its guard inside
  the transaction, under the lock, before the row. Each writer can join
  an open transaction. The v8 migration calls both `record_migration`
  and `import_event` inside one batch. Its rollback takes back both rows.
- `EventLogger` receives the event kind and each `Logged` entry when it
  occurs. A handler error propagates before the next retry pause or write.
  The fixture compares log levels, retry numbers and handler failures.
- No regular expression is used.

Fixtures (`gen_store_record_event`, `store_record_event_posix.jsonl`):
stores opened as `store_tx.jsonl`'s are; a second connection holding
`BEGIN IMMEDIATE` makes a real SQLITE_BUSY, `PRAGMA query_only` a
SQLITE_READONLY; `store_events.time` is a stub for each step whose
monotonic readings are scripted (the Rust test replays exactly the
readings taken) and whose sleep commits the blocker at a named pause;
`bettermemory.__version__` is fixed for the migration rows. Cases: the
plain write, the actor, `attempts` of 0 and below, the refused kinds,
busy with and without retries and `best_effort`, a blocker freed after one
and two pauses, deadlines with time for one more try, exactly the pause
left, a lowered wait given back, read-only stores, calls inside a
transaction, failing log handlers, a real keyless reader, signed columns with surrogates, a
submillisecond timeout and the timeout sampled at insertion, the v8
import with a control token in a note, the keys under
`v8`, under a needle with wildcards, after a row is rewritten to hold the
token as an earlier build kept it, the importer's re-run, migration rows
and capture rows with a guard that refuses, and a batch containing all
three writers that is rolled back or committed. POSIX only, as
`store_tx.jsonl`; `store_record_event_not_posix.rs` records the gap, and
the kills and robustness tests run everywhere.

`store::recorder::StoreEventSink` connects the recorder to `WritableStore`.

`store::rows` holds the leaves of `store_rows.py` that the fold and the
readers share. The fold's private copies moved here unchanged; the rest
is new. Reference lines are `store_rows.py` unless named.

| Function | Reference | Needs from the machine | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `iso_opt` | `_iso_opt` 66-67 | nothing | built |
| `upsert` | `_upsert_sql` 233-243 | nothing | moved from `fold` |
| `sync_links` | `_sync_links` 246-264 | a statement runner (argument) | moved out of `Applier::apply` |
| `Spec`, `SPECS` | `store_schema._MEMBERSHIP_SPECS` | nothing | moved from `fold` |
| `membership_values`, `membership_key` | `_membership_values` 687-716, `_membership_key` 745-756 | nothing | moved from `fold` |
| `columns_of` | `PRAGMA table_info` of `_table_rows` | a connection (argument) | moved from `fold` |
| `membership_spec` | `_membership_spec` 719-723 | nothing | built |
| `membership_spec_by_table` | `store_schema._MEMBERSHIP_BY_TABLE` | nothing | built |
| `membership_column` | `_membership_column` 726-728 | nothing | built |
| `sort_rows` | `_sort_rows` 731-742 | nothing | built |
| `known_columns` | `_known_columns` 759-777 | the linked SQLite | built |
| `verification_row` | `_verification_row` 475-483 | nothing | built |
| `event_from_columns` | `_event_from_columns` 816-838 (`_ROW_COLUMNS` 813) | nothing | built |
| `event_from_raw` | `store.py` `Store._event_from_raw` 2004-2010 | nothing | built |
| `is_mutation`, `is_membership_mutation`, `MUTATION_TABLES` | `store_schema.MUTATION_KINDS` 206-208, `MEMBERSHIP_MUTATION_KINDS` 248-250 | nothing | `is_mutation` moved from `fold` (re-exported there) |
| `CONTROL_KINDS` | `log.py` 172, 179, 208, 218 (the union of the four assignments) | nothing | built |
| `MEMBERSHIP_EVENT_KINDS`, `not_telemetry` | `store_schema.py` 214-247, `_NOT_TELEMETRY` 255 | nothing | built |

Not moved: `fold`'s private `schema_texts` reads the first two pinned
schema texts and `admission::schema_texts` all five, so they do not
concatenate the same texts and `fold` keeps its own. `sqlite_class` stays
in `fold`. `fold`'s refusal type `Fail` and its `item`, `get`, `text` and
`key_error` helpers moved with the membership checks that use them;
`fold::json_text` is `pub(crate)` for `membership_values`.
`records::rows::load_json` is `pub(crate)` for `verification_row`.
`records::rows::path_targets` is not reused: it serves the record
readers, whose rows always name an `id`, so it reads `row["id"]`
unconditionally (IndexError on a verification row, which names none,
where the reference skips the check), and it keeps only the first level
of each target map, which is all the model reads. `verification_row`
has its own whole `_path_targets`, with Python's `==` between the
record's id and the column.

Decisions:

- `sort_rows` reproduces `list.sort` with `key` and `reverse`, not a
  sort with an inverted comparator: the keys are made for every row
  first (a row without the column is KeyError, `str(exc)` the column's
  `repr`, before any comparison), the list is reversed for a leading
  `-`, sorted ascending and reversed back, which keeps equal rows in
  their order. Keys compare as Python compares the tuples `(value is not
  None, value or 0)`: the flags first, then `==` (never raising across
  types) and `<`, which across types (int or float against str or bytes,
  str against bytes) is the TypeError `'<' not supported between
  instances of 'A' and 'B'`, returned and never a panic. An int and a
  float compare exactly, as CPython does. The comparisons are CPython
  3.13's own at every length: `count_run`, binary insertion up to the
  minimum run, powersort's merge order (`powerloop`, `found_new_run`,
  `merge_force_collapse`) and the galloping merges (`merge_at`,
  `gallop_left`, `gallop_right`, `merge_lo`, `merge_hi`, `min_gallop`
  carried from merge to merge), each merge in place over the list with
  the shorter run copied aside. So a TypeError names its two types in
  the order CPython's first failing comparison does, and a NaN (which
  SQLite never returns) leaves the rows in the order CPython leaves them.
  The keys sort with each row's index; the rows are moved once per name.
  Rows are `records::rows::Row` values, as sqlite3 gives them.
- `known_columns` builds an in-memory database from `SCHEMA` and then
  `MEMBERSHIP_SCHEMA` (the first two pinned texts of
  `admission::schema_texts`), FTS5's table and shadow tables included,
  once per process. Its fixture names the reference SQLite and is gated
  on it on the Python side (`SQLITE_GATED`); the Rust test compares it
  strictly (class i), since the native build links its own SQLite and
  `gates_of` gates no file on SQLite but `models_stores.jsonl`.
- `event_from_columns` takes the payload as the column value: null and
  numbers are `json.loads`' TypeError, which propagates; a
  JSONDecodeError, a UnicodeDecodeError of bytes and the too-many-digits
  ValueError are None; RecursionError propagates. A non-telemetry kind
  is None before the payload is read.
- `verification_row` answers a list of name and field pairs: a column as
  sqlite3 gives it, or a decoded value; a refusal is the class.
- `verification_row` and `event_from_raw` read a column as `sqlite3.Row`
  does (`Row::item`): the first column whose name is equal, or equal
  ignoring ASCII case when both names are ASCII. `name in row.keys()`
  (`Row::has_key`) is exact. `Row::get`, which the record readers use,
  is unchanged.
- No regular expression is involved.

Fixtures (`tests/contract/gen_store_rows.py`): `store_rows_leaves.jsonl`
(upsert statements for the memory and tombstone columns, link rows,
`membership_spec` and `membership_column` over every kind, table and
column and bad names, sorts with nulls, ties under a descending name,
several names, int and float boundaries and mixed types, a sweep of
4,000 seeded lists of up to 63 rows of numbers or text as a digest, verification rows read
from a reference-built table (names repeated or in another case among
them), events over every kind of
`_NOT_TELEMETRY` and over payloads that are not JSON or not objects,
log rows through `Store._event_from_raw` (names repeated or in another
case among them), the five kind sets, and `_iso_opt`),
`store_rows_leaves_python.jsonl` (payloads nested around the recursion
budget, an attestation payload past it, the same sweep with mixed-type
lists, whose TypeError names the pair the release's sort compares first
(3.12 and 3.11 compare in another order than 3.13), lists of 32 to 63
rows that one run and two runs fail on differently, and 600 seeded
lists of 64 to 400 rows each over numbers with NaN and over mixed types;
gated on the Python release) and
`store_rows_columns.jsonl`
(gated on SQLite on the Python side only).

Left for later units: the rest of `store_rows.py` (the record writers and
readers that are not yet ported, `_table_rows` as a whole and the
mutation dispatcher outside the fold).

## The membership tables' store methods (`store::membership`)

`store::membership` ports `store_membership.py`, the `Store` methods the
membership model reads and writes through, with `Store.in_batch` and
`Store.membership_store_id` (`store.py` 1603-1620) and the parts of
`store_native.py` its reads and writes need (`row_key` 21-22,
`legacy_row` 25-38, `native_rows` 41-67, `matches` 70-77,
`require_native_writer` 81-86), all but `legacy_row` private here. Reference
lines are `store_membership.py` unless named. Line ranges were checked
against the source as it is now.

| Function | Reference | Needs from the machine | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `put_membership` | 47-80 | the store (write transaction), the log clock | built; the surrogate branch (59-77) in unit store_membership-2 |
| `delete_membership` | 83-104 | the same | built; the surrogate branch (91-101) in unit store_membership-2 |
| `_clear_native` | 107-125 | the same | built |
| `record_membership` | 128-137 | the same | built |
| `membership_rows` | 140-217 | the store (reads) | built |
| `next_membership_id` | 220-233 | the store | built |
| `next_membership_number` | 236-246 | the store | built |
| `committed_seq` | 249-262 | the transaction's rows; the connection | built |
| `membership_log` | 265-304 | the store | built (unit store_membership-2) |
| `wrote_record` | 307-326 | the store | built |
| `reissue_membership_store_id` | 329-354 | the store, `secrets.token_hex` (`Provider::membership_store_id`) | built (unit store_membership-2) |
| `Store.in_batch`, `Store.membership_store_id` | `store.py` 1603-1620 | the store | built |
| `row_key`, `native_rows`, `matches`, `require_native_writer` | `store_native.py` 21-22, 41-77, 81-86 | the store | built (private) |
| `legacy_row` | `store_native.py` 25-38 | nothing | built (unit store_membership-2) |

The writes. Each runs on a `Transaction` as a nested entry
(`Transaction::scope`, as `_transaction` joins a batch), or on a
`WritableStore` in a transaction of its own, whose arguments are checked
before `BEGIN` as the reference checks them before its `with`. A row is
the mapping's items in order (`&[(PyValue, PyValue)]`), so `dict(row)`
needs no answer of its own. `Transaction::mutate_membership` appends and
applies a membership table's own kind under a savepoint, the two
`native_member` kinds after `require_native_writer` (as `_mutate`'s
`prepare_mutation` checks them); no such kind names a record for the
`returned` marks. `Transaction::append_control` appends a control row of
design 8.10 (`MEMBERSHIP_EVENT_KINDS`, `store_forked` among them) and
changes no table. A put or delete whose row or key holds a lone
surrogate is written as the reference writes it (unit store_membership-2,
below). `_clear_native` writes `native_member_delete` after the put or delete
when the row has a native twin, under the same writer check.

The reads take the connection. `membership_rows` reproduces the
reference's order of checks (the table, the native rows, each `where`
column, each `order_by` name with every leading `-` stripped, the
`column_in` column), `dict.fromkeys`' de-duplication by Python equality
(TypeError for an unhashable value), batches of `_PROVENANCE_BATCH`
(500) values, the native rows read as `native_rows` reads them (a row
that does not parse to an object, fails the table's checks or does not
carry its own key is None), legacy rows with a native twin dropped and
the matching native rows appended, and `_sort_rows` only when native
rows exist or more than one batch ran. The sort reuses `store::rows`'
`sort_rows` (CPython's merge order): a dict row is carried as its order
columns, a text value spelled so that byte order is code point order with
lone surrogates included. A statement parameter binds as `sqlite3` binds
it: an int past 64 bits is OverflowError, a list, dict, tuple or path is
ProgrammingError. `next_membership_number` reads `int()` of each native
value (`'12'` is 12, `5.5` is 5, other text ValueError with the
reference's words) and `int(value or 0)` of the SQL maximum.
`committed_seq` is the row before the first a transaction appended and
no rollback took back, None before any; on a `WritableStore`, 0 while the
connection is still in a transaction no call owns (`!is_autocommit()`),
else None. `in_batch` is true on a `Transaction`, false on a
`WritableStore` (`_tx_depth` is 0 outside one, a residue included).

Decisions. sqlite3's own exceptions are refusals by class only, their
text being the interpreter's. Values this build does not carry the way
the reference does are refused as `WriteNotPorted::Value`: `bytes` from a
BLOB column, a datetime bound as a parameter (sqlite3's deprecated
adapter), an int past 128 bits in a counter (the next number after a
native value of 2**127 - 1 included), and a sort over a value
other than None, int, float and str (a bool included, though Python
sorts it as an int). A non-integer `min_writer_revision`
answers ValueError without the reference's text (a store `open` refuses
first). No regular expression is involved.

The defer point was reached: the unit passed 600 lines, so
`membership_log` and `reissue_membership_store_id` moved to unit
store_membership-2 with the surrogate write branches.

Fixtures (`tests/contract/gen_store_membership.py`):
`store_membership.jsonl` (3 cases, 100,863 bytes), each case run as
`store_records_b.jsonl`'s (each step's log rows, clocks, state digest,
index, and the refold at the end): puts and deletes with every refusal
of the row checks, control rows, reads with `where`, `column_in`
(duplicates, empty, unhashable) and descending names, the id counters
(an empty table, a `_` prefix, tables without a minted id),
`committed_seq` and `in_batch` outside and inside a batch, a batch that
fails and writes nothing, `wrote_record` before and after a home,
`membership_store_id` with meta's row present and deleted (its path
spelled `<store>`), reads past one batch recorded as a count and a
SHA-256, native rows put in directly (a twin, a surrogate key, a wrong
key, rows that do not parse, text and float counters), the twin cleared
after a put and a delete, and a store held to revision 4 (the surrogate
put the native build refuses is pinned by the kills test instead: its log
row spells an escape `host_fact` reads as a host path). Gated as
`store_records_b.jsonl`: Unicode, pydantic-core, POSIX only.

Tests: `golden_store_membership.rs`, `store_membership_kills.rs` (13),
`store_membership_robustness.rs` (5; a `column_in` ten times larger,
of duplicates or of distinct values, reads within 30 times as long), `store_membership_not_posix.rs`.

### Unit 2, built

Unit store_membership-2 builds the rest of the module: the surrogate
branches of `put_membership` and `delete_membership` with
`store_native.legacy_row`, `membership_log` and
`reissue_membership_store_id`. Line ranges were checked against the
source as it is now.

The native writes. A put whose row holds a lone surrogate
(`has_surrogates` over the whole mapping; a key that holds one fails the
row's checks first) is checked as before outside the transaction, then
inside it: `require_native_writer`, the legacy `<kind>_put` of
`legacy_row`'s row when it answers one, then `native_member_put` of
`{"native_member": {"member_kind", "key_text": row_key, "row_text":
encoded_json(dict(row))}}`, whose row is the answer. No `_clear_native`
runs on this branch, so a native put over its own twin logs no delete. A
delete whose key columns hold one logs `native_member_delete` of
`{"member_kind", "key_text"}` alone, the legacy row untouched. A legacy
row whose replacement is None in a NOT NULL column (a surrogate in
`machines.minted`, say) fails SQLite's constraint as the reference's
does: IntegrityError, the whole call taken back. `legacy_row` is None
when a key column holds a surrogate; else the row in its order with each
value that holds one replaced: a `_json` column's by `[]` for a list or
tuple and `{}` for anything else (a str included), a `name`, `line` or
`reason` str by `utf8_text` (a pair of halves stays two escapes), any
other by None. `legacy_row`'s domain is a row the put's checks passed
(`_membership_values`: a dict of the table's columns named by str, each
key column non-empty text); outside it its answer is not the
reference's, which raises KeyError for a missing key column, TypeError
for a row that is not a mapping and AttributeError for a column name
that is not a str, and keeps `[]` or `{}` for a `_json` column whose name
holds a surrogate. `put_membership` never hands it such a row.
`WriteNotPorted::NativeMember`, the refusal unit 1 put in their place,
had no caller left and is gone.

The depth budget. The reference's `has_surrogates` recurses, two Python
frames a level (the function and its generator), and runs on every put
and delete, so a `_json` value nested about 500 deep raises
RecursionError inside the transaction, on the plain branch as on the
surrogate one, before anything is written; how deep follows the
caller's stack. The port counts the same frames against
`SURROGATE_FRAMES` (998: CPython 3.13.13's limit of 1000 less the
module's frame and the method's own, as from a module's top level).
`has_surrogates(row)` is frame 1; each value takes its frame and the
next (the generator over a str's characters, `Mapping.__instancecheck__`
for anything else, the generator over a container's items); a
container's keys and values are two frames further; the walk goes in the
reference's order and stops at the first surrogate. So a `facts_json` of
497 nested lists around a str or an int is written and 498 is
RecursionError, 498 nested lists whose innermost is empty are written
and 499 are not, as 3.13.13 answers called from a module's top level
(900 and 5,000 levels are RecursionError in both); a deeper caller in the
reference raises sooner. The port counts `Mapping.__instancecheck__` as
one frame, which it is once the process has checked that type against
`Mapping` (the ABC caches the answer). A type's first check in a process
runs `__subclasscheck__` too, some frames more: in a fresh 3.13.13
process whose first int, None, float or bool checked against `Mapping`
is the value's innermost, 494 lists around it are written and 495 are
RecursionError, where a process that checked that type once before (at
any depth) writes 497. A str never reaches the check, and a list or a
dict is checked at a shallower level of the same walk first (the row is
a dict). A RecursionError inside that first
check leaves the cache cold, and `ABCMeta.register` anywhere empties
the negative caches. Like the caller's stack, the cache is the
process's state, which the port cannot see; it answers as a warm cache
does. `legacy_row` runs beside `has_surrogates(row)`
and walks each value one frame shallower, every value to its end, so a
value the put's own walk never reached (a surrogate in an earlier column
ends that walk) raises there at 498 lists around a str. Each level costs
two frames and the budget is even, so that one frame changes no answer
from a module's top level (3.13.13 agrees: 497 lists written, 498
RecursionError), and a walk started a frame deeper cannot be told apart
by any test. Past `json::MAX_DEPTH` the row's own checks raise
RecursionError first, before the transaction, as the reference's JSON
encoder does past its own limit. A delete's key is text alone and
reaches no depth.

`membership_log` takes the kinds as the collection's items: the
reference's `set(kinds) & allowed` raises TypeError at an unhashable item
(a list, a dict, a tuple holding one) and drops one that is not a str or
not a membership kind; the names are sorted and bound as the reference
binds them, `since_seq` is an `i64` the caller has already passed through
`int()` (a bool is its int), and the checkout test is the reference's
SQL, `CASE WHEN json_valid(payload) THEN json_extract(payload,
'$.checkout') END = ?`, left to SQLite: a JSON `true` reads as 1, so a
checkout of `True`, `1` or `1.0` matches it and `"1"` does not, and an
array or object reads back as its JSON text. A checkout bound as
`sqlite3` binds it: a text holding a lone surrogate is UnicodeEncodeError
with `str.encode`'s words (the first run of surrogates, one by its
escape, several by their positions), a list, dict or tuple is
ProgrammingError. With no membership kind left the reference returns
before binding anything, so a checkout that cannot be bound is no error
there. Each row is read as `LogRow(int, str, ...)` reads it (a NULL
session stays None, any other value is its `str()`). The reference is a
generator: its checks and its statement run at the first `next()`, and
each row is read at the `next()` that yields it. `membership_log_each`
reads the same way, handing each row to a visitor that answers
`ControlFlow::Continue` to read the next or `Break` to stop, so a row past
the one a caller stops at is never read: a later row whose TEXT column is
not UTF-8 fails only a read that reaches it (OperationalError), as it
fails only the reference's caller that iterates that far
(`membership_alias._first_remotes`, for one, stops at its first match).
`membership_log` is `list(...)` of it, every row or the first error.
Rows written between two reads are seen as SQLite's statement sees them.

`reissue_membership_store_id` on a `WritableStore` draws the new id
(`Provider::membership_store_id`, `secrets.token_hex(16)`) before
`BEGIN`, as the reference draws it before its `with`: a store whose
transaction cannot begin has still drawn it. A draw that fails is
`WriteError::Clock`. Inside one savepoint it reads the old id
(`membership_store_id`, RuntimeError naming the store's path when meta
has none), runs `UPDATE meta` and appends `store_forked` with
`{old_store, new_store, record, source}` through `append_control`, so a
failure leaves meta and the log as they were (a `store_forked` append
whose clock read fails inside a batch that catches it takes back the
`UPDATE meta`, as the reference's nested savepoint does); it answers
`(old, new)`.
On a `Transaction` (a batch) the caller passes the id it drew and the
store's path, since the transaction's provider is its own.

Fixtures (`tests/contract/gen_store_membership.py`, `generate_native`):
`store_membership_native.jsonl` (4 cases, 123,374 bytes), run as
`store_membership.jsonl`'s: a surrogate in a key column and in each kind
of non-key column on every membership table (`_json` lists, tuples,
dicts and strs, nullable columns, `name`, `line` and `reason`, NOT NULL
columns that refuse), the tables after the writes and the refold, a
native twin a later plain put clears, surrogate deletes, a store held
to revision 4 and one without the meta row, native writes inside
batches, `membership_log` with kinds None, empty, foreign, mixed and
unhashable, `since_seq` at its edges and as `True`, checkouts of each
type, a payload that is not JSON and one cut short, and reissues with a
scripted token (`secrets` patched in `store_membership`), in and out of
a batch and without an id. A log read is recorded as its rows'
sequence numbers and the SHA-256 of their `encoded_json` text (each row
is in its step's log rows already), a table of more than eight rows as
its count and digest. A text the file would spell with four
backslashes in a row (a native row's escape inside a payload inside the
line) trips the golden directory's `host_fact` guard, so an answer or a
payload holding two backslashes in a row is written as its UTF-8 hex.
The surrogate checkout's UnicodeEncodeError text is the interpreter's and
is pinned in the kills test instead. Gated on Unicode (the index text)
and POSIX only, as the other store fixtures are; no row comes from
pydantic.

Tests: `golden_store_membership_native.rs`,
`store_membership_native_kills.rs` (17), and
`store_membership_native_robustness.rs` (5; a hundred thousand log rows
read within 30 times the time of ten thousand, by the wall clock since
the read waits on the database file; a `_json` value 10 deep written and
900, 5,000 and 100,000 deep RecursionError with nothing written),
`store_membership_native_not_posix.rs` (the gap, class os).
`store_membership_kills.rs`'s surrogate refusal became the built answer.
The kills cover a legacy row written for a surrogate key, `[]` and `{}`
swapped, the native put before the legacy one, `_clear_native` after a
native put, a log read kind by kind, a checkout compared outside SQLite,
the token drawn inside the transaction, the depth budget moved by a
frame either way (a str, an int, an empty list, a surrogate and a dict's
key at the bottom, and a value only `legacy_row` walks),
`require_native_writer` checked after the legacy put (a store at
revision 4 answers StoreVersionError before any clock read, and before a
legacy row's IntegrityError), the log's kinds taken from a slice that
holds `quarantine` (every record and quarantine kind's row is absent,
with `kinds` None and named), a checkout bound with no membership kind,
a log read past the row its caller stopped at, and the reissue run
without its savepoint. The answers were read from the reference under
CPython 3.13.13. A port that binds the kinds unsorted answers every row the
same (the statement orders by `seq`), so no test can tell it apart.

No regular expression is involved. Left for later units: binding the
membership model's seams (`MembershipStore`, `MembershipLog`,
`ScopeReader`) to the store (store_membership-3).

## The search pool, by caller

`store::pool::PoolReader` draws the pool a caller's request ranks from a
store file opened read only, as `handlers.search.resolve_search_pool`
draws it, and `SearchPool::rank` ranks it as `_rank_pool` does
(`search.search` over the pool, priced with the pool's statistics, the
configured half-life and lane, no rescue leg):

- `PoolReader::new(&StoreFile)` (through the process's document
  frequency memo) or `PoolReader::with_memo(&StoreFile, &DocFreqMemo)`;
  `resolve_search_pool(query, &Filters, size, digest_fingerprint) ->
  Result<SearchPool, PoolError>`: the first `size` rows the request
  admits (`POOL_SIZE` 200) in the full-text index's order for the query
  (`bm25()`, then row number), or newest first for a query empty after
  `str.strip`, each read into the record model as `light_many` reads it,
  the rows decided through the memo as `_admitted_candidates` decides
  them (the index's best 800, or the whole ranking a batch at a time, or
  the newest 800 at a time: unit poolmemo, in the memo's section);
- `Filters` (scopes, excluded scopes, admission, client, model):
  `search.candidate_admitted` over each row's admission inputs (scopes, the
  project its `homes` row names, the declared writer);
- `SearchPool::statistics(terms)`: `Store.ranking_statistics` through the
  memo (the admitted collection's size, each term's document frequency in
  the body and in the body or scopes, the admitted rows' average BM25
  length from the digest; inside a transaction the uncached read, with no
  average);
- `SearchPool::rank(query, now, mode, max_results, stats_seen)`;
  `clamp_search_width`, `MAX_SEARCH_RESULTS`.

The caller arrives resolved, as data: `pool::Admission` holds what the
reference's `admission.Admission` answers for one store's rows (each
project's admission, and a global record's by its scope list); membership,
`location.resolve_caller` and git are not ported. Anchoring is not read:
in the reference it reaches only each hit's drift report. Not here: each
hit's signals (staleness, drift, claim checks), relations, `expand_top`,
`since_prior_session`, the search's log row, the response.

What differs, by design of a read-only port (`pool.rs`'s module docs
have the whole list). The average BM25 length comes from the digest, and
any write leaves the digest behind the log: the reference's next search
brings it current (`digest_mark(build=False)`, a write) and reads its
lengths, and this port brings the same rows forward in memory over the
same log rows (each mutated id's entry rewritten from its memory row, or
dropped), writing nothing. Where `digest_mark` answers None (no digest
state, another fingerprint, a payload or record that does not read) there
is no average here either. The reference answers None for a digest
behind also when SQLite itself cannot write the store (a read-only file,
a busy lock); a `Store.open` that the key ring marks read-only still
catches the digest up and writes it. This port answers as a reference
whose SQLite can write. The reference pays the catch-up once and writes
it; this port, which never writes the digest, pays it each time the
memo reads the store's inputs (once per memory head for the process,
while the memo keeps the store). Its cost is linear in the unseen rows
(`catching_up_is_linear_in_the_unseen_rows`); a payload of 20 MB in an
unseen row costs about 300 MB while it is parsed. An unseen row's id is
read through `str()` for a string, an int, null, a bool or a float, and
its payload from TEXT or from UTF-8 bytes (a leading BOM dropped, as
`json.loads` does for bytes; a TEXT payload with a BOM and bytes that are
not UTF-8 give no average, as there). Not ported, giving no average where
the reference answers: an id that is a list or an object, and a payload
in UTF-16 or UTF-32 bytes. The
digest fingerprint (`store_digest.fingerprint`, which reads the
supersession rules) is passed in, not computed; with none the digest is
never trusted. The rows' admission inputs and each term's hits are the
process's document frequency memo's (`store::docfreq`), keyed by the
store's path as opened and its id, at the memory head, with the
fingerprint in the key where it is not the one this build computes. The reference reads pool records with
`seed_tokens=index_spelled_here()` (token streams split from `body_fts`
where the log's tokenizer stamp is this build's); this port reads the
stamp as the reference does and tokenizes the body, which agrees wherever
`body_fts` is the stamped tokenizer's spelling of the body, as on every
row the reference writes. `rank`'s
half-life (30 days) and lane (on) are constants because
`config.FIXED_SETTINGS` fixes both. A scope list holding anything but
strings is refused (TypeError); `int()` of a digest row's number or
length is Python's (a REAL length truncates, a TEXT row number that is no
integer is ValueError), past 64 bits OverflowError.

The fixture. `search_store.jsonl` (generator `gen_store_path`) holds the
schema every store here shares and, per store, its tables' rows (the
tables a search reads, every other table empty, the values the clock and
the key mint give masked, the log cut to the rows the digest's mark and
catch-up read; the generator checks each copy holds the same memory rows
(row number, body, updated, scopes, writer) in the same newest-first order,
keeps each mutation's record id, ranks its queries, reads
the same admission inputs and digest rows, finds the digest in the same
state and names the same mutations after its mark, as the store did), the
SQL a case applies after the rows, each caller's admission as data, and
the digest fingerprint. Floats are recorded as IEEE-754 bits. The stores:

- the main one (18 records): 81 run lines of 7 runs (offline and three
  callers on two surfaces) and 36 `hostile` lines of 2 (FTS5 operators
  and column filters, quotes, NUL, punctuation, stopwords only, empty,
  whitespace, 46,000 and 20,000 characters; the reference raised on none);
- `big` (236 records, 222 active matches for one query, bodies repeating
  every 12 records for exact `bm25()` ties, `updated` repeating every 4,
  tombstones, one and two scopes, five writer shapes including client
  `""`, records homed in two projects, `global` and nowhere): 51 lines
  over scope, excluded-scope, client and model filters and their
  combinations, an empty scope list, pool sizes and widths (200/10,
  50/5, 5/10, 1/1, 300/50, 20/10) and callers including the write
  review's surface (`review_strata`), whose admission tells a global
  record's scope lists apart;
- 19 small stores whose digest is current, one, three or fifteen writes
  behind, behind by an update, a tombstone or a restore, under another
  fingerprint (alone and one write behind), gone, or holds a REAL length
  or a TEXT row number, or is behind by one unseen row whose id is null,
  a float or true, or whose payload is UTF-8 bytes (with and without a
  BOM), bytes that are not UTF-8, or text with a BOM: 4 lines each. The reference raises ValueError for
  the TEXT row number and reads the REAL length as `int(3.5)`.

`golden_search_store` rebuilds each store, opens it and compares 639 runs
on the main store and 127 store lines (pool, every statistics call, hits),
and holds the 81 offline runs to `search.jsonl`'s in-memory ranking.
SQLite: the reference draws the pool with its SQLite (3.50.4 here, 3.53.1
on the runners), the native build with 3.54.1; the pool's order is
`bm25()` then row number, and FTS5's scores were bit-equal across those
versions on every query so far (`sqlite_spike`, `store_real`).

Timing the pool and its ranking: every main-store run line's query and
mode, offline and for each caller's admission (567 calls a pass), store
opened once:

```sh
cargo test --offline --release --test golden_search_store -- --ignored --nocapture
../.venv/bin/python tools/bench_search_store.py 20
```

On an Apple M-series laptop at 20 passes, three runs each: the reference
63.58, 63.32 and 63.35 ms a pass (median), native 18.31, 18.35 and 18.22
ms (about 3.5 times). The prediction of at most a fifth is missed. The
two sides do not do the same work: the reference also runs
`search.search`'s second filter pass (`_filter_candidates`, with
`admission.prime`) and builds a snippet per hit, and keeps its token
cache and each term's document frequencies warm between calls, while
native builds its ranker's corpus and reads each term's hits from the
index on every call. Per call native spends about 8 microseconds in the
FTS5 match, 11 reading and validating the pool's records, 5 building the
corpus, 5 in the statistics' index reads and 5 ranking.

## What a caller is admitted to see

`store::caller` reproduces, as pure functions over data, what the
reference's `admission.Admission` answers for a caller its resolution
describes: `membership_records.relation` and `admitted` (design 3.5's
table: `IN_PROJECT_POLICY`, `OUTSIDE_POLICY`, the seven `SURFACES`, the
write review's `review_strata` among them), `Admission.nothing`,
`project_home`, `admits_project`, `admits_row`, `admitted_projects`,
`admits_global`, and the membership reads they make (`canonical`,
`chain_of`, `named`, `project`, `projects`).

- `Resolution::from_json(text)` / `from_value`: the dataclass as
  `dataclasses.asdict` writes it (a field missing or of another type is a
  `ResolutionError`).
- `Membership::read(&Connection)` (a `StoreFile`'s or a pool reader's
  connection; it only reads), `Membership::from_projects(rows)`.
- `Admission::new(surface, Option<&Resolution>, &Membership)`, its
  answers (`Result<_, ModelError>`), and `pool_admission(&Connection) ->
  pool::Admission`: the data form the native search takes, computed for
  every project a `homes` row or the projects table names and `global`,
  and every scope list of a memory or a live digest row, so a recorded
  resolution drives `PoolReader::resolve_search_pool`. The data form stays
  as it was.

Inputs. Of the resolution: `outcome`, `project`, `chain`, `tenant` (the
other fields are parsed and not read). Of the store: the `projects`
table's `id`, `name`, `merged_into`, `provisional`, `parent`, `tenant`
(the read selects all nine columns, so a missing one or text that is not
UTF-8 in any raises), and the `project` rows of `native_membership_rows`
(`key_text`, `row_text`), which replace the legacy row their key names.
Nothing else: no `homes` row is read for an answer (a record's recorded
project is the question's input), no checkout, view or witness.

The rule in plain words. A caller whose resolution raised is admitted
nothing; one whose outcome is `indeterminate` or `deferred`, or that
names no project, says so in `nothing`. A record's home is its recorded
project with merges followed (`canonical`; a falsy result falls back to
the recorded id), that project's chain (itself and its parents, each
parent's merges followed, nearest first) and its own row's tenant; it is
`unresolved` while that row's `provisional` is `indeterminate` or
`deferred`. The relation: `unknown` for a caller with no project;
`global_named` for a `global` record whose `projects:<name>` scopes
(case-folded) name a project on the caller's chain (or the caller's
project when its chain is empty) and the caller is not outside any
project, else `global`; `other_tenant` when the home's tenant and the
caller's differ (empty reads as none); `other_project` for every project
record when the caller is outside any project; `same_project` when the
home's project is on the caller's chain; `sub_project` when the caller's
project is on the home's chain; `other_project` otherwise. The surface
admits the relation by the in-project or the outside policy, except that
an unresolved home is admitted only as `same_project`, and `unknown`
never. A record with no home row is admitted nowhere.

Special cases, each a fixture table: merges and merge chains (a merge
into a missing row, into `global`, into `""`); parents and nested
sub-projects (a parent merged away, a missing parent); boundaries and
tenants (an empty tenant); provisional and unresolved projects (merged
into, and below, an unresolved one); names folded (`ß`, final sigma) and
names held only by a native row; cycles in `merged_into` and `parent` (a
cycle stops where it would revisit a project) and 40-long chains; native
rows that replace, add, and malformed ones that still remove the legacy
row they key; a missing native table, a native table missing a column,
a missing projects table or column; values of other types in a table
with no column affinity (Python's `==`, truthiness and `str()` decide);
a blob id or mixed number and text ids beside a native row (TypeError);
text that is not UTF-8 (OperationalError).

A native row's JSON held as bytes is read as `json.loads` reads bytes:
`json.detect_encoding` (the UTF-32, UTF-16 and UTF-8 BOMs, then the NUL
pattern of the first four bytes, or of two), then the decode with
``surrogatepass`` (a surrogate's UTF-8 spelling and a lone UTF-16 or
UTF-32 surrogate are kept); bytes that do not decode (an odd UTF-16
length, a UTF-32 length not a multiple of four, a code point past
U+10FFFF, any other invalid UTF-8) make the row malformed, which still
removes the legacy row of its key. The reads are linear in the rows: the
native keys are hashed as Python's dict files them (an int, an integral
float and a bool of one value are one key). A resolution whose `tenant`
is not text is not a `Resolution` here. Any SQLite error of the read is
OperationalError, as Python's `sqlite3` classes the ones these reads meet.

The fixture. `caller_admission.jsonl` (generator `gen_caller_admission`,
no gate: ASCII and casefold-stable names, no ranking): 23 table cases,
each a store `Store.create` built, its rows put through `put_membership`
or written by direct SQL (the case says which), the two tables recorded
as rows with typed cells, one of them native rows whose JSON is bytes in
every encoding `json.detect_encoding` names, whole, odd, truncated and
empty; 145 resolution cases (none, `global`,
`indeterminate`, `deferred`, and each table's own of `silent`, `ask` and
`new`), each with `nothing` and, per surface, `admits_project` of every
key, `admits_row` of every scope list and home, `admitted_projects` and
`admits_global`; `project_home` of every key per table. Its header holds
`search_store.jsonl`'s main store's projects rows and its three callers'
resolutions (the scratch path in `lines` written `<scratch>`).

Tests. `golden_caller_admission` (class i on `caller_admission.jsonl`:
`every_case_answers_as_the_reference`, 168 cases; class iii on
`search_store.jsonl`: `main_store_callers_compute_the_tabulated_admission`,
which computes the six admissions of the main store's callers from their
resolutions, holds each to the tabulated one, and draws and ranks the
486 caller runs through them). `caller_admission_robustness`: cycles,
100,000-long chains closed into cycles, every value type in every
column, missing tables, columns and rows, malformed, nested and large
native rows, native bytes of every short shape, resolutions that do not
parse: typed outcomes, no panic; and `reading_native_rows_is_linear`
(best of five reads of 2,000 and 20,000 legacy rows each replaced by a
native row: at most sixty times as long plus 50 ms, where linear is ten
and quadratic a hundred).

## The settings

`toml::loads` is `Lib/tomllib/_parser.py` rule for rule, over the bytes of
the `&str` (every syntax character is ASCII, so positions and slices agree
with the reference's code-point indexes; a message's column is counted in
code points). Three outcomes are not `TOMLDecodeError` in the reference and
are kept apart (`toml::Error`): an integer of more than 4300 decimal digits
is `int()`'s ValueError, which `tomllib` does not wrap, so the product
reports it without its `malformed config in <path>:` prefix; and nesting
past the stack is RecursionError, which the product does not catch at all
(`config check` and `config show` stop with a traceback; here
`Err(Raised { class: "RecursionError", .. })`). The reference's depth limit
is its stack: from a fresh interpreter's top it takes 497 nested arrays and
331 nested inline tables (two and three Python frames a level) and fails
past them, and fewer when called deeper. Here a level costs the same two
or three and more than 995 is refused, which is the top-of-stack limit
exactly for either kind alone; a mixed nesting near the limit, or the
reference called deep in a stack, can differ (the corpus keeps its deep
documents at 50 and 150 levels and at 400 and more). The parse runs on a
thread with a 16 MiB stack, so an unoptimised build fits the deepest
document the budget admits on any caller's thread; what it returns is at
most 497 levels deep, is dropped without recursion, and is walked by the
reports within that depth (`config_robustness` runs check, show, path and
the audit over values at the budget on a 2 MiB thread). A hostile document costs
linear time (`config_robustness`: a 45 MB document of a million keys, a
6-million-item array and a 10 MB string loads in 4.5 s unoptimised; 2,000
integers of 4300 digits in 1.1 s; a million `[` in 1.3 ms).

`config` takes everything a load reads as data: the environment is a map
(`config::Env`), every file and path operation goes through `config::Fs`
(the tests hand in the generator's world; `report::SystemFs`, over the
real file system, is not for use yet, below), and the platform's locations (`config::Locations`: the
user config file, the managed file or registry value, the default keys and
state directories, the system prefixes) are inputs. The loader's one-shot
notices (`_DEPRECATED_KEY_WARNED_PATHS`) are a `config::Guards` the caller
holds. The fixture records each command as a CLI process of its own runs
it, with the set cleared before each of check, show and the audit, and the
tests give each command a fresh `Guards`; a caller that runs several
commands in one process and holds one `Guards` across them gets the
reference's in-process behaviour (a notice logged once is not logged
again). A path built from text (a location variable, `[storage]
directory`) is spelled as `str(Path(text))` spells it (`config::pure_path`:
`PurePath._parse_path` and `_format_parsed_parts` over `posixpath` and
`ntpath.splitroot`, compared under both flavours with CPython's spelling of
800 texts in `settings_python.json`'s `pure_paths`), and a relative one is read
against the working directory. The flavour is the world's
(`Locations::flavour`), never the platform the crate was built for, so the
tests' POSIX world reads the same on every runner and a Windows caller
passes `Flavour::Windows`. A NUL in a path that is stat'd or resolved
raises as `os.lstat` does (`config::nul_in_path`), and a first segment
`~name` that does not expand raises `Path.expanduser()`'s RuntimeError
(`config::no_home`): `config path` stops on it, check finds nothing
(`_system_dir_findings` catches it) and show never reaches it. The test
world has one user, so a `~name` that does expand is not covered. Its file
system has a root (`/`, and `//`, which `Path` keeps as two), and the
fixture holds no case that resolves above `<scratch>`: the reference prints
the host's own directory there, and `gen_config._within_scratch` refuses a
case whose output names any place outside `<scratch>` but the root. The
recorded config files are the text the reference read: the scrubber sees
only what the commands printed. The three
commands return `(text, exit code)`, the text being `json.dumps(document,
indent=2, ensure_ascii=True, default=str)` and a line feed; `Err` is an
exception the reference lets escape. The difflib guess (`_close`) is
`SequenceMatcher` with autojunk, ported (`config::difflib`), and the
`utf-8-sig` decode reproduces CPython's `UnicodeDecodeError` text, its
position counted after a byte-order mark.

The settings fixtures are split by how far their bytes hold.
`settings.json` (ungated) holds what reads the same under every Python the
suite runs and on every platform: the catalogue, the fixed settings, the
coercion table, `config path` in the generator's own environment, and the
cases worded by bettermemory alone (each regenerated identically under
3.11.15, 3.12.13 and 3.13.13 here; 3.14 and Windows were not run, and the
reason to expect the same there is that nothing in them is the
interpreter's or the OS's wording, and the paths they print are under the
run's directory, which the scrubber rewrites). `settings_python.json`
(Python-gated) holds the cases whose text is the interpreter's (a `tomllib`
or codec message, `int()`'s digit limit, a float conversion, `repr`,
RecursionError, bare NaN) and `pure_paths` (3.11's pathlib spells 307 of
the 800 otherwise). `settings_paths.json` (POSIX only: not generated on
Windows, read by `cfg(unix)` tests, recorded as class "os" by
`settings_paths_not_posix.rs` elsewhere) holds the `config path`
environments and the cases whose directory is expanded and resolved;
`settings_paths_python.json` (both) holds a NUL in a path, whose ValueError
3.11 words otherwise. `toml.jsonl` is Python-gated: its 927 documents read
the same under 3.11.15 and 3.12.13 (only the header's `python` differs),
though their `tomllib` sources differ from 3.13.13's by 14 lines.

Accidents of the reference reproduced and pinned (the settings fixtures):

- `[daemon] port = inf` (any integer setting read from an infinite float)
  is an OverflowError that escapes `_parse_one`'s `except ValueError`:
  `config check` and `config show` stop with a traceback (case
  `inf_port`). `port = nan` is a ValueError without the `malformed config
  in <path>:` prefix, so check's finding reads "cannot convert float NaN to
  integer; the config does not load." (case `nan_port`).
- An integer past 4300 digits in either file is reported un-prefixed, from
  `int()` (cases `int_past_the_digit_limit*`).
- The managed loader's refusal of a top-level value prints it with `repr`
  (`datetime.datetime(1979, 5, 27, 7, 32, tzinfo=...)`, `[{'enabled':
  False}]`), where every other message spells values as TOML.
- A NUL in `[storage] directory` (either file) makes `config check` stop
  with `ValueError: lstat: embedded null character in path` from
  `Path.resolve()` (`_system_dir_findings` catches OSError and
  RuntimeError only), and `config path` too wherever the directory chooses
  the store; `config show` and the audit answer (cases `nul_*`,
  `directory_*_nul`). A location variable cannot hold a NUL (`os.environ`
  refuses one, as `execve` would), so no case sets one; natively the same
  error is raised.
- `config show --json` prints a non-finite float a file holds bare, as
  `Infinity`, `-Infinity` or `NaN` (`json.dumps` with `allow_nan`), which
  is not JSON (case `non_finite_floats`).
- Configs with 494 to 497 nested arrays, or 329 to 331 nested inline
  tables, make the reference CLI stop with a RecursionError (its entry
  point runs `tomllib` a few frames down the stack; measured through
  `cli.main` in a fresh interpreter), where native loads them: the budget
  is `tomllib`'s at the top of a stack, which `toml.jsonl` pins.
- `config check` reads the managed file through `read_config_file`, so its
  `unreadable` finding says `malformed config in`, while the load (`show`'s
  error, check's `load_error`) says `malformed managed config in`.

Not ported: reading the Windows registry value (`ManagedSource::Registry`
takes its text, or its error, from the caller; no crate here reads the
registry), Cygwin's and MSYS2's planted-file refusal (`_refuse_planted`),
the text (non-`--json`) renderings, and
argument parsing. `report::SystemFs` is not for use until a later unit
compares it with `pathlib` on a real tree (a symlinked home, `..` through
a symlink, `~user`, relative paths, a config path that is a directory, an
unreadable file, prefixes that differ in case): its `resolve` pops `..`
after canonicalising, `expanduser` takes only `~` and `~/`, `under` is
case-sensitive and `is_dir` follows symlinks. No entry point uses it by
default; every compared case goes through the test's world.

### The first-run write (unit config-2)

`config::create::load_config_creating` is `config.load_config(path,
create=True)` (`config.py` 1319-1367 at 606ebe94): `parent.mkdir(parents=True,
exist_ok=True)`, then `Path.exists`, and where it says no file,
`_fsutil.atomic_write_bytes(path, DEFAULT_CONFIG.encode())` with neither
mode, the notice `[bettermemory] created default config at {path}` on
stderr, and `_overlay_managed(read_config_file(path), path)`, the same
overlay `load_config` (create=False) uses, now `config::overlay_managed`.
It returns whether it wrote and the load; the caller prints
`create::created_notice(path)` when it wrote, and the notice stands even
when the read then fails (the reference prints before reading). A file
gone between the write and the read is FileNotFoundError, not the
defaults `create=False` reads a missing file as.

| function | reference | needs from the machine | status |
|---|---|---|---|
| `create::DEFAULT_CONFIG` | `DEFAULT_CONFIG`, 67-286 | none (`default_config.toml`, `include_str!`, 11,870 bytes, checked by sha256) | built |
| `create::load_config_creating` | `load_config` with `create=True`, 1340-1367 | `create::Create` and `config::Fs` | built |
| `create::SystemCreate::mkdir_parent` | `Path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` | `std::fs::create_dir`, `is_dir` | built |
| `create::SystemCreate::exists` | `Path.exists` (3.13) | `std::fs::metadata` | built |
| `create::SystemCreate::write_atomic` | `atomic_write_bytes(path, data)` | `store::write::replace_retrying` | built |

The effects go through a trait of their own, `config::create::Create`
(make the parents, `exists`, the atomic write), so `config::Fs`, `World`
and every test world are unchanged. `SystemCreate` is the real one; the
golden tests run it in a scratch directory under the system's temporary
directory, reading through `report::SystemFs`, which for a plain file
under that directory reads as `Path.read_bytes` does. Decisions:

- `mkdir_parent` is `pathlib.Path.mkdir` ported step for step (a
  FileNotFoundError makes the parent first, any other error stands only
  where the path is not a directory), not `create_dir_all`, so the class
  of a failure is the reference's: a parent that is a file is
  FileExistsError naming it, a grandparent that is a file is
  NotADirectoryError naming the parent's parent. A path with no parent
  text makes `.`.
- `exists` is CPython 3.13's: a stat error other than a missing entry,
  ENOTDIR, ELOOP, EBADF (on Windows the winerrors 2, 3 and 6, which CPython
  maps to ENOENT and EBADF, and 21, 123 and 1921) raises, EINVAL and
  Windows' ERROR_DIRECTORY (267) among them; a NUL answers false. 3.14 answers false for a file in a directory this
  account cannot search, and its write then fails; 3.11 to 3.13 raise
  PermissionError from `exists`. Both end in a PermissionError out of
  `load_config`, which is all the fixture keeps.
- The new file's mode is the temporary file's, 0o600 whatever the umask
  (`tempfile.mkstemp` there, `store::create::new_private_file` here), recorded on
  POSIX as the reference produced it, not assumed. `replace_retrying` adds
  the reference's Windows retry of a rename a reader holds open: as
  `_fsutil.replace_atomic`, only the rename is tried again, on
  PermissionError, at most 5 attempts with a pause doubling from 10 ms.
- A NUL in the final name passes `mkdir` (the parents are made, and an
  error on the way raises as there) and raises
  `ValueError('open: embedded null character in path')` from the write (the
  3.12 to 3.14 text; 3.11 says `embedded null byte`, so the fixture keeps
  the class only); a NUL in a parent raises from `mkdir`.
- On Windows an error reads `[WinError N] text: 'path'`, as Python's
