### Unit pyre-6a, built (`pyre::regex`)

`pyre/regex.rs` holds `re.Pattern` and `re.Match` for the methods that
find matches. A `Regex` is built from the pattern's own text and flags as
`re.compile` builds it, and its methods call `exec::exec` and nothing
else of the matcher. It holds 497 lines of Rust source. The reference
is `Lib/re/__init__.py` `_compile` (the flag and type checks) and
`Modules/_sre/sre.c` of 3.13.13 (`pattern_new_match`, `scanner_search`,
`pattern_findall`), whose C text is not on the build machine: their
answers are compared by value with the interpreter.

| function | reproduces | needs | status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Regex::new`, `new_str`, `new_bytes` | `re.compile(pattern, flags)` for a `str` or a bytes pattern: `parse` (with `fix_flags` and the engine's refusals), `lower`, `exec::supports`, then each distinct class compiled once by `compile_class` | `parse`, `lower`, `charset`, `exec` | built |
| `Regex::pattern`, `flags`, `groups`, `names` | `Pattern.pattern`, `Pattern.flags` (the state's flags: the flags given, UNICODE for a `str` pattern, the leading inline flags), `Pattern.groups`, `Pattern.groupindex` by number | nothing | built |
| `match`, `fullmatch`, `search` and their `try_*` | the three calls with `pos` and `endpos`, answered as a `Match` | `exec` | built |
| `finditer`, `try_finditer` | `scanner_search` in a loop: a search from `pos`, then from the end of each match, with `must_advance` after an empty one | `exec`, `advance` | built |
| `findall`, `try_findall` | `pattern_findall`: the same scan; the whole match with no group, the group with one, the tuple of groups with more, an empty piece for a group that took no part | `exec`, `advance` | built |
| `advance` | the attempt after an empty match (`must_advance` read at `SUCCESS` in `SRE(match)`) | `lower::Program` | built |
| `Match` (`regs`, `span`, `group`, `pos`, `endpos`, `lastindex`, `lastgroup`) | `pattern_new_match`: unset groups as `(-1, -1)`, `pos` and `endpos` as clamped, `lastgroup` the name of `lastindex` | nothing | built |
| `CallError` | `_sre`'s TypeError for a text of the other type, with its message; `Memory` and `Budget` of `try_*` | nothing | built |

Decisions and their reasons:

- **The attempt that must advance is a second copy of the program.**
  After an empty match at `p`, `_sre` runs the next attempt at `p` with
  `must_advance` set: its `SUCCESS` fails when the position is still `p`,
  and backtracking goes on (`re.findall('a*?', 'aab')` is `['', 'a', '',
  'a', '', '']`; a scan that steps to `p + 1` loses the `a`s). Only that
  first attempt carries the flag; when it fails the search goes on from
  `p + 1` as usual. `exec` has no such rule and its file is not changed
  by this unit, so `advance` builds, once per pattern, a program of two
  copies: copy B is the program as it is; copy A is the same nodes before
  anything is consumed. In A, `MATCH` is `FAIL`, a unit leads into B, and
  a single-unit repeat of minimum 0 is split, in its own order of trial,
  into its counts from 1 (into B) and its count 0 (staying in A): a
  greedy one tries the counts from 1 first, a lazy one the count 0 first.
  A lookaround's body stays in B, since what it reads is not consumed.
  The first path that reaches `MATCH` in B is the first path of the
  reference's attempt that ends past `p`, with the same marks. Every
  attempt of a scan otherwise is a plain `exec` search, so the step
  counts of the two differ only on this attempt.
- **A class is compiled once.** `exec` asks a `ClassTest` for membership
  with the arena's `Class` itself; `Regex` compiles every distinct class
  of its program when it is built and finds it again by the address of
  its members (an `Arc` that unrolled copies share) and its flags. A
  class the compiler refuses is a failed build (`RegexError::Class`).
- **A failed build is a value.** `RegexError` carries what `parse`,
  `lower` and `compile_class` answer; what `exec::supports` refuses is
  carried by its name (`Debug`), so the unit names no variant of
  `exec::Unsupported` and builds unchanged once lookarounds are run. A
  pattern of the reference held as a static is a
  `LazyLock<Result<Regex, RegexError>>` built from its text.
- **Flags past a C `int` overflow.** `_sre.compile` takes the flags as
  a C `int`, so flags of 2**31 or more raise OverflowError after `parse`
  and `_code` have run; `Regex::build` answers
  `RegexError::FlagsOverflow` at the same point, after `lower`.
- **A refusal can come before `re.error`.** Where `parse` refuses a
  possessive repeat or a conditional group (units pyre-3a to pyre-3c)
  before a later position at which `re` raises `re.error`, the build
  answers `Build(Unsupported)` where the reference raises: `'.?+?'` is
  `Possessive` at 2 against "multiple repeat at position 3", `'(?(1)a)'`
  is `Conditional` at 0 against "invalid group reference 1 at position
  3". Both refuse to build; the kind and position differ. The order of
  those checks belongs to `parse`, left for a later unit.
- **`groups` and `groupdict` answer spans.** `Match::groups(default)`
  answers each group's span from 1, or `default` where it took no part;
  `Match::groupdict(names, default)` pairs each name of `Regex::names`,
  in group order as `groupindex` holds them, with the same.
- **The text's type is checked as `_sre` checks it.** A method takes any
  `Subject` (`[u32]` for a `str`, `[u8]` for bytes); the other type is
  `CallError::Type`, whose text is the TypeError's.
- **The window.** `pos` and `endpos` are `isize` (`Py_ssize_t`), passed
  to `exec` unchanged. `endpos` has no default: a caller passes
  `isize::MAX` for `re`'s default of `sys.maxsize`. `Match.pos` and
  `Match.endpos` are the clamped values
  (`re.compile('a').search('xa', -5, 99).pos` is 0). A scan stops when
  its start passes the clamped `endpos`, so a reversed window finds
  nothing through `finditer` and `findall`.
- **Plain and `try_*`.** The plain methods have no budget and end on an
  allocation failure as the rest of the crate ends
  (`handle_alloc_error`); `try_*` answer `Memory` and `Budget`. In a scan
  the budget holds for each run of the matcher, not for the whole scan.
- `findall` hands back pieces of the text (`Vec<u32>` or `Vec<u8>`),
  never `None`: a group that took no part is an empty piece, as `''` is
  in the reference, while `Match::group` answers `None` for it.

Patterns: this unit reproduces no call site of the reference. Its sweep
builds the first 60 of the reference's literal patterns
(`gen_pyre_atom._literals`) that the engine builds and that hold no
lookaround, from their own text, and pins all five methods on them; the
engine's inventory gains nothing new.

answers: the spans and `lastindex` of a match, those of each match of
`finditer`, and the code points of each piece of `findall`.

| part | rows |
| --- | --- |
| `api.sweep` | 60 inventory patterns, each over every text of at most 10 code points over a two-symbol alphabet (7 over three symbols) taken from the pattern's own literals: every window in `[-1, n + 1]` up to 6 code points (4 over three symbols), four windows past it, by count and SHA-256. The ordered windows are in `pyre_api.jsonl` (in `pyre_unicode.jsonl` when the pattern folds case or its alphabet goes past ASCII); the reversed windows, whose `match` and `fullmatch` answers are 3.13.13's, in `pyre_python.jsonl` |
| `api.fuzz` | the decision's fuzz: the first 300 patterns of `gen_pyre_parse._fuzz_case` the engine builds, each with a digest of its five methods over every text over `ab` of at most 4 code points and every ordered window, and the first 100 it refuses or `re` rejects, by name |
| `api.kill` | calls written out: the attempt after an empty match, `findall`'s shape, a group that took no part, `lastgroup`, clamped and reversed windows, with `pos`, `endpos` and `lastgroup` of each match |

The sweep does not take every window of every text of up to 12 code
points, as the task planned: that is about 25 times the calls, which the
Rust tests in debug do not finish in minutes (pyre-5a made the same cut).

| `pyre_api_robustness` | 5 | a scan of 200,000 empty matches, every window bound, an exponential shape under a budget, nesting and 3,000 groups, scans linear at ten times the text |

### Unit pyre-6b, built (`pyre::replace`)

`pyre/replace.rs` holds a second `impl Regex` block: `Pattern.sub`,
`subn` and `split` as CPython 3.13.13 answers them
(`Modules/_sre/sre.c` `pattern_subx` and `pattern_split`, called by
`Lib/re/__init__.py` `sub`, `subn` and `split` through `_compile`). The C
text is not on the build machine; the answers are compared by value with
the interpreter. The file holds 228 lines of Rust source; `regex.rs`
gains 12 lines and loses 7 (the scan's bound and two visibilities).

| function | reproduces | needs | status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Regex::sub`, `subn`, `try_subn` | `pattern_subx` with a literal: the text between matches kept, each match replaced, the rest appended; the count of replacements | `Regex`'s scan | built |
| `Regex::sub_with`, `subn_with`, `try_subn_with` | `pattern_subx` with a callable: each match handed over as a `Match` (`pos` 0, `endpos` the text's length), its answer appended, `None` as nothing | `Regex`'s scan, `Match` | built |
| `Regex::split`, `try_split` | `pattern_split`: the text before each match, then each group (`None` where it took no part), then the rest, even when empty | `Regex`'s scan | built |
| `ReplaceError` | `Template` for a literal holding a backslash; `Call` for what the scan answers (the type check, `Memory`, `Budget`) | nothing | built |

Decisions and their reasons:

- **One scan.** `sub` and `split` run the scan of `finditer`
  (`Regex::scan`, with its attempt after an empty match); it gains a
  bound `limit` checked before each search, as the loops of
  `pattern_subx` and `pattern_split` check their count (`while (!count
  || n < count)`), so no search runs once the count is met and a budget
  that a later search would pass is not met. `finditer` and `findall`
  pass `usize::MAX`.
- **The count.** It is `Py_ssize_t`: 0 is no bound and a negative count
  finds nothing (`re.compile('a').subn('-', 'aaaa', -1)` is
  `('aaaa', 0)`, `split` answers the whole text). The text's type is
  still checked: it is checked by `state_init` before the loop.
- **A template is refused, first.** A literal that holds a backslash
  (0x5C, in a `str` or a bytes literal) is a template in the reference
  (`re._compile_template`); the engine builds none (decision section 4:
  the only template of the reference, `gitconfig.py:1718`, is built by
  hand, and the 25 literal replacements hold no backslash).
  `pattern_subx` compiles the template before `state_init`, so its
  `re.error` comes before the TypeError of a text of the other type; the
  refusal is answered at the same point, before the type check. The
  refusal type is local to this file, not a `tree::Feature`: it belongs
  to the call, not to the pattern.
- **Types are the signature's.** The literal, the text and a function's
  answer share one unit type (`u32` for a `str`, `u8` for bytes), so the
  reference's TypeError for a replacement of the other type, or for a
  function answering neither `str` nor `None`, cannot be asked.
- **Plain and `try_*`** as in pyre-6a: the budget holds for each run of
  the matcher.

Patterns: this unit reproduces no call site of the reference; the
engine's inventory gains nothing. The call sites of `sub` and `split`
(25 literal and 4 function replacements, the splits of `supersession`,
`search_lexicon`, `models` and others) are ported with their own units.

### Unit pyre-7, built (the inventory proof, tests only)

The unit adds no crate source. It proves the engine on every pattern of
the reference it is to run, each built from the reference's own text
and flags, and reproduces no reference function of its own: what it
pins is `re.compile`, `Pattern.match`, `fullmatch`, `search`,
`finditer` and `findall` of CPython 3.13.13 over those patterns, and
`sub`, `subn` and `split` over those the reference uses through them.

**The sites.** `tests/contract/_pyre_sites.py` finds them anew at each
generation: an `ast` scan of `src/bettermemory` for every call of `re`
that takes a pattern (216 sites), and the patterns the modules build at
import, read in a child interpreter with `re`'s functions wrapped (262
instances, every import-time builder among them: `_PHRASE_REGEXES`,
`_ENVELOPES`, `_ALIAS_ANCHOR_PATTERNS`, `_PATTERN_OVERRIDES`). A site is
named without a line number (file, enclosing functions, the name the call
is bound to, an ordinal). Each is one of three kinds: `hand` (90, matched
by a hand-written matcher already built, listed by id in
`gen_pyre_inventory.HAND`; pyre-8 proves them), `builder` (5, a pattern
built per call from data, `BUILDERS`), `engine` (121, every other).
The child interpreter puts the scanned tree first on its path and fails
when `bettermemory` was imported from anywhere else, so a copy of the
tree or a non-editable install reads the tree scanned, not the one
installed.

**The methods.** Each site records the calls it is used through, as the
method, the count of positional arguments and the keywords
(`split/2`, `search/1:pos`): the function itself for a call of `re`
other than `compile`, and for `compile` every pattern method called on
the name it is bound to, in the binding scope and, for a module-level
name, in every module importing it by name. A pattern kept in a list or
a dict, or handed on otherwise, has no method read (57 sites, most of
them lists such as `_TODO_PATTERNS`).

**The tripwire.** The site lines (id, kind, eight hex digits of the
SHA-256 of the site's instances, the methods) are pinned by
`SITES_SHA256`: a new site, a changed pattern text or flag, a method
added or gone, a `pos`, `endpos`, count or `maxsplit` argument added or
gone, or a site gone fails the generation and names the lines that
differ from the committed `inventory.sites` row. The tripwire runs in
the generator; the Rust test reads the row's shape (every engine site
has a pattern row, every method is one of the eight). A new site is classed and the constant moved in
the same change.

**The texts.** Each distinct `(pattern, flags)` of the engine sites is
one row (168). Its texts are every text over the pattern's own cell
representatives (its literals, each range's ends and the code point past
it, a member of each category, a fixed base) up to the largest length
with at most 300 texts, then 300 texts joined from up to 12 fragments
drawn from the tree (a match or a near miss) and alphabet symbols by the
seeded `Lcg` of `gen_pyre_tree`, then the witnesses the mutants needed.
The Rust test regenerates the texts by the same rule (`texts` in both)
and compares the five methods over the windows `(0, n)` and `(1, n)` by
count and digest. Fragments and witnesses are committed, so the Rust side
holds only the join rule, not the tree walk. A row one of whose sites
is used through `sub`, `subn` or `split` (`replace`, 14 rows) also runs
its texts through `subn` with `<>`, `subn` with the function `_swap` of
`gen_pyre_api` and `split`, each with the counts 0 and 1 (the
reference's `maxsplit=1` sites), by count and digest. The other
methods' empty matches, counts and groups are pyre-6b's sweep; this
check runs them on the reference's own patterns.

**Mutants** (generator side only, decision section 4). Each pattern is
rewritten the ways an engine could be wrong: greedy and lazy swapped, a
bound off by one, `$` for `\Z` and back, `^` for `\A`, a `\b` dropped,
the first two alternatives swapped, a flag dropped, ASCII classes. A
mutant no committed text and no text of a hidden pool four times as
large tells apart is equivalent (327); every other one (373) is told
apart by at least 20 committed texts, or the generator draws more: the
hidden texts that tell it apart become fragments, then near misses of 40
more tree witnesses (a symbol before or after, a code point dropped, the
fragment twice) and ten further seeded pools become witnesses, and a
mutant still short fails the generation. 66 witnesses were needed, most
for `$` against `\Z`, which differ only on a text that ends in a match
and one newline. The `no fold table` mutant of the decision is the ASCII
one under IGNORECASE; an engine without its fold tables is held by
pyre-1's sweeps.

**The four data-built families** (`inventory.builder`): the patterns
`_project_name_matches` and `_declared_root_spans` of `scope_match.py`,
`rf"\b{column}\b"` of `store_schema._add_membership_tables` (two sites,
one family) and `packed_names` of `githead.py`. The generator pins each
site's pattern argument as `ast.unparse` prints it, so a changed builder
fails it, and writes inputs; the Rust test builds each pattern by the
same string code with the port's `re.escape` and runs it over the input
with every prefix and suffix of a fixed list, by count and digest.

**The replay.** `native/tools/pyre_differential.py inventory FILE`
writes every text of every row with its two answer lines;
`pyre_inventory_differential_file` (ignored, `BM_PYRE_INVENTORY_DIFF`)
reads it and names the first text that differs, which turns a digest
mismatch into an input.

Every pattern builds: no inventory pattern, builder or fragment found a
refusal or a difference. Per decision rule 5 a refusal would fail
`golden_pyre_inventory`, never be respelled.

### Unit pyre-5b, built (lookarounds in `pyre::exec`)

The unit adds `_sre`'s ASSERT and ASSERT_NOT (`sre_lib.h`,
`SRE_OP_ASSERT` and `SRE_OP_ASSERT_NOT`, CPython 3.13.13) to the loop of
`Run::attempt`, established by differential against `re` since the C
source is not on the machine. `Unsupported` keeps its name with no
variant, and `supports` answers `Ok` for every program.

| function | reproduces | needs | status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Run::attempt`, `Op::Look` | ASSERT and ASSERT_NOT: the width check, the body entered at `pos - width` | nothing | built |
| `Run::attempt`, `Op::LookEnd` | the body's success: its choice points cut, the position restored | nothing | built |
| `Run::attempt`, `Frame::Look` | the body's failure: ASSERT fails, ASSERT_NOT goes on at its `next` | nothing | built |

Decisions and their reasons:

- A body runs as a sub-attempt on the same heap stack: entering it
  pushes `Frame::Look` (the node, the position, the trail's length). At
  `LookEnd` every frame above the topmost marker is dropped with it, so
  the body is atomic as sre's child match is (`(?=(a|ab))ab` leaves the
  group at `a`). A backtrack that pops the marker is the body's failure.
  The Rust call stack does not grow with nesting.
- The width of a lookbehind is checked against the string's beginning,
  not `pos`: with `pos` past the start, `(?<=a)b` on `ab` at `pos=1`
  matches and `(?<!a)b` does not. Too few characters fail ASSERT and pass
  ASSERT_NOT without running the body. A lookahead's body stops at
  `endpos` as every unit does.
- The refusal of pyre-3c (`parse::refusal`) refuses a capture inside a
  lookaround (`CaptureInLookaround`) and a choice inside a lookbehind
  (`ChoiceInLookbehind`), so no call of the crate hands the matcher a
  lookaround body holding a `Mark`. The matcher still carries `_sre`'s
  rule for one, faithful to ASSERT and ASSERT_NOT: marks and `lastindex`
  a positive body wrote stay on success and stay on the trail, so a later
  backtrack takes them back; a negative body's are taken back whether it
  matched or not, as ASSERT_NOT's `LASTMARK_RESTORE` does. When the
  negative body matched, the explicit unwind is redundant: the backtrack
  that follows unwinds every frame to a trail no longer than the
  marker's, so no answer can tell it apart, and it is kept only to
  mirror the reference. The decision
  makes every construct outside the subset a failed build and asks
  nothing of the matcher's code beyond it, so the rule is kept for the
  day the subset widens, and the tests that pin it reach the matcher
  below the refusal: from `re._parser`'s tree in the `exec.beyond.` rows,
  never through `parse`. `kills::a_lookaround_body_holds_no_mark_after_the_refusal`
  checks that every way of writing a group inside a body is refused by
  name and that no lookaround of an admitted pattern holds a `Mark`
  (for pyre-9's memo).
- Inside the subset the cut of a body's choice points shows in the
  stack, not in an answer: a body cannot be backtracked into with a
  different outcome once the position is restored, so a matcher that
  kept the body's frames answers the same and holds more frames
  (`kills::a_matched_body_leaves_no_choice_point` pins the peak).

Patterns: this unit matches no pattern of the reference by itself; the
reference's lookaround patterns wait for `Regex` (pyre-6). Seven of
them, or their shortest faithful cuts, are fixtures (`exec.kill`): the
inventory of the engine gains no entry.

#### Fixtures and tests of pyre-5b

`gen_pyre_exec.py` gains 22 sweep patterns admitted by the subset
(lookahead and lookbehind, positive and negative, at the start of the
string and at `endpos`, nested lookarounds, choices inside lookaheads,
and four cut from the reference's sentence, hex and punctuation
patterns) over every `(pos, endpos)` pair of the short texts, and 17
written-out calls: a lookbehind at `pos > 0` reading before `pos`, a
lookbehind wider than the text before it, a lookahead at `endpos`, marks
set before a failed or negated lookaround, and seven patterns of the
reference. Six sweep patterns and eight calls hold a capture inside a
lookaround (`BEYOND_PATTERNS`, `BEYOND_KILLS`): their rows are the parts
`exec.beyond.sweep` and `exec.beyond.kill`, each naming the refusal it
meets under `refused`, with answers made by `re` as every row's are.
Reversed windows go to `pyre_python.jsonl` as pyre-5a's do (28 rows, six
of them beyond). `golden_pyre_exec` builds every row's pattern through
`parse::parse` and `lower` as well: an admitted row must build the
program its tree lowers to, a beyond row must be refused with the feature
it names.

### Unit pyre-9, built (`pyre::memo`)

The memo: what one call of a pattern remembers of where the rest of the
pattern has already failed, so that the hostile texts of the reference's
patterns cost steps in proportion to their length. It ports no function
of `src/bettermemory` and changes no answer of the engine. Its reference
is the decision record of 2026-11-19 (section 4, conditions 4 to 8;
section 5 rule 6; section 8 risks 3 and 4), the design's section "The
three devices, and why none changes an answer" and the prototype
`proto_small_backtracker.py` (`_run`, `_failed_ends`, `_prepare`, the
drivers).

| function | reference | what it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `memo::Memo` (`new`, `wake`, `failed`, `set`, `rep`, `failed_ends`, `finish`) | `_prepare`, `_failed_ends`, the `failed` set and `ivs` of `_run` | one bit per (Split or Rep1 node, position), a row allocated on its first bit through `try_reserve`; per Rep1 node the run of its unit read last and one interval of failed ends; the switch |
| `memo::Way`, `Setting` | `memo_mode` (`off`, `on`, `auto`), `use_iv` | off, on from the first step, as shipped (`Auto`, the switch at `64 * (len + 64)` steps), and `After(b)` for a forced budget; the intervals on or off |
| `memo::Stats`, `last_call` | `Regex.steps` of the prototype | the steps and peak stack of a whole call (every run it made), whether the memo started and the bytes it held, for the last call of a `Regex` method on the thread |
| `memo::premises` | decision condition 6 | an exhaustive match over `Op` with no wildcard: an op added to the arena stops the build until the memo is argued sound for it |
| `exec::exec_with`, `Frame::Memo` | `_run`'s `F_MEMO` frames and reads | one run of a call that owns the memo; `exec` runs it with the memo off, so its callers and step counts are unchanged |
| `Regex::with_memo` (hidden), `Regex::scan` with one memo per call | the drivers | every public method runs as shipped; the tests set the other ways |

Decisions, with their reasons:

- The memo is owned by the call (`Regex::one` for `match`, `fullmatch`
  and `search`; `Regex::scan` for `finditer`, `findall`, `sub`, `subn`
  and `split`) and handed to each run of the matcher. The switch counts
  the call's steps across its searches: counted per search, a text with
  many matches would spend the switch once per match, which is
  quadratic (`pyre_memo_kills`: `the_switch_counts_the_whole_call`).
- Soundness. After lowering no op reads a mark and there is no counter,
  backreference or conditional (`parse::refusal`; a loop over a nullable
  body is `lower`'s `NullableLoop`), so whether the rest reaches an
  accepted end from (node, position) is a function of that pair for one
  text, one `endpos` and one acceptance rule. A bit is written only when
  its marker frame is popped by backtracking: a marker cut by
  `Op::LookEnd` (a lookaround's body matched) or left under an accepted
  match records nothing. A body's bit says the body cannot reach its
  `LookEnd` from there, which does not depend on where the lookaround was
  entered.
- The attempt that must advance runs `advance`'s program, whose nodes
  below `n` (copy B) are the plain program with the plain acceptance,
  entered only once a unit is consumed or as a lookaround's body. It
  reads and records the bits and intervals of those nodes as every
  search of the call does; copy A (nodes `n` and above) has no bit and
  no interval. This departs from the prototype's `nowrite`: with the
  attempt reading only, `(?:a|aa)*?(?<!a)` with `finditer` over a run of
  `a` stays exponential as shipped (the attempt after the empty match at
  0 tries every way to split the run; 1,542,985 steps at 24 characters,
  10,574,084 at 28), and recording copy B makes it linear, 80 steps per
  character at a megabyte (`pyre_memo_robustness`:
  `the_attempt_that_must_advance_is_linear`, and a family of
  `pyre_memo.jsonl`). The review's random differential of the recording
  attempt against `re` and against the memo off, 1,850,520 short-text
  calls under on and under a forced switch, found no difference.
  Writing copy A's bits would be sound as well (a node of copy A is only
  ever at the attempt's own start, and no later attempt of the call
  starts there) and would save nothing.
- One memo never outlives a call, so `fullmatch` and the others never
  share bits.
- Unlike the prototype, the intervals and runs also wait for the switch:
  below it a call runs exactly as before this unit, step for step, so no
  step count pinned by an earlier unit moved. Above it the memo costs a
  call that had nothing to save as well (see the stated limits).
- `last_call` holds the stats of the last call of a method on the
  thread, a call refused by the type check included: every method makes
  its memo before the check, so a refused call records zeros.
- A greedy repeat's ends are written as failed when its marker is popped
  (every count from the minimum to the run was tried or known failed); a
  lazy repeat's when it is popped stopped by the text. A lazy repeat that
  reaches its maximum writes nothing (sound, only less remembered).
- What a step is. The steps of `exec` are unchanged (node visits, units
  read by a repeat, frames popped). A bit test and an interval skip are
  made inside a node visit or a frame pop, which counts one step, and a
  marker frame popped counts one step like any frame; a run read before
  costs the visit's step and nothing per unit skipped. No bit test or
  skip is made without a step, so a pin in steps bounds the work done.
- The first-character scan filter (decision risk 4) is not built: it is
  pyre-9b. Without it a megabyte with no match as shipped took the steps
  pinned in `pyre_memo_robustness` (for example 5 steps per character
  for a backtick never closed).

The hostile families (`gen_pyre_memo`, `pyre_memo.jsonl`): the 33 of the
decision record and three shapes outside the inventory, `(?:a|aa)+b` over
a run of `a`, `(?:\w+\s?)+$` over a word and `!`, and `(?:a|aa)*?(?<!a)`
with `finditer` over a run of `a`. The record names a site by file and
line at 3a26051a; the generator maps each to the inventory's file and
bound name (the mapping is in its module text) and fails when a site is
gone. A family's row holds both: `record`, the record's `file:line`
written in the generator as a fixed string (never read from the source,
so an edit of the reference does not move the file's bytes), and `site`,
the inventory's id, from which the pattern is read anew. Every engine
site builds from the reference's text, the hand-matched `_BACKTICK_RE`
included; none is refused. The reference's answer is pinned at 250 to
2,000 characters for the 33 families and at 12, 16 and 20 for the three
shapes, which are exponential for `re`; at a megabyte
the reference takes minutes to hours (the record measured `re` at 32,000
characters: 9.2 s for `_DRIFTING_COUNT_RE` on `1.` repeated, 5.5 s for
`_PROPER_NOUN_RE`, 2.7 s for `_TEST_TOTAL_RE`, 1.5 s for the `state` field
of `_LAUNCHCTL_FIELDS`, the rest under half a second), so there the port
is held to linear steps with the ways agreeing at 4,000. Every family is
linear as shipped: growth 2.000 from half a megabyte to a megabyte, with
at most 119 steps per character (`_DRIFTING_COUNT_RE`, 118.5). The
reference-quadratic families are recorded as reference findings, not
reproduced in time. The most memory the memo held at 16 KiB was 45,848
bytes (`_GENERIC_KEYWORD_RE`, prefix words); at a megabyte 2.5 MB for the
same family.

Stated limits. Only failures are remembered, so a lookaround that
succeeds after a scan is run again at every start: `(?=[^b]*?b)a` with
`finditer` over `a * n + b` takes 1,007,010 steps at 1,000 and 4,014,010
at 2,000 (pinned). The census of condition 8 over the inventory flags
four sites whose lookaround bodies hold an unbounded repeat:
`_COMMIT_HASH_RE`, the third and fourth `_PATTERN_OVERRIDES` of
`durability.py`, and `_PREFERENCE_RE`. Each body is entered only at a
word boundary after a fixed literal or at the boundary that opens a hex
run, so the scans of two entries do not overlap; that is a reading of
the patterns, not a measurement. One interval per repeat is a heuristic.
Every node of the plain program (and of copy B) is recorded by every run
of the call, and copy A is entered only at an attempt's start and left at
its first unit, so its cost depends on the pattern alone; the worst case
argued is then polynomial, not exponential: a lookaround that succeeds is
run again at each entry, so one holding an unbounded repeat is quadratic
(above), and each lookaround that succeeds nested inside a repeat of one
that succeeds adds a factor of the length: `(?=(?:a(?=[^b]*?b))*)c` with
`finditer` over `a * n + b` is cubic in steps in every way, as plain
backtracking and `re` are (364,212 steps at 100, 2,788,412 at 200,
pinned in `pyre_memo_kills`: `a_nested_successful_lookaround_is_cubic`).
Until the attempt that must advance recorded copy B no such bound held
(the case above); no other exponential case is known, and the review's
differential with a budget of 2,000,000 steps per run was cut only by
that one.

The switch does not tell a hostile call from a merely long one. Once a
call has spent `64 * (len + 64)` steps the memo starts, even where plain
backtracking had nothing to repeat: a wide alternation fails at every
position after trying each alternative, so it reaches the switch, writes
a full row for each of its Split nodes, and only adds marker frames. The
memo's memory is at most one row of `len / 64 + 1` words per Split or
Rep1 node, about `nodes * len / 8` bytes, which at the 4,096-node cap is
512 bytes per character. Measured in review in a release build (neither
call makes an attempt that must advance, so recording copy B moves
neither): an alternation of
300 three-letter literals with `search` over a megabyte of `a` took
1,233,872,830 steps and held 39,192,920 bytes, against 942,669,825 steps
with the memo off; 300 alternatives of a two-member class and a digit
with `finditer` over a megabyte of `z` held 39 MB and took 9.6 s against
6.0 s off, and 1,300 such alternatives 170,272,920 bytes, 43.6 s against
36.9 s (`re` held 20 MB and took 2.96 s at 256 KiB). The answers are the same and the
steps linear. No pattern of the reference comes near: the inventory's
largest has 59 Split and Rep1 nodes (at most about 7.4 bytes per
character), and none of its eight largest woke on a megabyte of prose.
There is no cap on the bits beyond `MAX_NODES`.

Pins of earlier units that moved: three tests held a budget against an
exponential blow-up, `(?:a|aa)*c` over 60 `a` (`pyre_api_robustness` and
`pyre_replace_robustness`: `a_pathological_pattern_is_bounded_by_its_budget`)
and `c|(?:a|aa)*b` over `c` and 40 `a` (`pyre_replace_kills`:
`the_scan_stops_at_the_count`). As shipped the memo ends those calls in
linear steps under the budget, so they now build the pattern with the
memo off, which is what they test: the budget cuts plain backtracking.
The budget after the memo has woken is pinned here instead
(`pyre_memo_robustness`: `the_budget_cuts_a_call_after_the_memo_woke`,
`(?=[^b]*?b)c` with `try_search` over 1,000 `a` and a `b` and a budget of
1,000,000 steps, which as shipped wakes the memo and is cut). No step
count of an earlier unit moved.

#### Fixtures and tests of pyre-9

| test | what |
| --- | --- |
| `golden_pyre_memo` | every family at 250 to 2,000 characters (the three shapes at 12, 16 and 20) against `re`'s count and SHA-256, under every way (off, on with and without the intervals, as shipped, switched on after 0 to 40 steps) |
| `pyre_memo_three_ways` | every text of `pyre_exec.jsonl`, `pyre_api.jsonl`, `pyre_inventory.jsonl` and their rows in `pyre_unicode.jsonl` and `pyre_python.jsonl` through the five methods (and `subn`, `subn` with a function and `split` for the replacing rows) under every way, held to the answer with the memo off; a sweep or fuzz row's texts run over three windows (`(0, n)`, `(1, n)`, `(0, n - 1)`), not every window, and a sweep row keeps its 300 shortest texts and an even sample of about 300 of the rest, so the file ends within the battery's bounds in a debug build; the inventory rows run every text |
| `pyre_memo_kills` | the unsound writes (a marker cut inside a positive and a negative lookaround, bits across calls, an interval written with counts left, the switch per search), the attempt that must advance recording copy B, failed ends that start at the minimum and merge only when they touch, a known run read to its true end, over every text of a small alphabet under every way; the memo off never waking; a refused call's zeros in `last_call`; the premises of condition 6; the census of condition 8; the stated quadratic limit and its cubic nesting |
| `pyre_memo_robustness` | each family at a megabyte as shipped (64 KiB in a debug build): steps at most `c * (len + 64)` with `c` per family (also the budget of each run, so a broken memo fails the pin instead of running for ever), growth under 2.2, peak stack pinned; the ways agreeing at 4,000; the exponential shapes, the attempt that must advance linear at a megabyte; the budget cutting a call after the memo woke; the steps of every family with the memo on from the first step, with and without the intervals, pinned exactly as two sums (a skip that saves less changes no answer, only these); a 64 KiB thread; the memo's memory; `MatchError::Memory` when growth is refused |

## The text helpers of `models.py`

`models_text` is unit 2 of `models.py` (unit 1 is the record models, in
`records`). It holds the text helpers of lines 884-1127: they need
nothing from the machine but the Unicode tables, and come to 284 lines of
Rust source.

### Map, by function

| function | reference lines | needs from the machine | status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `_SLUG_RE`, `_LEADING_DATE_RE` | 884-892 | nothing | built (by hand) |
| `make_slug` | 895-909 | `str.strip`, `str.lower`, `re`'s `\d` and `\s` (the crate's `unicode`) | built |
| `build_filename` | 912-914 | `strftime`'s `%Y` | built |
| `_SENTENCE_END_RE`, `_ABBREVIATIONS` | 920-956 | nothing | built (by hand; `ABBREVIATIONS`) |
| `_word_ending_at` | 960-972 | `str.isalnum` | built (`word_ending_at`) |
| `_BODY_TERMINALS`, `looks_truncated` | 981-1027 | `str.strip` | built |
| `first_summary_line` | 1030-1054 | `str.strip`, `str.isalnum`, `str.lower`, `re`'s `\s` | built |
| `snippet_for` | 1057-1068 | `str.strip` | built (moved from `search_dedup`) |
| `snippet_window` | 1071-1108 | `str.strip` | built |
| `_truncate_at_word` | 1111-1127 | nothing | built (`truncate_at_word`, moved from `search_dedup`) |

The rest of `models.py` past the record models (`validate_path_targets`
and its helpers, 1154 on) is left for a later unit.

### What each function reproduces, and the decisions

- **Text and integers.** A text is code points, indexed as Python
  indexes a `str`. The integer parameters (`max_words`, `max_chars`,
  `start`, `end`) are `i64`; the arithmetic on them (`max_chars - 3`,
  `max_chars - 40`) is done in `i128`, so `i64::MIN` and `i64::MAX` do
  not overflow, and every slice follows Python's rule for a negative
  bound (`words[:-1]` drops the last word).
- **`make_slug`.** `str.strip`, then `str.lower` (full case mapping,
  so `İ` becomes two code points), then the text before the first
  `str.splitlines` boundary (`\n`, `\r`, `\v`, `\f`, U+001C to U+001E,
  U+0085, U+2028, U+2029). `_LEADING_DATE_RE.sub` without a flag can only
  match at offset 0, once. The words are the runs of `[a-z0-9]`, so a
  letter `str.lower` leaves outside ASCII splits a word (`façade` gives
  `fa-ade`). The join is cut at `max_chars` code points, then dashes are
  stripped from both ends; an empty slug is `memory`.
- **`_LEADING_DATE_RE`, by hand.** Every part after the date is optional
  and the trailing class is a star, so nothing after a part can fail and
  the greedy choice at each step is the match: no backtracking changes
  the answer. `\d` is `unicode::is_re_digit` (Unicode decimals, so
  Arabic-Indic digits form a date); `\s` in the trailing class is
  `unicode::is_space`. The zone `[+\-]\d{2}:?\d{2}` tries the colon first
  and then none, as `:?` does; a zone that matches neither way is left
  in the text (`+02:0` stays).
- **`build_filename`.** `<YYYY-MM-DD>-<slug>.md` with the year spelt as
  the host's C library writes `%Y` for a year before 1000, as the
  reference's `strftime` does: unpadded on Linux with glibc
  (`cfg(all(target_os = "linux", target_env = "gnu"))`), padded to four
  digits everywhere else (macOS, Windows, and musl, which pads by its
  source). `datetime::year_field(year, pads)` spells it and
  `datetime::STRFTIME_PADS_YEAR` says what this target's C library does;
  `DateTime::strftime`'s `%Y` uses the same two, so the two never
  disagree. Those years go in the platform-gated file, made on each
  system and compared there.
- **`_SENTENCE_END_RE`, by hand.** One of `.!?` followed by a code point
  `str.isspace` holds or by the end. `$` would also match before a final
  newline, but `first_summary_line` replaced every newline with a space
  first, so only the end remains. The matches are single code points, so
  the scan is a walk over the text.
- **`first_summary_line`.** A `.` whose alnum/dot run, lowered, is in
  `_ABBREVIATIONS` is skipped; the first other boundary decides: the
  stripped text before it if non-empty and within `max_chars`, else the
  scan stops. Then the whole text if it fits, else `_truncate_at_word`.
- **`_word_ending_at`.** `end` past the text raises `IndexError` in the
  reference (`text[end - 1]`); the port answers `None`. A negative `end`
  never enters the loop and answers the empty slice.
- **`looks_truncated`.** The last code point of the stripped body
  against the sixteen terminals, `»` among them.
- **`snippet_window`.** `start <= 0` is `snippet_for`; else the tail from
  `start` (empty past the end) with the leading `...` charged to the
  budget `max_chars - 3`.
- **`_truncate_at_word`.** The cut, then the last space, newline or tab
  (only those three) if it lies at or past `max_chars - 40`, then
  `rstrip(" ,;:.-")` and `...`. The reference's "none found" is `-1`, and
  `-1 >= max_chars - 40` holds when `max_chars <= 39`: the cut is then
  sliced at `-1`, one more code point gone (a reference finding, below,
  which the port reproduces).

No regular-expression crate is used: the three patterns are matched by
hand as described, and no crate was added.

### Reference findings

- `_truncate_at_word(text, max_chars)` with `max_chars <= 39` and no
  whitespace in the cut drops one more code point than the cut:
  `_truncate_at_word("abcdef", 3)` is `"ab..."`, not `"abc..."`. It is
  reachable from `snippet_window` with `max_chars <= 42` and from
  `first_summary_line` with `max_chars <= 39`.
- `make_slug` lowers before splitting on `[^a-z0-9]+`, so a letter
  outside ASCII is a separator: `make_slug("Ünïcödé façade")` is
  `"n-c-d-fa-ade"`.
- `build_filename` of a year before 1000 depends on the C library's
  `strftime`: macOS's and Windows' pad it to four digits, glibc writes it
  unpadded (`999-01-02-y.md`). The port follows the host's C library, as
  it does for `strerror`'s texts; `models_text_kills` pins both spellings
  and which one this target uses.

### Fixtures and tests

`tests/contract/gen_models_text.py` writes `models_text.jsonl` (ASCII
texts, class i: each branch and bound of every function, and a digest row
over 6,000 inputs drawn by splitmix64 from a fixed seed, each answered by
six functions), `models_text_unicode.jsonl` (texts past ASCII and a lone
surrogate, and a digest row of seven answers for every code point, gated
on Unicode) and `models_text_platform.jsonl` (years before 1000, gated on
the platform and the Python release). A digest row records the rule, the
count and the SHA-256 of the answers as 4-byte code points; the Rust test
regenerates the inputs by the same rule. Together the files hold 17 KB.
`golden_models_text` checks every case; `models_text_kills` (16) pins
inputs a plausible wrong port answers otherwise (the date only at the
start, Unicode `\s` and `\d` in the date pattern, the short zone, the
`str.splitlines` boundary, a negative word bound, the `-1` slice, the
ellipsis charged to the budget, the abbreviations' case and the space
after a boundary, the scan stopping at the first long sentence, a
superscript as alnum, the terminals, `IndexError`, only `.` read as an
abbreviation's end, the year below 1000 padded or not as the C library
writes it);
`models_text_robustness` (4) shows the summary scan, the slug and the
snippets linear (the fastest of five runs at 2,000,000 code points
within four times the fastest at 1,000,000 plus 200 ms) and feeds the `i64` extremes and
every lone surrogate. The reference takes 0.63 s, 0.42 s and 0.14 s on
the three linear texts at 2,000,000 (Apple M-series).

## The result models of `models.py` and the store-free half of `standing.py`

Two small leaves, built together (units models-3 and standing-1). Both
need nothing from the machine; together they come to 461 lines of Rust
source (`src/records/summaries.rs` 189, `src/standing.rs` 272), comments
included. No pattern of `re` is involved.

### `records::summaries` (models.py 509-618, 703-719)

| function | reference lines | needs from the machine | status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `MemoryHit` | 509-599 | nothing | built (`MemoryHit::new`) |
| `MemorySummary` | 601-618 | nothing | built (`MemorySummary::of`) |
| `TombstonedSummary` | 703-719 | nothing | built (`TombstonedSummary::of`) |
| `SimilarHit` | 721-747 | nothing | built earlier as `search_dedup::SimilarHit` |
| the scope filter of `list_summaries`, `list_tombstones` | store_records.py 1054-1112 | nothing | built (`summaries`, `tombstone_summaries`) |

None of the three models is ever `model_dump`ed in the reference, and
every construction site passes records already validated
(`search._build_hit`, `store_records.list_summaries` and
`list_tombstones`), so they are plain structs: no pydantic validation and
no JSON spelling. `MemoryHit::new` takes the seven required fields and
sets the rest to the model's defaults in its order (relevance `"medium"`,
empty lists, zero counts, None, `query_unique` 0); the caller sets what
`_build_hit` passes beyond them. `score` is the `f64` given. `of` fills
`summary` with `models_text::first_summary_line(body, 80)` and copies
the other fields as the listings do: `MemorySummary` carries `actor`,
`TombstonedSummary` `removed`, `removed_reason` and `removed_session`.
The filter is the reference's `if scopes`: None or an empty list keeps
every record; otherwise a record is kept when it shares a scope with the
list (a set, so the filter is linear), in the input's order. The store's
listings themselves (reading every record) are the store's and are not
in this unit.

`RELATED_CAP` (11), `RELATED_TEXT_CHARS` (600) and `STANDING_STATEMENT`
are `review`'s (unit review-1) and are re-exported here, so `BATCH` and
`record_text` read them through `standing` as before. `asking(tau_set)` takes the review's switch
(whether `current_tau()` is set) and `answered_by(actor)` the request's
actor (`identity::Published::current_actor`); an empty client or model
counts as none, as `or` reads it. `is_standing` compares the category to
`"ambient"` as text.

The errors are one local `StandingError { class, text }` (`ValueError`
or `OverflowError`), which a later caller maps into the store's
`WriteError`. `check_probability` takes a `PyValue`: a bool or any value
but an int or a float is `ValueError` naming `type(value).__name__` as
the reference spells each of `PyValue`'s variants (`NoneType`, `str`,
`list`, `tuple`, `dict`, `datetime`, `PurePosixPath`); an int is
converted as `float(int)` does, the text's nearest double rounding half
to even (Rust's `f64` parse), so `OverflowError` exactly when its
magnitude is at least 2**1024 - 2**970; a range failure prints the
original value's repr (an int in full, a float by `float_repr`, so `nan`
and `inf` as Python prints them; -0.0 passes). `answer_of` checks the
source first (its repr), then the probability, then names who answered,
and stores the probability as `PyValue::Float`. The line builders count
with the id list's length and join ids with `", "`; `record_text` strips
with Unicode whitespace and windows with `models_text::snippet_window(text,
0, 597)`.

`tests/contract/gen_models_hits.py` writes `models_hits.jsonl` (25 KB,
class i): seven memories and five tombstones in its header (each its
`model_dump(mode="json")`, which the Rust test validates again), the two
listings under seven scope filters (None, empty, one, two, a repeated
scope, an unknown one, another case), and four hits with their defaults.
`tests/contract/gen_standing.py` writes `standing.jsonl` (51 KB, class
i): the constants in its header, and every branch of each function
(`check_probability` over None, bools, ints at and beside the overflow
bound, floats including nan, inf, -0.0, 1.0000000000000002 and the
subnormals, texts, containers, a datetime and a path; `answer_of` with a
bad source and a bad probability together; the line builders at 0, 1,
11, 12 ids; `record_text` at 599, 600, 601 code points and with
surrounding whitespace). `golden_models_hits` and `golden_standing` check
every case; `standing_kills` (11) pins the bool refusal, the overflow
bound and its neighbour, -0.0 and nan, the order of `answer_of`'s
checks, an empty client, the case of `ambient`, the 600 window, the
counts and cap of the line builders, the question's key order, the empty
scope filter and the hit's defaults; `standing_robustness` (3) feeds ints
of 100,000 digits and a list nested 100,000 deep, and holds `record_text`,
the held lines and the scope filter to `timing::TENFOLD` at ten times the
input.

### `standing` (standing.py, unit 2: the store reads)

Unit standing-2 is `src/standing/reads.rs` (481 lines), re-exported
from `standing`. Its reference lines were confirmed against
`src/bettermemory/standing.py` as it is now: the memo 131-139,
`_current` 190-213, `answers` 216-220, `Backlog` 223-231, `backlog`
234-245, `guarded_ids` 248-259, `makes_standing` 262-294, `held_ids`
297-311, `standing_ids` 314-350, `refusal_rows` 364-385,
`held_by_removal` 399-415.

The store is the trait `StandingStore`, which extends
`in_force::LinkReader` (so `in_force` runs over the same store), with
one method per `Store` read the reference makes: `body_of`,
`standing_rows` (rows as the struct `StandingRow`, its dict's keys as
fields), `digest_unanswered_ids`, `returned_rows` (the marked ids in the
dict's order; the marks' values are not read here),
`standing_candidate_ids`, `get_many` (`records::Memory`) and
`tombstone_links` (`ReadError::NotFound` for no tombstone). The
admission is the trait `Admission: RecordView` with `admits_row`, shaped
as `store::caller::Admission::admits_row`; `EveryRecord` implements it.
Whether the write review is in force (`review.current_tau()` set) is the
argument `tau_set` of `held_ids` and `held_by_removal`, as `asking`
takes it. An implementation of `LinkReader::held_ids` over a real store
calls `standing::held_ids` with its own switch; an error there cannot
cross that trait method, which answers a set. So where the reference's
`in_force` raises `UnicodeEncodeError` from `held_ids` (a held candidate
whose body holds a lone surrogate, for an id `standing_ids` never hashed
itself), `standing_ids`, `guarded_ids` and `makes_standing` cannot
return `ReadError::Unencodable`: the implementation drops the error or
panics. Closing this gap is a change to `in_force::LinkReader`.

The memo is one process-wide `Mutex` around an ordered map: a hit moves
its key to the end, an insert of a new key goes to the end and an insert
of a present key keeps its place (a dict assignment), and the oldest are
popped while the map holds more than the bound. A row without `log_mac`
is hashed on every read and never memoized. `clear_shas` empties it (its
registration with `_caches` is wired when that lane folds),
`set_sha_bound` rebinds the bound as a caller may rebind the module
global, and `sha_count` is `len(_SHAS)`. `body_sha256` hashes the body's
UTF-8; a body holding a lone surrogate is `ReadError::Unencodable`, the
reference's `UnicodeEncodeError`.

Kept as the reference has them: `standing_ids`' pre-filter on the raw
probability (a non-ambient row without one is skipped before the
admission is asked), the rows' order, a held record only when `held` is
passed; `makes_standing`'s checks in order (not standing after, history,
held, an unchanged body already standing); `backlog`'s rows from the
digest's ids or every row; `answers` as a dict (a repeated row keeps its
first place and its last value); `refusal_rows`' keys `id`, `scopes`,
`updated`, `text`, then `admitted: false` only when not admitted, the
date of `updated` in UTC, and the ids deduplicated first-seen before
`get_many` while `prime` sees them as given; `held_by_removal`'s
`supersedes` targets deduplicated first-seen and kept when held. A naive
`updated`, which the reference reads as the machine's local time, is
`ReadError::NaiveUpdated`; an instant outside years 1 to 9999 is
`ReadError::Date`.

One stated difference: ids cross the traits as `String`, so an id
holding a lone surrogate (a record id or a tombstone's `supersedes`
target) is spelled with U+FFFD before `admits_id`, `held_ids` and the
first-seen dedup, and two ids that differ only in such a code point are
one id here. Record ids are ULIDs, which hold none.

`tests/contract/gen_standing_reads.py` writes `standing_reads.jsonl`
(36 KB, class i) over an in-memory store and admission that log every
read: 41 cases, each a list of operations on one memo, with
probabilities at 0.3 and its two neighbouring doubles, a memo bound
rebound to 2 and 0, refusal dates across the UTC day boundary, and
tombstones with every link type. `golden_standing_reads` checks every
operation's answer and its reads in order; `standing_reads_kills` (11)
pins the unmemoized row, the hit that moves to the end, the inclusive
threshold, the pre-filter, held and history, the review off, the
refusal keys and dates, the removal dedup, the repeated row, the two
errors and the category of `makes_standing`'s first row of two; the
memo's own unit test pins that an insert of a present key keeps its
place; `standing_reads_robustness` (4) holds the memo at its bound past
65,536 rows, hashes a body of two megabytes and holds `standing_ids` to
`timing::TENFOLD` at ten times the rows, and `answers` the same (an
index beside the ordered pairs keeps it linear). No pattern is matched here.

## The write review's sealed tables (`review.py`, unit review-1)

`review.py` (about 1,250 lines) is cut into units, leaves first. Unit
review-1 is built in `src/review/mod.rs` and `src/review/related.rs`;
the answers units add `review/answers.rs` and `review/decision.rs`
beside them.

| Function | Lines | Needs from the machine | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `RELATED_TOP`, `RELATED_CAP`, `RELATED_TEXT_CHARS`, `RELATED_CONSTANTS`, `ROSTER_TEXT_CHARS` | 84-112 | nothing | built (review-1) |
| `TAU_UNSAFE`, `TAU_SECRET`, `Tau`, `current_tau`, `tau_override`, `tau_unset` | 121-171 | a process-wide cell | built (review-1) |
| the labels, `LABEL_CHOICES`, the four statements | 177-219 | nothing | built (review-1) |
| `QUESTIONS`, `questions_payload`, `canonical_json`, `questions_sha256`, `constants_sha256`, `seal_shas` | 222-307 | nothing | built (review-1); `canonical_json` is `json::review_canonical_json` |
| `RelatedEntry`, `RelatedSet` | 311-377 | nothing | built (review-1) |
| `_SENTENCE_BREAK_RE`, `related_text`, `related_entry` | 380-417 | nothing | built (review-1) |
| `related_for` | 420-528 | the store, the engine, the cue code | review-3 |
| `RosterLine`, `_write_sentences` | 531-540, 572-575 | nothing | built (review-1) |
| `roster_candidates`, `roster_for` | 543-674 | the store, the engine | review-3 |
| `ReviewAnswerError`, `ANSWER_FORMAT`, `NAMED_FORMAT`, `UPDATE_ANSWER_FORMAT`, `ReviewAnswers` (`to_event`, `is_zero_attestation`), `_score`, `_chain_keys`, `parse_answers`, `parse_update_answers`, `check_answered_ids`, `check_named` | 677-942 | nothing | built (review-2, `review/answers.rs`) |
| `ACTION_*`, `DETECTOR_*`, `REVIEW_LINK_NOTE` | 949-959 | nothing | built (review-1) |
| `ReviewDecision` and `to_event`, `_DISPUTED`, `replaced_ids`, `apply_review` | 963-1167 | nothing | built (`review/decision.rs`) |
| the review-issued rows and their chains | 1172-1335 | the store | the review chain unit |

What review-1 reproduces, and why it is built as it is:

- **The thresholds** are one process-wide cell, a `Mutex` of
  `(Option<f64>, Option<f64>)` seeded with the sealed 0.3 and 0.3, as the
  two module attributes are. `current_tau()` reads it at call time and is
  the only way product code reads tau. `tau_override` and `tau_unset`
  return guards that put back the pair they found when dropped, also
  while a panic unwinds, as the reference's `finally` does; a guard
  dropped out of order restores what it found, so two overrides left out
  of order end where the reference's two `__exit__` calls in that order
  end. `tau_patched` is what `mock.patch` of the two attributes does in
  the reference's tests, which can leave one of them None.
- **The serializing lock.** Tests in one binary run on threads of one
  process, while the reference's module attributes are read by one test
  at a time. Every guard therefore holds a serializing lock for its life:
  a counted lock (the holding thread and its count of live guards, with
  a `Condvar`), so a second thread's override waits until the first
  thread's guards are all dropped. It counts rather than being a plain
  `Mutex<()>` because the reference nests overrides on one thread, which
  a plain mutex would deadlock.
  Two differences from the reference follow and are stated here. A
  thread that holds a guard and then joins a thread that itself takes
  an override deadlocks, where the reference's second thread just sets
  the attributes. `current_tau()` takes no part in the lock, so a test
  that takes no guard can read another thread's override; every test
  that reads tau therefore holds a guard (`tau_patched(TAU_UNSAFE,
  TAU_SECRET)` for the sealed pair). `TauGuard` is not `Send`, so its
  count is released on the thread that took it.
- **The guard is the override.** `tau_override` returns only the
  `#[must_use]` guard, and the yielded `Tau` is `guard.tau()`, so the
  `Tau` cannot be kept while the guard is dropped in the same pattern.
  The override ends when the guard is dropped, where the reference's
  ends with its `with` block.
- **`QUESTIONS`** is built once as a `PyValue` tree in the reference's
  key order and only lent out; `questions_payload` is a clone. The shas
  are SHA-256 over `json::review_canonical_json`.
- **`RelatedSet`** keeps the cue report as `Option<CueReport>`:
  `supersession.py` is not built, so `CueReport { supersedes, conflicts }`
  holds the memory ids of the report's two lists in report order, the
  shape the supersession unit converts its report into. None is the
  `write_supersession` switch off.
- **`related_text`** reads tokens through
  `search_dedup::raw_content_token_set`; the reference's cache
  (`RawTokenCache`) changes no answer here. The window comes from
  `models_text::snippet_window`.
- **`related_entry`** renders `updated` in UTC as `date().isoformat()`;
  `astimezone`'s OverflowError (year 1 or 9999 pushed past the range) is
  `RelatedError::Date`, and a naive `updated`, which the reference reads
  as the machine's local time, is declined (`NaiveUpdated`). Its
  `claim_sized` is `store::digest::claim_sized`, the port of
  `supersession.claim_sized`, made public for this; the supersession
  unit re-exports it.
- **`RELATED_CAP`, `RELATED_TEXT_CHARS` and `STANDING_STATEMENT`** moved
  here from `standing`, which re-exports all three; `standing::BATCH`
  stays.

The pattern: `_SENTENCE_BREAK_RE` (`(?<=[.!?])\s+|\n+`, class T2) is a
`pyre::regex::Regex` built from the reference's own text with no flags,
called through `finditer` in `related_text` and `split` in
`_write_sentences` (the pyre decision's rule 1). It is in the engine's
inventory through `gen_pyre_atom`'s scan of the reference's source.

Fixtures: `gen_review_tables` writes `review_tables.jsonl` (ungated: the
constants, the payload in sorted and in reference key order with both
shas, the tau overrides, `to_dict`, `RelatedSet`, `to_line`,
`related_text` and `_write_sentences` over long and short bodies with
breaks, `!?.` runs and line feeds, `related_entry` across UTC dates and
both overflow edges, and a seeded sweep of 2,000 cases as one digest
row) and `review_tables_unicode.jsonl` (`UNICODE_GATED`: `\s` and the
tokenizer past ASCII). The generator reads tau only inside `with`
blocks of `tau_override` and `tau_unset`. Tests: `golden_review_tables`,
`review_tables_kills` (the guards out of order, under a panic and across
threads), `review_tables_robustness` (long bodies, runs of breaks, odd
code points, linear growth).

### Unit review-2: the answers (`review/answers.rs`)

Unit review-2 ports lines 677-942: the answer readers, their teaching
errors and the two answer checks. It imports the labels,
`LABEL_CHOICES` and `LABEL_UNRELATED` from `review/mod.rs` and defines
none of the sealed tables again. Nothing it does reads the store, the
clock or the environment, and it holds no pattern.

- **`raw`** is the `review` argument as `json::loads` gives it, an
  `Option<&PyValue>`: Rust None and JSON null are both a first call, as
  is an empty dict; any value other than a dict is the teaching error.
  The relation must be a `PyValue::Dict` (`Mapping`); `named` a list or
  a tuple of str.
- **The errors** are `AnswerFault::Teach` with the reference's text in
  code points, or `AnswerFault::Py` for another exception the reference
  raises on the way: `float` of an int past the float range
  (OverflowError: Rust's decimal parse rounds half to even as CPython's
  `float(int)` does, so 2**1024 - 2**970 overflows and one less does
  not), `sorted` of unknown keys of types `<` refuses (TypeError), and
  `repr` of a review_id nested past `json::MAX_DEPTH`
  (RecursionError, as `pyvalue::repr` models it).
- **The order of the checks** is the reference's: unknown keys,
  review_id, relation, named, said, then unsafe, secret and standing in
  the order the dataclass's arguments are evaluated.
- **`_score`** tests bool before the number test, then `float`, then
  `math.isfinite` and the bounds; the shown value is `pyvalue::repr` of
  the value as given (an int stays an int, a float goes through
  `float_repr`). `type(value).__name__` is spelled per variant
  (`datetime` for a `DateTime`, `PurePosixPath` for a `Path`).
- **The orders.** The relation keeps a repeated id at its first place
  with its last label, as a dict does; `named` keeps each id at its first
  appearance (`dict.fromkeys`); unknown keys and foreign ids sort by code
  point, and the lists print as Python's repr of a list. `said` is
  `" ".join(said.split())` with `unicode::is_space`, and `said.strip()`
  is empty exactly when every code point is a space.
- **Set semantics** for unknown keys dedupe equal values after sorting;
  a dict JSON gives has str keys only, so `1 == 1.0 == True` among
  non-str keys is not modelled.
- **`ReviewAnswers`** holds the relation as ordered pairs; `to_event`
  is a `PyValue` dict in the reference's key order. `check_named`
  takes the roster and the shown ids as `HashSet`s and answers the
  named ids.

Fixtures: `gen_review_answers` writes `review_answers.jsonl`
(ungated: every text is ASCII or an escaped surrogate, no int reaches
the 4,300 digit limit, and `said` folds only ASCII whitespace there; the
three formats, every teaching error of both readers, the accepted
shapes with `to_event`, the review_id and `is_zero_attestation`, both
checks, and a seeded sweep of 3,000 label and score combinations as one
digest row). No module global is patched. Tests:
`golden_review_answers`, `review_answers_kills` (a bool score, JSON
null, the check order, the dedup orders, whitespace past ASCII, the int
bounds), `review_answers_robustness` (200,000 relation ids, 200,000
unknown keys, millions of spaces, a deep review_id, linear growth).

### The decision a write review makes (`review/decision.rs`)

`apply_review` reads the explicit `Tau`, related entries, answers and write
options. It checks the inclusive secret and unsafe thresholds in that order.
A conflict with a standing record refuses even when the writer quotes the
user. A restatement can refuse before the check for an unsaid replacement.
On a commit the decision records links, suggestions, filings and dropped cues
in related-entry order. An extends answer on a cue target both files the
disagreement and adds an extends link unless the writer declared the target.

`replaced_ids` preserves updated entries in order, then appends distinct
declarations, then undisputed cue targets absent from those two groups.
Repeated new cue targets survive the last step, as they do in the reference's
list comprehension. The implementation borrows code-point strings for lookup.
`apply_review_iter` and `replaced_ids_iter` accept fallible one-shot inputs.
A score refusal leaves both inputs untouched. Otherwise the decision consumes
standing IDs before declared IDs and returns any iteration error unchanged.
Only distinct IDs are retained while each source is consumed.
`ReviewDecision::to_event` emits fields in the reference's insertion order and
omits empty collections and a false `standing_write`.

`gen_review_decision` writes the ungated `review_decision.jsonl` from the pure
Python functions. Its 48 direct cases, a complete event and a seeded sweep
of 8,192 cases cover floating-point boundaries, rule order, writing options,
detector choice, duplicate IDs and lone surrogates. The golden test checks
the exact replacement list and ASCII JSON spelling. The kills tests pin the
branches that change a refusal, link or filing. The robustness tests cover
long code-point IDs, nonfinite scores and growth from 1,500 to 15,000 entries.
Store-backed review chains and related-set construction belong to later units.

## The write review's counters (`review_counters.py`)

`review_counters.py` (780 lines) reads the event log's review rows and
counts the write review's chains for `bettermemory eval` and `bettermemory
review samples`. It is cut into three units, leaves first. Unit
review_counters-1a is built in `src/review_counters.rs`.

| Function | Lines | Needs from the machine | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ANSWER_WINDOW`, `REVIEW_GRADE`, `REFUSAL_ACTIONS`, `DETECTORS`, `_STATUS_ACTION` | 46-70 | nothing | built (1a) |
| `_str`, `_ids`, `_session_of`, `_bucket_value` | 73-99 | nothing | built (1a) |
| `IssuedRow` (`chain_key`, `from_event`) | 108-152 | nothing | built (1a) |
| `DecidedRow` (`committed`, `zero_attestation`, `from_event`), `_score` | 155-245 | nothing | built (1a) |
| `GradeRow` (`from_event`) | 248-279 | nothing | built (1a) |
| `is_review_row` | 282-288 | nothing | built (1a) |
| `ReviewChain`, `build_chains`, `_in_window`, `chains_in_window`, `_share`, `_median`, `_iso_week`, `_Tally` | 296-610 | nothing (rows are arguments) | review_counters-1b |
| `ReviewReport`, `compute_review_report` | 613-780 | the event log's rows, the clock as an argument | review_counters-2 |

`review.py`'s `REVIEW_ISSUED` (`"review_issued"`) and `UNDECLARED`
(`"none"`) sit in `review/mod.rs` beside `ACTION_*`; they are the only
names of review.py's chain unit (review-4) the counters read.
`recall_settle.rs` keeps its own copy of `REVIEW_ISSUED`.

What review_counters-1a reproduces, and why it is built as it is:

- **An event is a `PyValue`.** The readers take the row as
  `json.loads` gave it. `.get(key)` is `PyValue::get`, the last value of
  a `str` key. A row that is not a dict has no `.get`: every reader
  answers `CountersError::AttributeError` with the type's name, as the
  reference raises. `actor`, `review_answers`, `relation` and each
  filing are read only when they are dicts (`isinstance(..., Mapping)`).
- **Texts.** `_str` is a non-empty `str`; `_ids` reads only a `list`
  (a tuple gives none, as `isinstance(value, list)` refuses it) and keeps
  its non-empty `str` items in order, repeats included. The session is
  the actor block's, then the row's own; the client and the model are
  the row's own, then the actor block's, then `UNDECLARED`. The actor
  block is read one level deep: an `actor` inside it is not followed.
- **`IssuedRow.from_event`** answers None without a review_id, without
  a time `parse_event_ts` reads, or with a `door` of any value but None
  (`false`, `0` and `""` are present: an update's standing roster).
  `response_chars` is an `int` that is not a bool, kept as `PyValue::Int`'s
  decimal text, since the reference keeps an `int` of any size.
  `pre_answered` is `is True` (an `int` 1 is not). `chain_key` is the
  parent's review_id, else the row's own.
- **`DecidedRow.from_event`** answers None without a review_id, a time
  or a non-empty `str` status. The action is `review_action` when it is
  a non-empty `str`, else `_STATUS_ACTION`'s entry for the status, else
  the status itself: an empty or non-`str` `review_action` falls to the
  map. The relation keeps the `str` to `str` pairs of the answers'
  `relation` in its order; a key held twice in the dict keeps its first
  place and its last value (as a dict built from those pairs does, and
  as `json::loads` already folds a key repeated in the log's text), and
  is then dropped if that last value is not a `str`. A filing is a dict
  row with a non-empty `str` id and detector.
- **`_score`** answers None for a bool and for anything not an `int` or
  a `float`; an `int` is `float(int)`, correctly rounded (Rust's parse
  rounds half to even, as CPython does), an `int` zero is +0.0 (an `int`
  has no negative zero, so `-0` text, which no reader makes, reads as
  `float(0)` does), and from 2**1024 - 2**970 on it
  raises OverflowError, which `from_event` does not catch: the answer is
  `CountersError::OverflowError`, the class only, since its text follows
  the release. The guards come first, so a row without a status answers
  None whatever its scores. NaN and the infinities pass as floats.
- **`zero_attestation`** compares both scores with 0 as floats (-0.0
  equals; NaN and None do not) and asks every relation label to be
  `unrelated` (true for no relation). `committed` is an action of
  `ACTION_COMMIT`.
- **`GradeRow.from_event`** needs `right_answers` and `right_action` to
  be bools (an `int` 1 is refused); `sample_ts` is read or None.
- **`is_review_row`** is `kind in (REVIEW_ISSUED, REVIEW_GRADE)`, a
  tuple's `==`, so a kind of any type, an unhashable list or dict
  included, answers False without raising; then a `write` kind with a
  `str` review_id, the empty one included (not `_str`).
- **`ANSWER_WINDOW`** is `ANSWER_WINDOW_US`, 30 minutes in microseconds;
  datetimes are `DateTime`s with the offset `parse_event_ts` gives.

The module has no regular expression.

`gen_review_counters` writes the ungated `review_counters_rows.jsonl`
(about 120 KB): the tables in its header with the three base events and
the sweep's pools; 219 event rows (each base with fields set or dropped
to reach every guard, a relation with one label unrelated and one
not, events that are not dicts, kinds of every type, and JSON texts with
a key held twice), each answered by all seven
readers; 36 rows of `_str`, `_ids` and `_score` on their own; and a
sweep of 10,000 events drawn field by field from the pools by count and
SHA-256 of the answers. `golden_review_counters_rows` checks every row
and the sweep (drawn here from the header's pools by the generator's
rule). `review_counters_rows_kills` pins the misreadings that move a
row into the wrong action, bucket, chain or verdict: an empty
`review_action` kept, a bool score read as 1.0, a huge `int` score read
as infinity, `right_answers` 1 taken as True, the actor's client before
the row's own, a false door read as absent, a list kind raising, a tuple
of ids read, a repeated relation key placed last, and a zero
attestation that asks any label, not every label, to be unrelated.
`review_counters_rows_robustness` reads rows of 100,000 ids, relation
pairs and filings (linear growth from 10,000), an actor nested 10,000
deep, every float extreme and `int`s past the float range, and texts of
200,000 code points, without a panic; it compares scores by their
bits, so a zero's sign is checked.

Known costs, both linear in the row's size. Each `.get` is
`PyValue::get`, the crate-wide linear scan of a dict's pairs from the
end, where the reference's dict lookup is O(1): the readers make about
20 lookups an event, so on an event of 1,000,000 keys
`DecidedRow::from_event` takes about 26 ms and `IssuedRow::from_event`
about 19 ms in release, where the reference takes a few microseconds
(the event's JSON parse, linear in both, stays the larger part end to
end). A relation of 200,000 keys of 200 code points takes 9.5 to 15
times the reference's time and 16 times its memory (188 MB against
11.5 MB): `str_items` hashes every key, and the row clones each key and
value as code points (4 bytes each) where the reference shares its `str`
objects; `IssuedRow` likewise clones the id lists it keeps.

Left for review_counters-1b: the chains and their window (`ReviewChain`
to `_Tally`); for review_counters-2: `ReviewReport` and
`compute_review_report`. The medians and the per-100 rates whose
rounding a report shows are theirs.

## The hook mains' argument parser (`argparse`, units argparse-1a and argparse-1b)

`hook.main` (`hook.py` 1251-1352) and `hook.prompt_main` (984-1063)
parse their argv through the standard library's `argparse`. The reference
is `Lib/argparse.py` of CPython 3.13.13, the release the contract
generators run; no line of `src/bettermemory` is ported here, and the two
mains' parsers are built again in the generator from the same calls.

The map, by function of `argparse.py`, with what each needs from the
machine and its status:

| function | lines | needs | status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ArgumentParser.__init__` (`prog`, `description`, `add_help`) | 1793-1871 | nothing | argparse-1a (`ArgumentParser::new`) |
| `add_argument`, `_get_positional_kwargs`, `_get_optional_kwargs`, the conflict check | 1468-1560, 1599-1697 | nothing | argparse-1a for `store`, `store_true`, `version`, `help`; the `ValueError`, `ArgumentError`, `IndexError` and `TypeError` of a bad spec (an empty name, `dest=` beside a positional name, `required=` on a positional, `help` or `version` as a positional) are classes (`SpecError`) only |
| `parse_args`, `_parse_known_args2`, `_parse_known_args` with `consume_optional` and `consume_positionals` | 1925-2282 | nothing | argparse-1a (`parse::parse_known`) |
| `_parse_optional`, `_get_option_tuples`, `_negative_number_matcher` | 2352-2441, 1427 | Unicode's decimal digits | argparse-1a |
| `_match_argument`, `_match_arguments_partial`, `_get_nargs_pattern` | 2313-2350, 2442-2482 | nothing | argparse-1a for `nargs` None and 0; argparse-1b for PARSER |
| `_get_values`, `_check_value`, `_get_action_name`, `ArgumentError.__str__` | 2520-2610, 728-768 | nothing | argparse-1a without type converters |
| `HelpFormatter._format_usage` with `get_lines`, `_get_actions_usage_parts_with_split`, `format_help`'s last pass | 286-497 | the terminal width (an argument) | argparse-1a without groups |
| `_VersionAction.__call__`, `_format_text`, `_fill_text` | 1175-1182, 500-504, 646-651 | the width | argparse-1a for a text that fits; `textwrap.fill` of a longer one is the `HelpText` hook's |
| `error`, `exit`, `_print_message` | 2658-2685 | stdout, stderr, the exit | argparse-1a, as an `Outcome` |
| `add_subparsers`, `add_parser`, `_SubParsersAction.__call__`, the leftovers of `_parse_known_args2` | 1185-1293, 1873-1903, 1945-1974 | the width | argparse-1b (`subparsers`); `title=`, `description=`, `required=`, `metavar=`, `prog=` of `add_subparsers` and `aliases=`, `deprecated=` of `add_parser` are not taken |
| `format_help`, `_format_action`, `_split_lines`, `textwrap` | 500-660, 2618-2640 | the width | argparse-2a (`help::DefaultHelp`) for the default English formatter and supported declarations |
| `nargs` `?`, `*`, `+`, integers, REMAINDER; `type=`; mutually exclusive groups; `fromfile_prefix_chars`; intermixed parsing; deprecation warnings | | | not needed by the two mains; not built |

**What each reproduces.** `ArgumentParser::new` adds `-h/--help` as
`add_help` does. `add_argument` derives `dest` as the reference does (the
first long option string, else the first, prefix dashes stripped and `-`
made `_`), marks a positional of one argument required, gives `store` a
default of None and `store_true` False unless one is given, and makes the
help and version actions' `dest` and default SUPPRESS; an option string
that looks like a negative number sets `_has_negative_number_optionals`.
`parse_args` returns the namespace (each dest in the order it was first
set, a later action of the same dest keeping the first one's place and
default) or an `Outcome`: what `SystemExit` would leave, its status,
stdout and stderr. Its parse follows `_parse_known_args` line by line:
the `A`/`O`/`-` pattern with everything after the first `--` an argument,
exact option strings, `--opt=value`, every prefix match in the order the
option strings were added (one is taken, two or more is the ambiguous
error naming them all), the single-dash cluster loop of
`consume_optional` with its `ignored explicit argument` errors, an
argument that looks like a negative number read as a positional, an
argument with a space read as a positional, the positionals matched
greedily up to each option and the first `--` of their run removed, the
required check before the unrecognized-arguments check. `error` prints
`format_usage()` and `prog: error: message`, status 2. The usage line is
`_format_usage` of 3.13.13 at the width given (the reference takes it
from `shutil.get_terminal_size` less two), wrapped by its `get_lines`
when the line runs past the width, with `prog` on its own line when the
prefix and `prog` take more than three quarters of it. The version action
prints its text with ASCII whitespace runs made one space and the ends
stripped by `str.strip`, as `_fill_text` does, then exits 0.

**Decisions.**

- Help text and long version text reach the parser through `HelpText`.
  `DefaultHelp` renders both. A caller that supplies `Unfilled` gets
  `NotPorted` for a requested formatting operation. A version text
  naming `%(prog)` is declined the same way (the reference applies `%`
  formatting to it).
- The width is an argument and may be any `i64`; the three-quarters test
  is computed in `i128`.
- Subparsers: `Kind::Parsers` is the PARSER variant. `match_argument` and
  `consume_positionals` answer `NotPorted` for it, so argparse-1b fills
  those arms without changing `parse.rs`'s shape.
- Texts are code points (`PyStr`), so argv may hold the surrogates
  `sys.argv` carries for undecodable bytes.
- An option string of one character with an explicit argument, which
  makes the reference raise IndexError (`option_string[1]`), answers
  `NotPorted`.

**Regular expressions.** `argparse` is not under `src/bettermemory`, so
its patterns are outside the inventory `gen_pyre_atom` scans, and none is
added to it. Each is matched by hand under rule 3 of the regular
expression decision (a leaf that starts before pyre-6, no nested choice),
and named here for pyre-8's cross-check:
`_negative_number_matcher`, `^-\d+$|^-\d*\.\d+$` under `match`
(`looks_negative`: a `-`, then decimal digits, or digits, a dot and at
least one digit; `$` also before a final newline, so `-1\n` is a
negative number); the `nargs` patterns `([A])`, `([AO]{0})` and
`(-*A-*)` over the private `A`/`O`/`-` alphabet (`match_argument`,
`match_partial`, greedy, which is the only match each can make); and
`_long_break_matcher`, `\n\n\n+` under `sub` (`usage::finish`). The
help formatter's `_whitespace_matcher`, `\s+` under ASCII, is matched by
hand in `format_version` over the six ASCII whitespace code points.

**Fixtures.** `gen_argparse.py` writes `argparse.jsonl` (not gated: the
cases that end in a namespace and use only exact option strings and
arguments that do not start with `-`; 3.11.15, 3.12.13, 3.13.13 and
3.14.10 write it alike) and `argparse_python.jsonl` (gated on the Python
release: every error text, usage line at widths from -5 to 78, `--`,
`=`, prefix, cluster, negative-number, help and version case, and a
sweep of 3,000 seeded argv vectors over 36 tokens pinned by count and
SHA-256). `golden_argparse` checks both, the help text handed to the
parser by a test `HelpText` that returns the case's stdout;
`argparse_kills` holds inputs a plausible wrong port misreads;
`argparse_robustness` holds every width an `i64` holds, arguments of
100,000 code points and surrogates, and ten times the argv within
`TENFOLD` times the time. `argparse_not_posix` is not needed: nothing
here reads the platform.

**Unit argparse-1b: subparsers.** `add_subparsers(dest, width)` adds
the `_SubParsersAction` as a positional of `nargs` PARSER whose choices are
the parsers' names; its `prog` prefix is what `format_help` of a formatter
given `add_usage(None, positionals, [], '')` writes at the width, stripped
(`usage::format_usage_with`), so it holds the parent's positionals added
