### As built

`cli::root` (`src/cli/root.rs`):

- `COMMANDS` holds the 31 subcommand names in `_build_parser`'s order,
  `hook` last; `DESCRIPTION` and `HOOK_HELP` are the reference's texts.
- `Command` is a command module as a trait object: `name`,
  `add_subparser(root, width)` (it calls `root.add_parser`; the
  reference's builder takes the `_SubParsersAction`, which the port keeps
  inside the root parser) and `run(args, root, sub) -> Exit`, the
  handler with the parsers its arm passes. `up`, `down` and `status` are
  three commands (the reference's `daemon_cmd.add_up`/`run_up` and
  kin); `serve`'s `run` is `run_serve`, which the reference calls with no
  argument, so its `args` is unused there.
- `build_parser(version, commands, width)`: `ArgumentParser(prog=
  "bettermemory", description=DESCRIPTION)`, `--version` with
  `"bettermemory {version}"`, `add_subparsers(dest="cmd")`, then each
  name of `COMMANDS` in order. A name with no `Command` registered is
  skipped, so it is no choice of the parser (the reference always
  registers all 31); where two are registered under one name the first
  is used. `hook` is always `add_hook_subparser`'s, whatever is
  registered under that name. The subparsers dict of the reference is
  `subparser(root, name)`, read from the root's subparsers action.
- `build_product_parser(version, width)` registers all 31 root commands
  and four log commands in their Python order. It builds the hook and
  log verify parsers with their real arguments. Each remaining command
  carries its parent help row and returns `NotPorted` on selection.
  `cli_registry.jsonl` checks the production declarations and portable
  parse results. The parser follows CPython 3.13.13 for error wording
  and for a leading `--` before a subcommand, which 3.11 rejects.
- `arm_parsers(cmd)` is `main`'s arm table: `(root, sub)` per name,
  both for `migrate` and `tombstones`, the root alone for
  `rename-scope` and `completion`, the subparser alone for the 17 others
  that take one, neither for `health`, `init`, `rollback`, `try`,
  `doctor`, `up`, `down`, `status` and `serve`; None for `hook` and any
  other name.
- `main(argv, version, commands, width, help, hook_main, shim)`:
  `route_hook_word` first (`Ended::Hook(code)`), then the parse; an exit
  of the parser (help, version, an error) is `Ended::Parser(outcome)`;
  `cmd` None runs the shim (`Ended::Shim`); a name with an arm and a
  registered command runs it (`Ended::Ran { cmd, exit }`); anything else
  is `parser.error(f"unknown subcommand: {cmd!r}")`, with
  `pyvalue::repr_str`. A `SpecError` from a builder is `Fault::Spec`
  (the reference raises), a decline of the parser `Fault::NotPorted`.
- `UsageError` for `ArgumentParser`: `prog`, and `error` at
  `DEFAULT_WIDTH` 78, the width `shutil.get_terminal_size` gives with
  `COLUMNS` unset and no terminal; a caller that knows another width
  calls `ArgumentParser::error` itself.
- `Formatted { parser, width }`: a parser as `main` hands it to
  `Command::run`, with `UsageError::error` at the width `main` was
  given, so a command's refusal wraps its usage line where the
  reference's `parser.error` does under that `COLUMNS`.

No regular expression is involved. The Windows flavour has no gap here:
nothing resolves a path.

### Fixtures and tests

`tests/contract/gen_cli_root.py` runs the reference `main` with every
command module's builder replaced by a stand-in (`add_parser(name,
help=, description=)` both `"<name> help"`, and `--opt`) and every
handler by one that records its arm and the `prog` of the parsers it was
passed; `hook_main` answers 7, the shim records that it ran,
`__version__` is `0.0.test` and `COLUMNS=80`. `cli_root.jsonl` (not
gated) holds the hook routes, the shim and every arm with its namespace;
`cli_root_python.jsonl` (gated on the Python release) holds the parser's
exits, whose texts are `argparse`'s, and argvs holding `--`. The Rust
tests are `golden_cli_root` (the same stand-ins in
`tests/common/cli_root.rs`), `cli_root_kills` and `cli_root_robustness`.

### Reference findings

- The hook subparser is said to be listed for `--help` and nothing else,
  but `--` before the word reaches it: `bettermemory -- hook stop` passes
  `route_hook_word` (its first word is `--`), parses to `cmd == "hook"`,
  which has no arm, and ends in `bettermemory: error: unknown subcommand:
  'hook'` (exit 2) instead of running the hook. The port reproduces it.

### Left for later

Individual command handlers, the hook client and the stdio shim have
their own units.

## The credential detectors

Read at 465bc600. `credentials.py` (639 lines). Nothing in it reads the
machine: no file, clock, environment variable, random source or child
process. Every function is a function of its text; the only data consulted
is `re`'s word class (`\w`, behind `\b`), which is the interpreter's
Unicode 15.1 data and the crate's `unicode::is_word`. No trait is needed
and none was extended.

### The module by function

| function or table | lines | needs from the machine | status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `_PREFIXED_DETECTORS` (twelve patterns) | 85-175 | nothing (Unicode `\b`) | built, unit 1 |
| `_MIN_BODY_DIVERSITY`, `_is_masked_token` | 184-189 | nothing | built, unit 1 |
| `_is_spent_run` | 192-197 | nothing | built, unit 1 |
| `_PLACEHOLDER_VALUES`, `_PLACEHOLDER_WORDS`, `_NUMBER_SUFFIX_RE`, `_is_placeholder` | 269-319, 362-378 | nothing (`str.lower`) | built, unit 2 |
| `_DATETIME_SHAPE_RE`, `_looks_like_secret` | 332-336, 381-472 | nothing (`str.isupper`, `isalpha`, `isdigit`, `\w`, `\d`) | built, unit 2 |
| `_GENERIC_KEYWORD_RE`, `_URI_USERINFO_RE` | 238-265 | nothing (`re.IGNORECASE`, `\s`, `\b`, a lookbehind) | built, unit 3 |
| `CredentialMatch`, `_CONTEXT_CHARS`, `_merged_secret_spans`, `secret_spans` | 475-546 | nothing | built, unit 4 |
| `_redact_all`, `_safe_snippet`, `find_credential_markers` | 549-632 | nothing (`\s` in `re.sub`) | built, unit 4 |

The whole module is more than 600 lines of Rust: the generic rule's
pattern alone (an IGNORECASE alternation with a bounded prefix repetition,
a lookbehind and conversational separators) and the value gate's six
patterns each need a hand-written matcher. The cut is by leaves: unit 1
(the prefixed shapes) stands alone; unit 2 (the value gate) stands alone;
unit 3 (the two value patterns) calls nothing but returns the spans unit 2
judges; unit 4 joins them into spans, snippets and markers.

### Unit 1, built (`credentials::prefixed`)

`Detector` (twelve variants in `_PREFIXED_DETECTORS`' order, `DETECTORS`),
`Detector::kind` (the reference's labels: both GitHub patterns are
`github-token`, both Slack patterns `slack-token`), `Detector::find_iter`
(`regex.finditer(text)`: each `Match` with its span, its `body` group's
span where the pattern names one, and whether the `spent` group took
part), `Detector::pattern` (the reference's pattern text, checked
against the golden header), `is_masked_token` (`_is_masked_token`: a body of fewer than
`MIN_BODY_DIVERSITY` distinct characters; a body span outside the text,
which only a hand-built `Match` can carry, is no mask), `is_spent_run`, and
`prefixed_spans` (the first loop of `_merged_secret_spans`: every hit,
detectors in order and each detector's matches in order, spent runs and
masks left out, before the sort and merge of unit 4). Texts are code
points and offsets are code point indices, as a `str` match's are.

Each pattern is a hand-written matcher; no regex crate is used and none was
added. Per pattern, why the matcher answers as `re` does for every input:

- Every pattern but the PEM header opens with `\b` before an ASCII letter,
  so a start needs the previous code point to be no word character
  (`unicode::is_word`, Unicode `\w`: a Latin-1 letter or a CJK ideograph
  before `AKIA` is a word character, a lone surrogate is not). Every
  closing `\b` is read the same way at the end.
- AWS, the classic GitHub token, Google and SendGrid have fixed-length
  bodies: the matcher checks the literal prefix, the exact count of the
  ASCII class and `\b` after it. With no repetition of variable length
  there is nothing to backtrack into.
- Stripe (`[0-9A-Za-z]{24,}\b`) and the fine-grained GitHub token
  (`[0-9A-Za-z_]{22,}\b`, its class all word characters): greedy over the
  class's run, then giving back one character at a time to the minimum
  until `\b` holds. Inside a run of word characters `\b` never holds, so
  only the run's end can close; the matcher still gives back in general.
- `sk-`: the two lookaheads ask whether the `[A-Za-z0-9_-]` run after
  `sk-` holds an uppercase letter and a digit (the run is the same set of
  characters the lookahead's `*` reads), then the body gives back from the
  run's end to 20 until `\b` holds (`-` is no word character, so a
  boundary can fall inside the run). When that fails the `spent`
  alternative takes the rest of the run. The optional `(?:ant-|proj-)?`
  needs no start of its own: both prefixes lie inside the run, add no
  uppercase letter or digit, and only move the minimum end later, so the
  largest boundary the option finds is the largest the bare start finds,
  and the match spans the same text either way.
- Slack (`xox[abceprs]-`) and the app token (`xapp-`): the same with one
  digit lookahead and a minimum of 10 over `[0-9A-Za-z-]`.
- Vault (`hv[sbr]\.`): greedy over `[A-Za-z0-9_-]` with give-back to 24.
- JWT: the first two parts' `{8,}` repetitions stop only at a `.`, which
  their class excludes, so each part ends where its run ends and giving
  back cannot find another `.`; the third part gives back to 8 until `\b`;
  otherwise `spent` takes the run after `eyJ`.
- The PEM header: `-----BEGIN `, at most one of the six labels (none of
  them a prefix of `PRIVATE`, so trying the empty option after a label
  never matches), `PRIVATE KEY-----`, then the lookahead: spaces and tabs,
  an optional carriage return, a line feed, and either 16 characters of
  `[A-Za-z0-9+/=_-]` or `Proc-Type:` or `DEK-Info:`. Giving back spaces or
  the carriage return leaves a space, tab or carriage return where a line
  feed is needed, so the first reading is the only one. The match ends at
  the header.
- The scan: no pattern matches the empty string, so after a match the
  next search starts at its end, otherwise one code point on, as
  `finditer` does.

Time: each attempt reads at most the run after its prefix, and a spent run
or a token moves the scan past that run, so the scan is linear in the text
as the reference's is (its `spent` alternatives exist for this). On
inputs of about 300 KB (a run of nothing but one prefix, a body giving back
across 300,000 hyphens, repeated tokens and headers) the reference takes
14 to 24 ms each on darwin-arm64 with CPython 3.13.13; the release build is
held to 0.25 s per input (the fastest of three runs, so a busy runner
fails no run that one quiet run passes) and takes under 10 ms.

#### What the reference does that looks wrong (not changed)

- The AWS comment says "16 base32 chars"; the class is `[0-9A-Z]`, which
  admits `0`, `1`, `8` and `9`. Reproduction:
  `find_credential_markers("AKIA" + "0189ABCDEFGHIJKL")` reports
  `aws-access-key-id`.
- The masked-token guard reads only the patterns that name a `body` group
  (AWS and both GitHub patterns), though its comment speaks of masks of
  "bounded-body detectors". A Google or SendGrid mask fires:
  `find_credential_markers("AIza" + "X" * 35)` reports `google-api-key`,
  `find_credential_markers("SG." + "x" * 22 + "." + "x" * 43)` reports
  `sendgrid-api-key`.
- `\b` is Unicode: a key followed or preceded by a letter past ASCII is not
  seen. `find_credential_markers("AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLEé")` is empty.
- The `sk-`, Slack and Vault bodies include a trailing hyphen when a word
  character past ASCII follows it: in `"sk-A" + "BCDEFGHIJ0123456789-é"`
  the match is code points 0 to 24, the hyphen inside.

### Unit 2, built (`credentials::gate`)

The line ranges were confirmed against the source as it is now: the
tables at 269-319, `_DATETIME_SHAPE_RE` at 332-336, `_NUMBER_SUFFIX_RE` at
339-359, `_is_placeholder` at 362-378 and `_looks_like_secret` at 381-472.

`PLACEHOLDER_VALUES` and `PLACEHOLDER_WORDS` (the two tables in source
order), `NUMBER_SUFFIX_PATTERN`, `DATETIME_SHAPE_PATTERN` and
`INLINE_PATTERNS` (the pattern texts, checked against the golden header),
`MIN_VALUE_LEN`, `MAX_VALUE_LEN` and `MIN_VALUE_DIVERSITY` (12, 1,024 and
8, the numbers the function spells inline), `is_upper` (`str.isupper` of
one character: `Lu` and `Other_Uppercase`, so Roman numerals and circled
letters are uppercase and a titlecase letter is not), `number_suffix`
(`_NUMBER_SUFFIX_RE.search`: the span its one match removes),
`is_placeholder`, `datetime_shape` (`_DATETIME_SHAPE_RE.fullmatch`),
`looks_like_secret` and `looks_like_secret_str`. Texts are code points, as
a `str` is; every length is in code points.

No regex crate is used and none was added. Per pattern, why the matcher
answers as `re` does for every input:

- `_NUMBER_SUFFIX_RE` (`[-_]?(?<!\d)\d+$`): `$` holds at the end and before
  a final line feed, so the match must end at one of the two. The
  lookbehind lets `\d+` start only where a run of `\d` (Unicode decimal
  digits, `unicode::is_re_digit`) starts, so the only match is the whole
  run that ends there, with the one `-` or `_` before it, which the
  leftmost search takes. After it no second match is possible (the next
  start follows a digit, or is past the line feed where `\d+` fails), so
  `sub("", ...)` removes that span alone.
- `re.split(r"[-_]+", ...)`: splitting at each separator rather than each
  run adds only empty tokens, which `all(not t or ...)` passes.
  `rstrip("0123456789")` is ASCII digits only.
- `_DATETIME_SHAPE_RE`: each optional part opens with a character nothing
  after it can start with (`:` the seconds, `.` the fraction, `Z`, `z`,
  `+` and `-` the zone), and the greedy `\d+` and `\d{4,6}` are followed
  by no digit, so one reading decides. The basic alternative cannot match
  where the extended one read a `-` after four digits. `\d` is Unicode.
- `(?:\.{0,2}/|~/|[A-Za-z]:/)` through `re.match`: a prefix test of `/`,
  `./`, `../`, `~/` and an ASCII letter, colon and slash.
- `[a-z0-9_.\-]+(?:/[a-z0-9_.\-]+)+` through `fullmatch`: `/` is outside
  the class, so the pieces between slashes are the only reading: each
  non-empty and of the class, with at least one slash (the test runs only
  when the value holds one).
- `[A-Za-z_][\w.]*` and `[A-Za-z_][\w.]*\(.*\)` through `fullmatch`: `(`
  is not in `[\w.]`, so the run ends where the run of `\w` (Unicode) and
  `.` ends and giving back cannot find a `(`; then `.*` takes anything but
  a line feed up to the final `)`.
- `[A-Z][A-Z0-9]*(?:_[A-Z0-9]+)+` through `fullmatch`: the pieces between
  underscores, each non-empty and of `[A-Z0-9]`, the first character
  `[A-Z]` and at least one underscore.

Past ASCII the gate reads the interpreter's Unicode 15.1.0 data:
`str.strip` (`unicode::is_space`), `str.lower` with its expansions and
final sigma (`unicode::lower`), `str.isalpha`, `str.isdigit` (which,
unlike `\d`, holds for superscripts) and `str.isupper`. `len(set(v)) < 8`
counts distinct code points and stops at eight.

Time: every step reads the value a bounded number of times, and a value
over 1,024 code points is refused after the strips, so the gate is linear
in its input. `is_placeholder` is linear in any length, as the
reference's anchored suffix pattern is (a 200,000-digit run behind
`changeme` is read once).

#### What the reference does that looks wrong (not changed)

- The suffix strip reads Unicode digits (`\d`) and the token strip ASCII

### Units 3 and 4, built (`credentials::spans`)

The line ranges were confirmed against the source as it is now:
`_GENERIC_KEYWORD_RE` at 238-251, `_URI_USERINFO_RE` at 262-265,
`CredentialMatch` at 475-489, `_CONTEXT_CHARS` at 492, `_merged_secret_spans`
at 495-525, `secret_spans` at 528-546, `_redact_all` at 549-557,
`_safe_snippet` at 560-588 and `find_credential_markers` at 591-632.
Both units were built together: unit 3 alone is two statics and two
calls, and every fixture of it is also a fixture of unit 4.

Per pattern (pyre decision, rule 4): `_GENERIC_KEYWORD_RE` (tier T3),
`_URI_USERINFO_RE` (T1) and `_safe_snippet`'s `\s+` (T1) are each a
`LazyLock<Result<pyre::Regex, RegexError>>` built from the reference's own
pattern text and flags (`GENERIC_KEYWORD_PATTERN`, `URI_USERINFO_PATTERN`,
`SNIPPET_SPACE_PATTERN`, the first two checked against the golden header,
IGNORECASE as the flag), run through `finditer` and `sub`; none is matched
by hand. All three are literal patterns of the reference, so the engine's
inventory already holds them (`gen_pyre_atom`'s scan and the tier table of
pyre-7); nothing was added to it.

- `generic_values`, `uri_values`: the `value` group's span of every match,
  read through `Match::group` by the group number the pattern's names give.
- `secret_spans` (`_merged_secret_spans` and `secret_spans`):
  `prefixed_spans`, then the generic and URI spans whose value passes
  `looks_like_secret`, a stable sort by start, and the union of overlaps
  keeping the first kind.
- `redact_all`: the markers spliced right to left.
- `safe_snippet`: the window `[max(0, start - 24), min(len, end + 24))`,
  with no trailing context for `private-key-pem`; every span that overlaps
  it spliced right to left with Python's slice clamping; line feeds to
  spaces; `\s+` to one space through the engine's `sub` with the literal
  `" "`; `str.strip` (`unicode::py_strip`); `...` on each cut edge.
- `find_credential_markers`: per detector the first match that is not a
  spent run or a mask (a kind already reported adds nothing), then the
  first generic and the first URI value that pass the gate. The merged
  spans are read once and shared by every snippet, which answers as the
  reference's call per snippet does. `CredentialMatch` holds the kind and
  the snippet. `_str` conveniences take a `&str`.

The engine runs with no budget, so it answers or panics on an engine
fault; it never answers a silent no-match. Rule 6's step claim is tested:
the steps of the longest run of `_GENERIC_KEYWORD_RE` over dense `_`,
`-`, `a_`, `-a` and long-segment runs, prose with and without keywords
and repeated `Authorization: Bearer` headers at 2n are within 2.2 times
the steps at n, and the same for `_URI_USERINFO_RE`.

## The server builder (`builder.py`)

Read at 42c271b6. Only the two pure schema scrubs are built; they read
nothing from the machine.

| function | lines | needs from the machine | status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `_strip_titles` | 294-332 | nothing | built |
| `_fold_nullable` | 335-378 | nothing | built |
| `_Served`, `build_server`, `_register_tools`, `_strip_schema_titles` | rest | the MCP server, the tool table, pydantic | later units |

`builder::strip_titles` and `builder::fold_nullable` walk a
`pyvalue::PyValue` tree in place with an explicit stack: each node's edit
reads only that node, and the walk then visits what the node holds after
the edit, so the order of visits does not change the answer. Both descend
into a dict held under `properties`, `$defs` or `definitions` by value
only, and into every other value and list item.

- `strip_titles`: `title` popped, `default` deleted when it is `None`.
- `fold_nullable`: `{"type": "null"} in branches` and `branches[1] ==
  {"type": "null"}` are true exactly when the branch is a dict of the one
  pair `("type", "null")` (one pair makes key order moot, a `str` value
  makes numeric equality across types moot), so that predicate is written
  instead of a general equality. The fold needs a list of two branches,
  one of them null, the other a dict whose `type` is a `str` and that has
  no `anyOf` or `$ref`, and no `type` on the node; then `anyOf` is
  deleted and the other's keys but `type` and then `type = [x, "null"]`
  are applied with `dict.update`'s rule (an existing key keeps its
  position, a new one is appended).

Fixtures: `tests/contract/gen_builder_schema.py` writes
`builder_schema.jsonl`, not gated: 54 hand-written trees (each guard of
both walks, the named maps, and two trees copied once in the shape
pydantic emits, so no row follows the installed pydantic), each as JSON
text with the tree after each walk and after both. Tests:
`golden_builder_schema.rs`, and the builder cases of
`credentials_spans_kills.rs` and `credentials_spans_robustness.rs`.

Stated difference: the reference recurses, so a tree nested past
Python's recursion limit (about 1,000 levels, less the caller's frames)
raises RecursionError; the port finishes it. The depth at which the
reference raises depends on its caller's stack and cannot be reproduced.

What the reference does that looks wrong (not changed): every value but
the named maps is walked as a schema node, so a `default`, `enum` or
`const` value that is an object loses its `title` key and its `default:
null` entry: `{"default": {"default": null, "title": "kept?"}}` becomes
`{"default": {}}`.

## What a memory claims (`claims.py`)

Read at 465bc600 (`claims.py`, 1,159 lines). The module holds the claim
record and its wire string, the path spellings a claim is looked for
under, the declare-time oracle that reads the worktree, and the drift
index that reads a `git log -p -U0` stream. Most of it needs
`ast.literal_eval` and `repr` of the values it returns, which the crate
does not have yet, so the module is cut into units, leaves first.

Unit 2 is the literal reader: `ast.literal_eval` over the expressions a
claim value and a changed line can hold (with the interpreter's
tokenizer, string prefixes and escapes, numbers, containers, unary and
binary `+`/`-` on numbers, the recursion limit) and `_canonical_repr`
over what it returns (float `repr` is `float_repr`; set order is the
sort of the canonical texts). Unit 3 is the index and the scoring, pure
over a stream of text. Unit 4 is the oracle, with the file system as the
`fsdata` trait; its symbol and literal kinds need `ast.parse` of a
module's top level, which is a unit of its own.

### Unit 1, built (`claims`)

`src/claims/mod.rs` (499 lines when built as `src/claims.rs`; moved
unchanged when unit 2 was added, no dependency added). Text is `&[u32]`, as in
`unicode`, since a claim path may hold a lone surrogate.

- `Claim { kind, rel_path, name, value }` with `Kind` (`path`, `symbol`,
  `literal`, `absent`) and `render`. The reference's `kind` is any `str`
  and renders the literal form for any kind it does not name; the port
  holds the four kinds `parse_claim` makes, so another kind cannot be
  written.
- `control_character`, `lone_surrogate`: the first such code point.
- `is_identifier` is `_IDENT_RE.match`.
- `claim_reason_is_indeterminate`: a substring test.
- `path_key`, `spellings_capped`, `stored_spellings` over `unicode`'s
  NFC and NFD, with `_component_forms`' order (as written, composed,
  decomposed, repeats dropped) and `itertools.product`'s order (the
  first component outermost). The product is taken with a saturating
  multiply: past `MAX_SPELLINGS` only the comparison is read.
- `claim_paths`: distinct paths in declaration order.
- `binding_token` (`_binding_token`), `hunk_lines`, `is_mark_hash`
  (`_MARK_HASH_RE.fullmatch`), `header_path` (`_header_path`) and
  `patch_header_path` (`_patch_header_path`, its two `set[str]` as
  `PathSet`s, hash sets, so each add is constant time as in the
  reference; order is no part of the answer).
- `claim_paths` drops repeats through a hash set, and
  `claim_reason_is_indeterminate` searches for the marker by Knuth,
  Morris and Pratt, both linear in their input as the reference is.
- `hunk_lines` answers the Python int as its decimal text: the two
  counts are summed digit by digit, so a count of any length within the
  limit is exact. `Err(IntTooLong)` is `int()`'s ValueError on a digit
  run past 4,300 digits, leading zeros counted. Only the two counts are
  read as ints: a start line of any length is accepted.

Each pattern is a hand-written matcher; no `regex` crate is used.

- `_IDENT_RE` `^[A-Za-z_]\w*$`: `re`'s `$` matches at the end and before
  one final line feed, so `"name\n"` matches; `\w` is `unicode::is_word`.
- `_DEF_RE`: `async` and one or more blanks (space or tab) are optional;
  then `def` or `class`, blanks, an identifier, blanks, then `(`, `[` or
  `:`. No backtracking can change the answer: every step after the
  identifier needs a character `\w` does not hold, and `async` without
  the blanks begins neither keyword.
- `_ASSIGN_RE`: the identifier and blanks are as above. The annotation
  `(?::[^=\n]+)?` can end anywhere before the first `=` or line feed
  after the colon, and the operator group holds no `=`, so a match
  through the annotation exists exactly when that first stop is a `=`
  at least two code points after the colon and not followed by another
  `=`. Without the annotation, a match is one of the twelve operators or
  none, then `=` not followed by `=`. Only existence and the identifier
  are read.
- `_HUNK_RE`: each `\d+` is maximal (the next character must be `,`, a
  space or nothing a digit is), and the optional `,\d+` is taken when
  present and skipped otherwise; skipping it where it is present always
  fails. `\d` is `unicode::is_re_digit`, and a digit's value is its
  place in its run of ten (as `int` reads it).
- `_MARK_HASH_RE` with `fullmatch`: exactly 40 or 64 of `[0-9a-f]`.

### Unit 2, built (`claims::literal`)

`src/claims/literal.rs` (343 lines, no dependency added), re-exported
from `claims`. It reads values with `pysyntax::literal::literal_eval`
and writes them with `pysyntax::literal::canonical_repr` (lane pylit),
and quotes a text in a message with `pyvalue::repr_str`. Line ranges
were confirmed against `claims.py` at 860b002d.

- `parse_claim` (234-303): `str.strip()` is `claims::strip`, whose space
  set is `unicode::is_space` (`str.isspace`, the set `str.strip()` uses);
  after `!` it is `lstrip()` of the same set, once. `str.partition` is
  taken at the first `::` and then the first `=`. The length cap counts
  code points (`len`), read after the strip and before `!` is dropped.
  Each message is the reference's text, em dash and backticks included;
  the absence message quotes the whole stripped claim, the others the text
  after `!`. Any failure of `literal_eval` or `_canonical_repr` (an int
  past 4,300 digits made by a hex literal, too deep a nesting) is the
  "is not a Python literal" refusal, as `except Exception` makes it.
- `parse_claims` (323-365): the count cap is read before any entry; then
  each entry in order, the first refusal ending the list; the control
  character and lone surrogate rules on the path with `U+%04X`;
  duplicates by `Claim.render` through a hash set, first kept.
- `load_claims` (366-382) takes a `PyValue` slice: an entry that is not
  `PyValue::Str` is skipped (`isinstance(entry, str)`), and a refused one;
  repeats stay.
- `claim_is_addressable` (448-503): every kind but `literal` is; a value
  that does not read back is not; a container (tuple, list, set, dict) is
  not. `literal_eval` never returns a `frozenset`.
- `governed_claim_paths` (505-518): `claim_paths` less every path whose
  `path_key` (NFC) an unaddressable claim holds, so one blocked spelling
  blocks every other.
- `rhs_repr` (`_rhs_repr`, 736-750), `string_fragment` (753-779) and
  `anchors_from_value` (782-803, `_MIN_ANCHOR_CHARS` as
  `MIN_ANCHOR_CHARS`, 12): `rstrip(",")` drops every trailing comma,
  `removesuffix(")")` and `removeprefix("(")` one each; anchors are the
  lines of a `str` value split at line feeds only, stripped, of at least
  twelve code points, first spelling first (`dict` order).

The pylex gaps, closed by unit claims-6: `literal_eval` answered
`LiteralError::NeedsIdentTable` for a name past ASCII whose NFKC is
`True`, `False`, `None` or `set`, and `LiteralError::NeedsNameTable` for a
`\N{...}` escape, and no longer answers either. Each function here
returns such a gap as its own error
(`ClaimError::Gap` from `parse_claim` and `parse_claims`, the
`LiteralError` from the others), never as the refusal or as `None`, so a
caller can tell "the reference refuses" from "the port cannot say";
`ClaimError::Gap` stays until unit 5d removes the variants.

No pattern of `claims.py` is read by this unit: it holds no `re` call,
so nothing is added to the engine's inventory.

### Reference findings (reproduced and pinned)

- `hunk_lines` reads any Unicode decimal digit: `hunk_lines("@@ -1,٩
  +1 @@")` is 10, and `build_binding_index` reads a hunk there. git
  prints ASCII digits only, so a file line shaped so is read as a hunk
  header. Pinned in `claims.jsonl`.
- `_patch_header_path` strips the target with `str.strip()`: a path
  ending in a space or in any Unicode space loses it (`"+++ b/x \t"`
  names `x`, `"+++ b/x　"` names `x`), so the index names a path
  that is not the file git changed. Pinned in `claims.jsonl`.
- `_IDENT_RE` accepts one trailing line feed (`"a\n"`). `parse_claim`
  strips the name first, so no claim reaches it with one.
- `string_fragment` removes one `)` before it removes the `(`, and only
  after `rstrip(",")`: the line `'a',)` (a string with a trailing comma
  closing a parenthesised group) is read as the tuple `('a',)` and gives
  `None`, so a changed line of that shape is not matched against a
  claimed value. `string_fragment("'a',)")` is `None` and
  `string_fragment("'a'),")` is `'a'`. Pinned in `claims_literal.jsonl`.

### Unit 3, built (`claim_drift`)

`src/claim_drift.rs`, read at 825-1159 of `claims.py` on `v9`. No
dependency added; nothing here reads a file, a clock or git. The module
is new beside `claims.rs`, which it reuses (`binding_token`, `hunk_lines`,
`is_mark_hash`, `header_path`, `patch_header_path`, `strip`, `PathSet`,
`COMMIT_MARK`).

- `LiteralLines` is the trait for the four literal helpers the index and
  the scoring call: `string_fragment`, `rhs_repr` (`_rhs_repr`),
  `anchors_from_value` and `claimed_str` (`ast.literal_eval(cite.value)`
  when it is a `str`). It has no error: every reference call site catches
  `Exception` and reads a failure as None or `()`. Unit 2 implements it
  over the literal reader; until then a caller supplies it.
- `Headers` is `_Headers`: the open section's path from `header_path`,
  the paths its extended header lines touch, and `only` (`header_only`),
  each touched path's commit recorded when the section closes. `copy
  from` is no header line (only `copy to` names a path); `rename from`
  and `deleted ` lines mark the path deleted.
- `build_binding_index(diff_text, lit) -> Result<Index, IntTooLong>`:
  `Index` has a field per key of the reference's dict. A binding's key is
  `(path, "def" | "assign", name)`, the reference's tuple. `Err` is
  `int()`'s ValueError on a hunk count past 4,300 digits, which the
  reference raises out of the function; it is read only where a hunk
  header matches and a path is set, as in the reference. A count is held
  saturated at `u64::MAX`: no stream holds that many lines, so the loop
  and the mismatch test answer as with the exact int.
- `claim_level_drift(cite, index, lit) -> Drift`: the eight keys. The
  reference's `hit` is `anchor_shas` itself (`hit = anchor_shas`, then
  `|=`), so `anchor_shas` holds every anchor and fragment commit; the
  port fills one set. The code points of the claimed value are gathered
  once; a fragment longer than the value or holding a code point the
  value lacks is not in it, and any other fragment is searched for by
  Knuth, Morris and Pratt. So a fragment foreign to a long value costs
  its own length, as with the skip table of `in`, and none costs more
  than the two lengths together. `Kind` has four members, so
  the reference's final `else` is the literal kind.
- `Index::render` and `Drift::render` give the reference's keys in order
  as a `PyValue`, each set a sorted list and each dict a list of `[key,
  value]` pairs sorted by key, which the fixtures compare after
  `json.dumps` with ASCII and compact separators.

Patterns: no new one. `_HUNK_RE` is `claims::hunk_lines` (already built
by hand, rule 3 of the `pyre` decision: a matcher built stays and gains
the engine's cross-check); past a match the header's shape is fixed, so
the two counts are read by a walk over it, not a second matcher.
`_MARK_HASH_RE.fullmatch` is `claims::is_mark_hash`. Nothing is added to
the engine's inventory.

Fixtures: `tests/contract/gen_claim_drift.py`, three files.

- `claim_drift.jsonl` (11 rows, not gated, class i): nine streams (each
  binding shape, extended headers of every kind, renames, copies,
  deletes, empty files, quoted and ` b/` paths, surrogates, content lines
  that read `diff --git`, `@@`, `+++` or a commit mark, `\ No newline`
  markers, short and long hunks, counts of 0, a Unicode digit and past
  `u64`, bad marks, a hunk before any path, an empty stream) with 32
  claims of the four kinds; a `vocab` row and a `sweep` row: 2,000 seeded
  streams of 24 lines (a 64-bit linear congruential generator, seed
  20261121) with five claims each, by SHA-256 of the renders. Each row
  records the literal answers it asked for and the test replays them, so
  the file does not follow the Python release.
- `claim_drift_unicode.jsonl` (17 blocks, gated on Unicode, class ii):
  every code point at both edges of a changed line (`str.strip`) and as
  a hunk count (`\d`), in blocks of 0x10000, by SHA-256.
- `claim_drift_python.jsonl` (8 rows, not gated, class i): counts of
  4,300 and 4,301 digits in either place, with and without a path. The
  generator sets `int`'s digit limit to 4,300 itself, the limit every
  supported release (3.11 to 3.14) has, and the rows hold no message, so
  the file is the same under every release.

Tests: `golden_claim_drift` (`claim_drift_every_case`,
`claim_drift_unicode_every_case`, `claim_drift_python_every_case`);
`claim_drift_kills` (12: the `\ No newline` marker, content read by
count, the backed-up short hunk, a bad mark keeping the last commit, a

20,000-line hunks linear in their
length, counts at and past `u64::MAX` and at 4,300 digits, 50,000

20,000 fragments foreign to a long claimed value,
odd one-line streams).

### Reference findings (unit 3)

- `+++ "b/sp ace.py"` (git's quoted spelling) names the path with its
  quotes, `"b/sp ace.py"`, since `_patch_header_path` strips only a bare
  `b/`; a claim on `sp ace.py` misses that section. Pinned in
  `claim_drift.jsonl` (stream `quoted`).
- A commit mark that is not a full hash keeps the previous commit for the
  lines after it, so its lines are credited to the commit before. Pinned
  (stream `mismatches`).
