## Symbol citations checked against a module (`symbols.py`)

Read at 65aea201 (`symbols.py`, 509 lines). The module parses the
two-token citation shape ("`name` in `pkg/mod.py`") out of a body,
resolves the cited module under the record's worktree root and asks the
module's AST whether the name is bound there. It is advisory: one caller
(`memory_verify`), no staleness input. Its parser needs two patterns the
regular expression engine is to run, and its index needs `ast.parse`, so
the module is cut into units, the checker first.

### The map, function by function

| function | lines | needs from the machine | status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `_MAX_CITATIONS_PER_BODY`, `_MAX_MODULE_PATH_LEN`, `_MAX_SYMBOL_LEN`, `_MAX_BODY_SCAN_CHARS`, `_MAX_MODULE_BYTES`, `_FILE_SUFFIXES` | 98-136 | nothing | built (symcheck) |
| `_SYMBOL_IN_MODULE`, `_SUPPRESSING_PROSE` (re.I), `_SUPPRESSION_LOOKBACK` | 137-182 | the regular expression engine | symbols-1b |
| `SymbolCitation`, `SymbolDriftReport` | 183-255 | nothing | built (symcheck) |
| `extract_symbol_citations` | 256-288 | the two patterns | symbols-1b |
| `check_symbol_citations` | 289-357 | the file system, `ast.parse` | built (symcheck), citations an argument |
| `_tier` | 358-378 | nothing | built (symcheck) |
| `_live_root` | 380-392 | `Path.resolve`, `is_dir` | built (symcheck) |
| `_resolve_module` | 393-421 | `Path.resolve`, `is_file` | built (symcheck) |
| `_module_bindings` | 422-451 | `stat`, `read_text`, `ast.parse` | built (symcheck), the parse a trait |
| `_top_level_names`, `_all_names` | 452-509 | the AST | with the Python parser (claims-5c) |

### Unit symcheck, built (`symbols`)

`src/symbols.rs` (382 lines, no dependency added). Text is
`&[u32]` (`PyStr`): a citation may hold a lone surrogate.

- The bounds are constants of the same names; the ones the checker does
  not read (the extraction's caps) wait for symbols-1b's use.
- `SymbolCitation` with `Binding` (the five strings), `text` is
  `__str__`. `SymbolDriftReport` with `missing`, `truthy` (`__bool__`)
  and `to_dict` (keys in the reference's order, `unconfirmed` only when
  there is one).
- `check_symbol_citations(citations, worktree_root, anchor, machine,
  names)`: `citations` is what `extract_symbol_citations(body)` answers,
  since the parser waits for the engine. `anchor` is `ClaimAnchor` as the
  checker reads it (`root`, `convicting`); it takes precedence over
  `worktree_root` as in the reference: with an anchor, its root alone is
  read, even when it is None. No citation answers the empty report before
  any root is resolved. One read per distinct module, in a map as the
  reference's `cache`.
- `ModuleNames::names(source)` stands for `ast.parse` and the two walks:
  None for SyntaxError, ValueError and RecursionError. The Python parser
  lanes implement it; the tests replay the reference's names by the
  SHA-256 of the text, so a text read otherwise than `read_text` reads it
  finds nothing.
- `Machine { fs, flavour, cwd }`: the file system is `fsdata::Fs`,
  `Path.resolve(strict=False)` is `fsdata::realpath::realpath` with the
  working directory an argument, `is_dir` and `is_file` are `Fs::stat`'s
  kind (any error is no, as `os.path.isdir` and `Path.is_file` read an
  error), `st_size` is `Fs::stat`'s.
- A path is `os.fsencode`d: UTF-8, U+DC80 to U+DCFF as the bytes they
  escape. A code point that does not encode (another lone surrogate) is
  written as a NUL: the reference raises UnicodeEncodeError, a
  ValueError, at the first `lstat` of the component holding it, and the
  walk raises ValueError on a NUL at the same place; both callers read it
  as None.
- `is_relative_to` is a component prefix test on the two resolved paths
  (`/` holds every absolute path).
- `read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")` is the bytes read
  through `Fs::open` and `Fs::read`, decoded with each bad sequence one
  U+FFFD (the crate's UTF-8 replace decode, `String::from_utf8_lossy`,
  which takes CPython's maximal subparts), then text mode's universal
  newlines: `\r\n` and a lone `\r` read as `\n`.
- The Windows flavour: `realpath` is not ported there (Linear ENG-124),
  so a call that resolves a root declines (`Declined::NotPorted`) where
  the reference on Windows answers. A call with no citation, or no root,
  answers the empty report on either flavour.

Patterns: the checker reads none. `_SYMBOL_IN_MODULE` and
`_SUPPRESSING_PROSE` are new patterns under the decision's rule 4: they
are never matched by hand and wait for the engine (symbols-1b), and both
go into the engine's inventory with that unit.

Fixtures (`gen_symbols`): each case a tree in a fresh scratch directory,
the citations given to `check_symbol_citations` in place of the parser's
answer, the root spelled relative to the case's directory, and the names
`ast.parse` gave each file with the digest of its text.
`symbols.jsonl` (ungated) holds the tiers, dotted names, the module
spellings refused before the file system is asked, roots missing, a
file, relative, dotted, with a NUL or a surrogate, the anchor's
precedence and conviction, the size bound (2 MiB read, one byte more
not), text that is not UTF-8, CRLF and CR newlines, a NUL, a BOM, a
syntax error and identifiers that NFKC folds. `symbols_platform.jsonl`
(gated on the platform and the Python release, and POSIX only) holds links (inside, out of, and to the
root, dangling, a loop), names that differ only in case, names ending in
a dot or a space, a FIFO and a mode-000 module; its native test writes
the tree to disk and reads it through `StdFs`.

### Reference findings

- On a file system that folds case (macOS, Windows), `is_relative_to`
  compares spellings: a root given as `<dir>/Root` for the directory
  `<dir>/root`, with a module reached through a link whose target spells
  `<dir>/root/...`, resolves outside the root by text though it is the
  same directory, and the citation is unresolved. Conversely `PKG/A.py`
  is checked against `pkg/a.py` there and unresolved on Linux.
- A module spelled with a trailing dot or space (`pkg/a.py.`) is
  unresolved on POSIX and, through Win32's name rules, the file `a.py`
  on Windows; the report then names a module spelling that is no file's.
- Under 3.11 and 3.12 `Path.resolve` raises RuntimeError on a link loop
  and neither `_live_root` nor `_resolve_module` catches it: a cited
  module that is a link to itself (`pkg/loop.py` -> `loop.py`) makes
  `check_symbol_citations` raise, so the verify call dies, where 3.13
  answers the citation unresolved. The port answers as 3.13; the row is
  in `symbols_platform.jsonl`, which is gated on the release.
- `read_text` translates newlines before `ast.parse`, so the size bound
  counts bytes the parse never sees; nothing turns on it.

### Left for later units

symbols-1b: `extract_symbol_citations` with `_SYMBOL_IN_MODULE` and
`_SUPPRESSING_PROSE` on the engine, and `check_symbol_citations` taking
a body. With the Python parser (claims-5c): `_top_level_names` and
`_all_names` as a `ModuleNames`.

## Python source as CPython reads it (`pysyntax`)

`claims.py` calls `ast.literal_eval(text)` at lines 296 (`parse_claim`),
497 (`claim_is_addressable`), 696 (`check_claim`), 748 (`_rhs_repr`), 776
(`string_fragment`), 793 (`anchors_from_value`) and 1131
(`claim_level_drift`), and `ast.parse` of a module at 672 (`check_claim`).
The reference is CPython 3.13.13 itself: `ast.literal_eval` strips `' \t'`
from the left, parses in eval mode and evaluates the tree's literals. The
module `pysyntax` reproduces that in lanes, each in its own file so that
none edits another's.

| part | reproduces | needs from the machine | status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `lex` | the eval-mode tokenizer (`Parser/lexer/lexer.c`'s `tok_get_normal_mode`), the newline translation of `_PyTokenizer_FromString`, the string decoders (`_PyUnicode_DecodeUnicodeEscapeInternal`, `_PyBytes_DecodeEscape`) and the number readers (`parsenumber`, `int`'s 4,300-digit limit) | nothing | built (unit pylex) |
| `literal` | the eval-mode parser over `lex`'s tokens, `literal_eval`'s evaluation and `claims._canonical_repr` | nothing | built (unit pylit) |
| `module_lex`, `fstring_lex` | the module-mode tokenizer for `ast.parse` at 672 (unit 5a) and its f-string modes (5b, first part); the statement grammar (5c) and the top-level binding read (5d) follow | nothing | 5a built (unit pymodlex), 5b first part built (unit pyfstring) |
| `module_expr` | the expression grammar of `ast.parse` over those tokens (5b2): acceptance, the first pass's actions, the parser's stack limit, `ast2obj`'s depth, and the tree with the names `symbols._all_names` reads | the C recursion limit of the host's CPython build (a `cfg` constant) | built (unit pyexpr) |
| the XID tables | whether a name past ASCII is an identifier (`verify_identifier`) | Unicode tables (`unicode::xid`) | built (unit claims-6) |
| `\N{...}` | the Unicode name table (`getcode`) | Unicode tables (`unicode::names`) | built (unit claims-6) |

### The tokenizer (`lex`)

`literal_tokens(text)` strips `' \t'` and calls `lex`, which refuses a NUL
or a lone surrogate (CPython raises for both, the second when it encodes
the text), translates `\r\n` and `\r` to `\n`, and returns the translated
text with its tokens: NAME, NUMBER (`Int` as canonical decimal text for
`PyValue::int_from_decimal`, `Float`, `Imag`), STRING (`Str` or `Bytes`,
decoded) and OP, each with its span, or one `LexError`. Comments,
continuation lines and blank lines yield nothing. No function recurses;
brackets are a stack held to `MAX_LEVEL` (200 open, the 201st refused).

- Lines: a line outside brackets whose first token is indented (spaces,
  tabs, form feeds resetting the column, continuation lines in between)
  is refused, as eval mode refuses an INDENT; a NEWLINE ends the
  expression, after which only blank and comment lines may follow;
  whitespace after the last newline is an indent too (`"1\n  "` raises).
  A backslash must end its line and a line must follow it.
- Names: a run of ASCII letters, digits, `_` and code points past ASCII.
  A run holding one past ASCII must be an identifier
  (`verify_identifier`: `unicode::xid::is_identifier` over the raw run,
  before any normalization), else it is refused; the NAME token keeps
  the raw text. The parser keeps such a name by its NFKC, so the literal
  reader reads it there (below).
- Numbers: `tok_decimal_tail` (one underscore between digits), the radix
  forms with an underscore allowed after the prefix (`0x_1`), a digit
  past the radix refused, leading zeros refused unless every digit is
  zero, fractions, exponents, `j`, and `verify_end_of_number`: a letter or
  digit after a number is refused unless it begins `and`, `else`, `for`,
  `if`, `in`, `is`, `not` or `or` (CPython warns there). Underscores are
  stripped; a decimal integer of more than 4,300 digits is refused, as
  3.13 refuses it at parse (radix literals and all-zero literals are
  exempt); radix literals are converted to decimal in limbs of 10**18;
  floats are read by Rust's correctly rounded parser (`1e309` is
  infinity).
- Strings: the prefixes `tok_get_normal_mode` accepts (`b`, `r`, `u`, `f`
  in any case and the orders it allows; `u` never with `r` or `b`, so
  `ur''` is a name then a string), single and triple quotes, a backslash
  skipping the next character while the end is found. Bytes hold ASCII
  source characters only, raw or not. Non-raw str: `\\ \' \" \a \b \f \n
  \r \t \v`, backslash-newline dropped, up to three octal digits (up to
  0o777), `\x` with two hex digits, `\u` with four, `\U` with eight (past
  U+10FFFF refused), lone surrogates kept, an unknown escape kept with its
  backslash (a backslash before a code point past ASCII included). Bytes:
  the same less `\u`, `\U` and `\N`, octal masked to a byte (`b'\777'` is
  `b'\xff'`). `\N{name}` in a non-raw str: the name runs to the next
  `}` and is read by `unicode::names::lookup`; an empty, unclosed or
  unknown name refuses the literal, at the first such escape.
- f-strings: an `f` prefix yields one `FString` token, its end found
  without reading the replacement fields, and lexing stops there: the
  literal reader refuses any text holding one, so what follows is not
  read (`"f'{1}' 0x"` lexes where CPython raises; both are a refusal for
  `literal_eval`). An f-string with no closing quote is refused.

Every failure is `LexError::Syntax` with a short kind; the callers catch
every exception, so only which texts fail matters.

No regular expression is involved: the reference is C code, not a pattern.

Cost: linear in the text, except the conversion of a radix literal to
decimal, which grows as Karatsuba multiplication does (about n**1.6 in
its digits). The digits are split at a power of two, each half converted
to limbs of 10**18 and the halves joined as `high * radix**m + low`, with
the powers `radix**(2**j)` kept; a few hundred digits are converted
directly. CPython converts a radix literal in linear time and keeps it
binary; the literal reader needs decimal text. `pysyntax_robustness`
holds ten times the digits under the bound for linear growth, which a
quadratic conversion fails, and `pysyntax_kills` checks the split
conversion against digit-at-a-time conversion across the split points.

### Fixtures

`tests/contract/gen_pysyntax.py` writes two files. `pysyntax.jsonl` is
not gated: for the escape, string, prefix, number, line and bound texts
it holds what `literal_eval` returns or raises (by exception type) and
nothing else, with the escape sweep below and a sweep of the number texts
without a sign by value, all of which 3.11, 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14 answer
alike; `pysyntax_values` checks that a refusal is a text `literal_eval`
refuses and one literal token's value equals its value.
`pysyntax_python.jsonl` is gated on the
Python release as a whole (the tokenizer's rules, the messages it is
classed by and the digit limit are 3.13.13's); under another interpreter
the generator writes the header alone, naming the interpreter, and the
Rust test sets that file aside. Each row holds the text, the tokens
`tokenize` reads, how `ast.parse` in eval mode ends (`ok`, `lex` for a
tokenizer or decoder error by its message, `syntax`, `other`) and what
`literal_eval` returns or raises. `golden_pysyntax` checks: a text the
parse reads lexes (a name past ASCII aside, which `literal_eval` refuses);
a `lex` error is refused (unless lexing stopped at an f-string); a refusal
is a text `literal_eval` refuses; the tokens equal `tokenize`'s; one
literal token's value equals `literal_eval`'s. Two sweep rows pin, by
count and SHA-256: every code point below U+0250 after a backslash in the
four kinds of literal, followed by nothing, `7` or `41` (7,104 texts),
and 20,000 texts of one to seven characters of number syntax drawn by a
fixed LCG. `pysyntax_kills` and `pysyntax_robustness` hold the rest.

### The literal reader (`literal`)

`literal_eval(text) -> Result<Literal, LiteralError>` reproduces CPython
3.13.13's `ast.literal_eval` (`Lib/ast.py`: `_convert`, `_convert_num`,
`_convert_signed_num`, the `set()` call and the complex `BinOp` rule)
over `lex::literal_tokens`. `canonical_repr(&Literal)` reproduces
`claims._canonical_repr` (`claims.py` 204-231). `Literal::is_container`
and `Literal::as_str` serve the callers in `claims`.

- Forms read: constants (str, bytes, int, float, complex, `True`,
  `False`, `None`, `...`), adjacent strings of one kind joined (str next
  to bytes is refused, as the parser refuses it), parentheses, tuples
  (`(1,)`, `()`, a bare `1,` or `1, 2` at the top only), lists, non-empty
  sets, dicts without `**`, the call `set()` (also `(set)()`, since
  parentheses make no node), one sign on an int, float or complex
  constant (`-(1)` too; never a bool, never a sign on a sign), and a
  signed int or float plus or minus an unsigned complex constant. Every
  other token sequence is one `LiteralError::Invalid`: a text that parses
  to a non-literal (ValueError) and one that does not parse (SyntaxError)
  are not told apart, since every caller catches `Exception`.
  A name past ASCII is read by its NFKC (`_PyPegen_new_identifier`):
  `set` is the name `set`, and every other is refused, those reading
  `True`, `False` or `None` included (the parser raises ValueError for
  them; they are no constants). `NeedsIdentTable` and `NeedsNameTable`
  from `lex` pass through, though `lex` no longer answers them.
- Arithmetic is 3.13's: `x + cj` is `complex(x, 0.0) + cj`, so the real
  part is `x + 0.0` (`-0.0+0j` is `0j`) and the imaginary part `0.0 + c`
  or `0.0 - c` (`0.0-0j` is `0j`); 3.14 changed mixed arithmetic, which
  is why the fixture is gated on the release. An int operand is rounded
  to a float correctly; past the float range it is refused
  (OverflowError). A minus on a complex negates both parts (`-0j` is
  `(-0-0j)`).
- Sets and dicts: each member is reduced to a key by Python equality
  (an integral number, bool, int, integral float or complex with a zero
  imaginary part, by its exact decimal text; another float by its bits;
  a complex by its parts with `-0.0` as `0.0`; str and bytes apart;
  tuples by their members), so `1 == 1.0 == True == (1+0j)`, `0.0 ==
  -0.0`, and a big int equals a float only when the float's exact value
  is that int. A list, set or dict member or key is refused (TypeError).
  A set keeps the first of equal members and a dict the first of equal
  keys with the last value, as CPython's `set` and `dict` do. Hashing the
  keys keeps a large set linear.
- `canonical_repr`: `set()` for an empty set, sets and dict items sorted
  by their canonical text (code point order, a dict's pairs as Python
  tuples sort), a one-element tuple with its comma, and the scalars by
  `repr`: `pyvalue::repr_str`, `float_repr::repr`, an int's decimal text
  (ValueError past 4,300 digits, which only a radix literal reaches,
  since `lex` refuses longer decimal literals), `bytes.__repr__` (`'`
  unless the bytes hold `'` and no `"`, `\t \n \r`, `\xhh` outside
  printable ASCII, backslash and the quote escaped) and CPython's
  `complex_repr` (the `'r'` format without `.0`, the real part left out
  only when it is +0.0, the imaginary part signed).
- Depth: `lex` holds brackets to 200, and one sign and one binary `+`
  or `-` are the most a literal holds per level (a second is refused
  where it is read, without recursion), so the parser's, the
  evaluation's and the canonical text's recursion is bounded by about
  three frames per bracket. That early refusal, like the others the
  reader makes (a `.` trailer, a bytes token after a str, the `set()`
  trailer's closing bracket, a float key that is not finite), bounds
  the work alone: the later steps refuse the same texts, so no answer
  depends on it.

No regular expression is involved: the reference is `Lib/ast.py` and the
C parser.

Fixtures: `tests/contract/gen_pysyntax_literal.py` writes
`pysyntax_literal_python.jsonl`, gated on the Python release, with every
text that holds an imaginary part and a `+` or `-` (3.14 changed mixed
real and complex arithmetic; under another interpreter the generator
writes its header alone), and `pysyntax_literal.jsonl`, not gated, with
every other text, which 3.11 to 3.14 answer alike. It imports
`claims._canonical_repr` from the reference. Each row holds a text and
its canonical text, or null where `literal_eval` or `_canonical_repr`
raises: every accepted form and its near misses, cross-type dedupe,
signed zeros and complex signs, ints at the 4,300-digit limit, at the
float range and past `i64`, bytes and str repr edges, and nesting to
the bracket limit. A sweep row in each file pins 20,000 texts drawn by a
fixed LCG by count and SHA-256: from 25 pieces in the gated file, from
the 24 without `1j` in the other.
`golden_pysyntax_literal` checks every row;
`pysyntax_literal_kills` and `pysyntax_literal_robustness` (a 100,000
element list and a 50,000 member set within ten times the time of a
tenth of the input) hold the rest.

### The module tokenizer (`module_lex`)

`check_claim` (`claims.py` 607-715) reads the target with
`read_text(encoding='utf-8', errors='replace')` and calls
`ast.parse(source)` at 672, catching SyntaxError, ValueError and
RecursionError alike as "does not parse". It then reads only the
top-level `FunctionDef`, `AsyncFunctionDef` and `ClassDef` names and the
value of the first single-target `Name` assignment, but whether the whole
file parses decides the answer. The cut, leaves first: 5a (unit
pymodlex, built) the module-mode tokenizer; 5b first part (unit
pyfstring, built) f-string tokenizing (PEP 701's FSTRING_START,
FSTRING_MIDDLE and FSTRING_END, nested fields and format
specifications); 5b2 the expression grammar over module tokens, with the
errors its actions raise and the binding facts `symbols._all_names`
reads; 5c the statement grammar; 5d `check_claim`'s and `symbols`'
reads of the parsed module (with symbols-2).

`module_tokens(text) -> Result<Module, ModuleError>` reproduces
CPython 3.13.13's tokenizer in module mode (`Parser/lexer/lexer.c`'s
`tok_get_normal_mode` over `_PyTokenizer_FromUTF8`) and returns every
token with its span in the translated source, as `tokenize` names them:
NAME, NUMBER, STRING, OP (read by `lex`'s reader, which `lex` now
exposes to its sibling), FSTRING_START, FSTRING_MIDDLE, FSTRING_END,
COMMENT, NEWLINE, NL, INDENT, DEDENT and ENDMARKER. It holds no recursion: the indentation stack and the
bracket stack are vectors.

- Source: a NUL anywhere is refused (`source code string cannot contain
  null bytes`), and a lone surrogate (UnicodeEncodeError, a ValueError,
  when `compile` encodes the text). `\r\n` and `\r` become `\n`, and a
  newline is added when the text does not end with one, as
  `_PyTokenizer_translate_newlines` does for exec input. A byte order
  mark is not skipped in a str source: U+FEFF is refused as an invalid
  non-printable character wherever it stands.
- Indentation: at the start of each line, a space adds one column, a
  tab moves to the next multiple of 8, and a form feed resets the
  column; a second column counts tabs as one (`altcol`). A backslash in
  the indentation continues the line, and the column at the first such
  backslash is the line's indentation. Blank and comment-only lines, and
  every line inside brackets, leave the stack alone and end in NL. Else
  a deeper column pushes one INDENT (refused past 99 levels, CPython's
  `MAXINDENT` of 100, "too many levels of indentation"), a shallower one
  pops a DEDENT per level and must land on a level ("unindent does not
  match any outer indentation level"), and in each case the tab-size-1
  column must agree (equal for an equal column, greater for a deeper
  one), or the line is a TabError. An unexpected indent is the parser's
  error, not the tokenizer's: the tokens are read.
- Lines: a line end at bracket depth 0 after tokens is NEWLINE, any
  other NL; a backslash must be followed by a line end and a line
  (`unexpected EOF while parsing` at the end of the text); at the end
  every level is popped and ENDMARKER follows, or an open bracket is
  refused.
- Names: a run of ASCII letters, digits, `_` and every code point past
  ASCII; a run past ASCII must be an identifier by
  `unicode::xid::is_identifier` (CPython's `verify_identifier` scans the
  raw run with `_PyUnicode_ScanIdentifier`; NFKC comes later, in the
  parser), else it is refused. `Module::name` gives a NAME's NFKC text
  for unit 5c.
- f-strings: a prefix with `f` hands over to `fstring_lex` (below).
- Strings and numbers decode as `lex` decodes them, which is how the
  parser decodes them: a bad escape, a byte past ASCII in bytes, an
  integer past 4,300 digits and every malformed number are refused.
  `\N{...}` is read with the name table since unit claims-6, so
  `'\N{EM DASH}\x4'` is refused as CPython refuses it. The branch that
  answered `NeedsNameTable` only when nothing else in the source is
  refused is no longer reached; it stays until unit 5d removes the
  variant.

`ModuleError::Syntax` carries a short kind; `check_claim` catches every
class alike, so only whether a source is refused matters.

No regular expression is involved: the reference is C code.

Fixtures: `tests/contract/gen_pysyntax_module.py` writes
`pysyntax_module.jsonl`, gated on the Python release (the tokenizer's
rules are 3.13.13's; under another interpreter the generator writes the
header alone). A row holds the source, whether the tokenizer refuses
it, the class `ast.parse` raises, and the tokens `tokenize` reads with
their offsets (by count and SHA-256 past 400 code points). Refusal is
read from the C tokenizer in the parser's mode
(`tokenize._generate_tokens_from_c_tokenizer` with `extra_tokens` false:
the `tokenize` module's own mode matches no brackets) plus the parse of
each STRING and NUMBER token alone, since `ast.parse` stops at the
first grammar error and never reaches a later tokenizer error; a
SyntaxError of `ast.parse` with a tokenizer's message is asserted to be
a refusal. The cases cover lines, line ends, indentation by spaces,
tabs and form feeds, continuations in and after the indentation,
brackets, every literal kind and its errors, names past ASCII, NUL,
surrogates, the bracket limit and the indentation limit at 98 to 101
levels. A sweep row pins 20,000 sources of one to twelve pieces drawn
by a fixed LCG by count and SHA-256. `golden_pysyntax_module` checks
every row (an f-string folded to one FSTRING from its last
FSTRING_START to each FSTRING_END, as the generator folds the `tokenize`
module's tokens) and allows a decline only for a source holding `\N`
(one row); `pysyntax_module_kills` and
`pysyntax_module_robustness` (100,000 lines and 200 descents to 99
levels within ten times the time of a tenth, hostile shapes without a
panic) hold the rest.

### The f-string modes (`fstring_lex`)

`fstring_lex` reproduces `tok_get_fstring_mode` and the f-string branches
of `tok_get_normal_mode` (3.13.13, PEP 701). The C source is not on the
build machine: every rule below was read from the interpreter's own
tokenizer in the parser's mode and is held by `pysyntax_fstring.jsonl`.
Each open f-string is a `Mode` (the C `tokenizer_mode`: quote, quote
size, raw, `curly_bracket_depth`, `curly_bracket_expr_start_depth`,
`in_format_spec`, and whether a literal part or a field is read next) on
a vector in `module_lex::read`; the field's tokens are read by the same
loop as any other, so nothing recurses.

- `open`: a prefix holding `f` (f, rf, fr in any case; never with b or
  u) followed by a quote is FSTRING_START over the prefix and the quote
  or three. Opening one with 149 already open is refused ("too many
  nested f-strings", `MAXFSTRINGLEVEL` 150).
- `literal`, at each step of a literal mode: a `{` not followed by `{`
  opens a field and no token is read; the closing quotes are
  FSTRING_END, and the mode is popped. Else a literal part is read to an
  FSTRING_MIDDLE, which may be empty (`f'{x:}'` holds one) and whose span
  spells it: `{{` and `}}` end the part after the first brace and the
  next token starts after the second. A single `{` (or any `{` in a
  format specification) opens a field; a `}` ends the part, and the
  regular mode then closes the field or refuses a single `}`. A `}}` is
  one brace only at bracket depth 0 outside a specification. After a
  nested field closes in a specification the mode no longer counts as
  in a specification (a release detail of 3.13.13): `{{` there is one
  brace, and a line end is "unterminated" rather than the specification
  message. A backslash takes the next character with it, except before
  `{` or `}` (the backslash stays in the part and the brace still acts);
  in a non-raw f-string `\N{` starts a named escape whose `}` ends the
  part. A line end in the literal part or the specification of a
  single-quoted f-string, or the end of the text, is refused. A field
  opened with three already open through specifications is refused
  ("f-string: expressions nested too deeply", `MAX_EXPR_NESTING` 3).
- In a field (`Mode::spec_colon`, `before_close`, `after_op`): every
  bracket counts in `curly_bracket_depth` and in the 200 brackets
  `lex`'s reader allows, the field's `{` included. A `:` at the field's
  own depth is OP and turns the mode to a format specification (so `:=`
  there is `:` and a specification `=`); `!=` stays one operator; a `}`
  closing the field's `{` returns to the literal mode. Line ends are NL,
  comments are read (in a single-quoted field a comment swallows the
  closing brace and quote), the same quote opens a nested string or
  f-string, and nothing moves the indentation stack.
- Decoding: each FSTRING_MIDDLE of a non-raw f-string, a specification's
  text included, is decoded as the parser decodes it
  (`decode_unicode_with_escapes`: `lex`'s str decoder, with a backslash
  left at the part's end before a brace taken as a backslash); a bad
  `\x`, `\u`, `\U` or `\N` refuses the source, an unknown name
  included (unit claims-6; the `NeedsNameTable` branch is no longer
  reached and stays until unit 5d). Raw f-strings decode nothing. The decoded text
  is not kept: the grammar unit decodes the span again.

Decisions. The three kinds replace the former single FSTRING token; the
module golden test folds them back as the `tokenize` module's tokens
were folded, so `pysyntax_module.jsonl` did not change. Errors of the
grammar (`f'{}'`, `f'{x!z}'`, a lambda without parentheses, an
expression that does not parse) are not the tokenizer's: those sources
are read into the reference's tokens and `ast.parse`'s class is recorded
for unit 5b2. For that unit, a field's expression tokens run from the
OP `{` after which the mode turned to the regular one up to the OP `!`,
`:` or `}` at the field's own depth; a specification is the FSTRING_MIDDLE
and field tokens after that `:` up to the `}` that returns to the literal
mode.

Fixtures: `tests/contract/gen_pysyntax_fstring.py` writes
`pysyntax_fstring.jsonl`, gated on the Python release. A row holds the
source, whether the tokenizer refuses it, `ast.parse`'s class, and the
tokens of the parser's mode (`_generate_tokens_from_c_tokenizer` with
`extra_tokens` false: no COMMENT or NL, operators as OP) with offsets,
by count and SHA-256 past 400 code points. A source is refused when that
tokenizer raises, when a STRING or NUMBER alone does not parse, or when a
non-raw FSTRING_MIDDLE does not decode by `_part_decodes`, a transcription
of `decode_unicode_with_escapes` over the `unicode_escape` codec; an
`ast.parse` SyntaxError with a tokenizer's message is asserted to be a
refusal. A UnicodeDecodeError of `ast.parse` is not one: its error pass
decodes a raw f-string's specification, so `Rf"""{x:\x4\}"""` followed
by an indented line raises it while the tokenizer accepts (a row holds
that case). `_generate_tokens_from_c_tokenizer` raises SystemError on
some sources `ast.parse` accepts (`f"""{x=:` newline `}"""`): such a row
holds `"tok": "unjudged"`, and the golden test holds the port to
accepting it; a SystemError on a source `ast.parse` refuses, or on a
sweep source, stops the generator. The 195 case rows cover every prefix, both quote
kinds and sizes, empty f-strings, doubled and single braces, fields with
brackets, nested strings and f-strings reusing the quote, line ends,
comments and continuations, `:` at and below field depth, `:=`, lambdas,
conversions, `!=`, `=`, specifications with text, nested fields, doubled
braces and line ends, backslashes before quotes, braces, `N{`, `x`, `u`
and line ends, raw and not, unterminated parts and fields, nesting at 149
and 150 and the bracket limit through a field. A sweep row pins 20,000
f-strings of one to eight pieces drawn by a fixed LCG (about 7,300 of
them accepted) by count and SHA-256. `golden_pysyntax_fstring` checks
every row and allows a decline only for `\N{...}` (at most three);
`pysyntax_fstring_kills` and `pysyntax_fstring_robustness` (100,000
fields, a megabyte of literal text and 200 nestings to 149 levels
within ten times the time of a tenth, the deepest nesting on a 64 KiB
thread, hostile shapes without a panic) hold the rest.

### Names past ASCII and `\N{...}` (unit claims-6)

Unit claims-6 closes the two declines `lex` answered. Reference: CPython
3.13.13 itself (`Parser/lexer`, `Parser/string_parser.c`,
`Objects/unicodeobject.c` and `Modules/unicodedata.c` are not on the
build machine; every rule below was read from the interpreter, by
`ast.literal_eval` and by calling the decoder's own lookup through
`ctypes`). 176 lines of Rust source outside tests were added (138 in
`src/unicode/names.rs`, 22 in `lex.rs`, 12 in `literal.rs`, 4 in
`unicode/mod.rs`), under the bound of 600; `src/unicode/name_tables.rs`
is generated data (391 KB, not counted).

| function | reproduces | needs | status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `unicode::names::lookup(&[u32]) -> Option<u32>` | `_PyUnicode_Name_CAPI`'s `getcode(name, len, &code, 0)` as the `unicode_escape` decoder calls it for `\N{name}` | `name_tables.rs` | built |
| `unicode::names::stored()` | every name and alias the table holds, by name (for the tests) | `name_tables.rs` | built |
| `lex` names | `verify_identifier`: `_PyUnicode_ScanIdentifier` over the raw run of a name holding a code point past ASCII | `unicode::xid` | built |
| `lex::decode_str`, `\N` | the decoder's `\N{...}` branch: the name to the next `}`, `getcode`, "malformed" or "unknown Unicode character name" | `unicode::names` | built |
| `literal` names | `_PyPegen_new_identifier`'s NFKC of a name past ASCII and its refusal of `True`, `False` and `None` | `unicode::nfkc_into` | built |

What `getcode` accepts (checked against `getcode` itself over every
name, its lower-case and mixed-case spellings and 300,000 mutations of
names, with no difference):

- A name compares with ASCII letters upper-cased against exactly one
  spelling per code point: `em dash` reads, `EM  DASH`, ` EM DASH` and
  `EMDASH` do not.
- The spellings: every name `unicodedata.name` gives; every alias of
  `NameAliases.txt` (473: `NULL`, `LF`, `BOM`, the corrections such as
  `LATIN CAPITAL LETTER GHA` beside the original); and, by rule, a prefix
  and the code point as `%04X` for the CJK unified ideographs, the CJK
  compatibility ideographs, Khitan small script characters, Nushu
  characters and the Tangut ideographs (U+17000 to U+187F7 and U+18D00 to
  U+18D08). `unicodedata.name` names no Tangut ideograph in 3.13.13, yet
  `\N{TANGUT IDEOGRAPH-17000}` reads; the port follows the decoder. The
  hex compares upper-cased too (`4e00` reads), and only its canonical
  form reads (`04E00`, `004E00` and `4E0` do not).
- A Hangul syllable is `HANGUL SYLLABLE ` and its three short names,
  each column read by `find_syllable`'s longest match (the first of
  equal length), the whole name used; the short names are upper-cased
  like the rest (`HANGUL SYLLABLE ga` reads).
- Named sequences (`KEYCAP NUMBER SIGN`) never read: the decoder passes
  `with_named_seq` 0. Control characters have no name but their aliases
  (`<control>` does not read).
- A code point past ASCII in the name never reads: the parser hands the
  decoder each one as `\Uxxxxxxxx` (`decode_unicode_with_escapes`), and
  no name holds a backslash. No length limit is reachable: no name is
  longer than 88 characters.

`decode_str` keeps its order: the first escape that does not decode
refuses the literal there; `\N` without `{`, `\N{}` and an unclosed
brace are malformed, an unknown name refuses alike. Raw strings and bytes
do not read the escape (`b'\N{X}'` keeps it, as an unknown escape).

Names past ASCII: the tokenizer reads a run of identifier characters and,
when the run holds a code point past ASCII, refuses it unless it is an
identifier as written (`ⓢⓔⓣ()` is refused, though its NFKC reads
`set`); the NAME token keeps the raw text, as `tokenize` shows it. The
parser keeps the name by its NFKC, and `literal_eval` evaluates no name
but `set` called with nothing, so `literal` reads a name past ASCII as
`set` when its NFKC is `set` (`ｓｅｔ()`, `𝐬𝐞𝐭()`, `ſet()` are `set()`)
and refuses every other; for `Ｔｒｕｅ`, `Ｆａｌｓｅ` and `Ｎｏｎｅ` the
parser itself raises ValueError ("identifier field can't represent
'True' constant").

Decisions:

- `literal.rs` gains the NFKC branch, outside the files the unit's brief
  listed: `lex` keeps the raw text in its tokens (the golden files pin
  `tokenize`'s raw spelling) and the literal reader reads a name from
  that text, so the reader is where the parser's normalization belongs.
- The rule ranges are data, probed through `getcode` for each prefix of
  `RULE_PREFIXES` (Unicode's NR2 prefixes); Khitan, Nushu and CJK
  compatibility names are stored names in CPython but read by the same
  rule here, which answers alike and keeps 1,880 names out of the table.
- The table is word-coded and decoded once, on the first lookup, into a
  list sorted by name for a binary search: lookup is logarithmic in the
  33,421 names and linear in the name's length.
- No regular expression is involved: the reference is C code.

Fixtures: `tests/contract/gen_unicode_names.py` writes
`unicode_names.jsonl`, gated on Unicode 15.1.0 (under another version it
writes the header alone). The header pins the 33,421 names and aliases
of the table, sorted by name, and the 116,865 names a rule makes (Hangul
from the short names it lists, then each range it lists by `%04X`), each
by count and the SHA-256 of `<name>\t<code point>` lines, every one
checked through `ast.literal_eval`. Then 1,267 texts with what
`literal_eval` returns or raises: case variants, every rule range at
both ends and one past, each rule prefix at the first code point of
every range of another prefix, hex spellings of up to nine digits (nine
overflow 32 bits), Hangul spellings, every alias and every named
sequence, malformed escapes, the decoder's order, a name holding a code
point past ASCII whose low byte would spell a name (`EM D\u{141}SH`),
and names past ASCII. A text holding two backslashes in a row is written as code points
(the golden files' host guard reads `\\` as a Windows share). Tests:
`golden_unicode_names` (both digests through `lookup`, the second from
the header's own short names and ranges, and every row through
`literal_eval`), `unicode_names_kills` (case on a rule prefix,
lower-case and padded hex, the range ends, aliases, named sequences,
Hangul composition, exact spacing, the decoder's order, the identifier
check on the raw run, and, apart from the Unicode-gated fixture, a code
point past ASCII whose low byte would spell a name, each rule prefix at
another prefix's code points and hex of seven to nine digits),
`unicode_names_robustness` (every `u32` boundary,
a 100,000-character name, 100,000 escapes, 50,000 lookups within ten
times the time of 5,000). The tests that asserted a decline
(`golden_pysyntax`, `pysyntax_kills`, `claims_kills`,
`golden_pysyntax_fstring`, `pysyntax_fstring_kills`,
`golden_pysyntax_module`) now assert the answer and allow no decline.

Hazard: a name table generated from another Unicode version than CPython
3.13.13's reads a different code point, or none; the generators refuse
any version but 15.1.0. Whether a later 3.13 release reads the Tangut
names alike was not seen here: the table and the fixture follow the
interpreter that writes them.

Cost: the table compiles alone in about 0.03 s; the first lookup decodes
it once.

### The expression grammar (`module_expr`)

`parse_expression_module(text) -> Result<Tree, ExprError>` reproduces
`ast.parse(source)` of CPython 3.13.13 for a module of expression
statements: `module_tokens`, then each logical line as
`star_expressions NEWLINE`, then ENDMARKER. `Grammar/python.gram` and
the C parser are not on the build machine: every rule below was read from
the interpreter and is held by `pysyntax_expr.jsonl`.

- The machine. `Parser` holds the module's tokens (COMMENT and NL left
  out), a position, the arena and a vector of frames: an operator
  awaiting its operand (`-`, `not`, `await`, a binary operator, `**`,
  `*`, `:=`, a lambda's body, a conditional's `else` part) or an owner
  awaiting its next element (the statement's `star_expressions`, a
  parenthesis, list, brace, call, subscript, comprehension, lambda's
  parameters, string concatenation, f-string and replacement field).
  One loop reads an operand (prefixes, then an atom, or a new owner),
  then its trailers, then an infix operator, closing operator frames by
  level; a token no operator takes ends the operand, and the owner
  under it reads that token. Nothing recurses, so the deepest source the
  reference accepts is read on a 64 KiB thread. Each slot has a level
  (named expression, expression, disjunction, inversion, bitwise or,
  factor, primary) that decides which prefixes open it and which
  operators may follow inside it: a comparison takes no `not`, a
  comprehension's `in` and `if` parts take no conditional or lambda, a
  target takes a primary only. Keywords are NAME tokens whose raw text
  is a keyword (`ｉｆ` is the name `if`); a Name keeps `Module::name`'s
  NFKC text.
- First-pass actions that refuse: bytes beside str or an f-string
  (`_PyPegen_concatenate_strings`); `<>` (`_PyPegen_check_barry_as_flufl`
  without the future flag); an identifier whose NFKC is `True`, `False`
  or `None` (`_PyPegen_new_identifier`, a ValueError, for a Name, an
  attribute, a keyword, a parameter, a walrus target, a conversion); an
  f-string conversion other than `s`, `r` or `a`, or not right after its
  `!` (`_PyPegen_check_fstring_conversion`). The grammar alone refuses a
  walrus whose target is not a name, a generator beside other call
  arguments, `*` after `**` and a positional argument after a keyword in
  a call, a starred group, `*` before `or` in a display, a parameter
  without a default after one with one, a bare `*` with no keyword-only
  parameter, `/` first or twice or after `*`, anything after `**k`, a
  conversion after `=`, an empty field. `ast.parse` runs neither the
  compiler nor the symbol table: a repeated keyword argument, a
  repeated lambda parameter, a lone `*a`, `yield` and `await` outside a
  function, `__debug__ :=` and `for *a in` are accepted.
- Trees. Each node is an `ast` class with its span, its context (Load,
  or Store for a walrus target and a comprehension's target, through
  tuples, lists and starred), its identifier (Name, Attribute, `arg`,
  `keyword`) and its children in field order; operators are nodes, as
  `ast.walk` meets them. A span is a pair of code point offsets into
  `Module::source`, `ast`'s `col_offset` and `end_col_offset` on one
  line: a display, call or subscript spans its closing bracket, a
  keyword its name or `**`, a generator argument its parentheses, an
  Expr its expression, and a node whose first part is parenthesised
  starts at the outermost `(` while that part keeps its own span
  (`(x) * y`: BinOp 0 to 7, Name 1 to 2). An f-string's literal parts and a specification's
  JoinedStr carry the string's or the field's span instead; operators,
  `arguments` and `comprehension`, which `ast` gives no position, an
  empty one. Adjacent strings are one Constant, or a
  JoinedStr whose literal parts (FSTRING_MIDDLE decoded, plain strings,
  a field's `=` text) are joined where adjacent and dropped where
  empty; a field is a FormattedValue with its specification as a
  JoinedStr.
- The parser's stack. CPython counts every rule call against
  `MAXSTACK` (6,000) and raises MemoryError ("Parser stack overflowed")
  past it, which `check_claim` does not catch (below). The port counts
  the calls on the path to each operand's atom, which the parser seeks
  whatever token follows (an operand-less chain overflows where a named
  leaf would): 31 from a statement to a name, one
  per `-`, `+`, `~` and `not`, two per `**` and lambda body, one per
  conditional `else` part, three into a comparison's right side, two
  into a later `and` or `or` operand, two into a statement's later item,
  minus five under a statement's `*`, one more for a number or `...`,
  four for a string, seven for an f-string. These are exact: each chain's
  deepest accepted and first refused source is pinned. Brackets are
  bounded, not counted: the rule calls into a bracket's elements depend
  on the element's place and on which alternative first parsed it (a
  statement tries assignment targets first, which reach a leading
  bracket's contents 19 calls sooner), so each bracket adds a range
  (parenthesis 22 to 29, list and brace 23 to 29, call 24 to 27,
  subscript 24 to 26, field 28 to 33, wider after the first comma, a
  comprehension target -40 to 11 past its bracket, a specification's
  field -10 to 9 past its field) and the first bracket lowers the least
  estimate by 60. A source whose least estimate passes 6,000 is refused
  as `stack` where the operand is sought, so nothing past it is read
  (a million `-` cost what ten thousand do, past the tokens); one whose
  most passes and least does not is declined (`stack bound`). Between
  the two lie only sources thousands of calls deep inside brackets. The
  first-pass actions come after the stack: a NAME whose identifier is a
  constant overflows first, except at a slot `:=` may open, where
  `assignment_expression` makes the identifier up to 22 calls above the
  atom (that slot answers ValueError within 22 calls less than its least
  estimate, else declines), and a lambda's parameter, whose identifier
  is made one call past its slot's atom; the concatenation check follows
  the strings' rules.
- The second pass. A first pass that ends in SyntaxError (not
  ValueError, which ends the parse) makes `_PyPegen_run_parser` read the
  whole source again with its `invalid_*` rules, which go deeper (7
  calls past a leaf on a `-` chain) and read past the first failure
  (`[*` + `lambda: ` * 2,979 + `1]` fails at the first `lambda`; the
  second pass reads the lambdas and overflows), and its MemoryError
  stands. The port bounds any reading of each logical line by its tokens
  (`Parser::reach`: 38 per open bracket, and since its opening the most
  each prefix, operator and keyword may add, nothing taken off before
  the bracket closes) and declines (`stack bound`) a refusal whose bound
  with 20 calls more passes 6,000. Below that the refusal stands
  (`-` * 5,902 + `x $` is SyntaxError; 5,963 MemoryError). Two error
  rules nest on a flat line: `invalid_legacy_expression`
  (`NAME !'(' star_expressions`) reads the rest of the bracket or line
  inside every expression that opens with a NAME a possible operand
  follows, six calls deeper each (`x + x, ` * 994 + `x $` raises
  MemoryError, 993 SyntaxError), and `invalid_arithmetic` and
  `invalid_factor` read the inversion after an arithmetic operator's
  `not` eleven calls deeper (`x` + ` + not x` * 543 raises MemoryError).
  The bound counts six for every NAME after a token an expression may
  follow (a bracket, `,`, `=`, `:`, `:=`, `else`, `yield`, `from`, `for`,
  a prefix `*` or `**`) that a possible operand other than `(` follows,
  kept to the bracket's or line's end, and eleven for every `not` after
  an arithmetic operator; where such a NAME does not open an expression
  the rule takes it, the bound counts more than the parser goes, and a
  line of about a thousand such elements is declined below the
  reference's edge.
- `ast2obj`'s depth. `ast.parse` converts the tree with a recursion check
  against `Py_C_RECURSION_LIMIT` (10,000 on unix, 3,000 on Windows x64,
  1,000 on Windows arm64: `C_RECURSION_LIMIT` by `cfg`, the rule
  `recursion_answer(depth, limit)` tested at all three) from the C depth
  its caller already holds: 3 when a script calls it, 30 under pytest
  (the interpreter's last converted sum is 9,995 terms from a script and
  9,967 under pytest). A left-nested chain
  (`x+x+...`, `x.a.a...`) reaches it long before the parser's stack: a
  tree deeper than the limit less 3 is refused as `recursion`, one within
  100 of that is declined (`recursion bound`), since a deeper caller
  (an asyncio server's) starts further down.
- Statements. A logical line opening with a statement keyword or `@`, or
  holding outside brackets `;`, `=` or an augmented assignment, or a `:`
  no `lambda` before it takes, is declined (`statement`) where every
  line before it parses: unit 5c owns statements. `match`, `case` and
  `type` statements hold such a `:` or `=`, so `match(x)` stays an
  expression. INDENT and DEDENT refuse, as an unexpected indent does.
- Entries for unit 5c: `Parser::new(&Module)`, `star_expressions` and
  `expression` (named or not), each reading from the position to the
  first token it cannot use; `statement_line`.

Reference finding (not a defect of the port): a source nested past the
parser's stack makes `ast.parse` raise MemoryError, which
`check_claim` (`claims.py` 671-677) does not catch with SyntaxError,
ValueError and RecursionError, so the reference raises out of
`check_claim` for such a file (`-` * 5970 + `x` is one). The port
answers `Refused("stack")` so that unit 5d can reproduce that, and
declines where it cannot tell MemoryError from another answer.

Stated difference: the port reads every token before the grammar, and
the reference's parser drives its tokenizer, reading a token only when
a rule asks for it. A tokenizer refusal later in the source therefore
comes first in the port where the reference's parser overflows before
reaching it: `[a, ` * 201 + `x` + `]` * 201 is refused as `too many
nested parentheses` (the reference raises MemoryError inside the 200th
bracket), `-` * 5,970 + `x '` as `unterminated string` and `-` * 5,970
+ `x)` as `unmatched bracket`.
`pysyntax_expr_kills::a_tokenizer_refusal_comes_first` pins all three. Only
a source within the parser's stack bound and a tokenizer refusal is
concerned; reading tokens on demand would need a streaming
`module_lex`.

No regular expression is involved: the reference is the C parser.

Size: the module is about 2,000 lines of Rust source after `cargo fmt`,
more than three times the 600 planned; the planned cut (comprehensions, lambda
parameters and f-string fields as a unit 5b3) would have removed about
450 and is not made.

Fixtures: `tests/contract/gen_pysyntax_expr.py` writes
`pysyntax_expr.jsonl` and `pysyntax_expr_posix.jsonl`, both gated on
the Python release (under another interpreter each generator writes the
header alone). The second holds the rows whose answer follows the C
recursion limit (a source the parser reads into a tree deeper than
Windows' `ast2obj` converts, and the sums near the limit), is POSIX
only (`golden_pysyntax_expr_not_posix` records the gap on Windows) and
its generator declines on a host whose limit is not 10,000; the first
holds every other row, which every host answers alike. A row holds the
source, the class `ast.parse` raises or `ok`, and for an accepted source
the names `symbols._all_names` reads from expressions (Store Names,
`arg`s, attributes, keywords) and the tree's shape in preorder by class
(by length and SHA-256 past 300 characters), which holds every count
`ast.walk` gives. The cases: every form above and its near misses, the
statements the port declines (`want` `D`, by the generator's copy of
`statement_line`), every `pysyntax_fstring.jsonl` case, raw f-strings
with an upper-case `R`, each exact
chain's boundary pair found by bisection over the interpreter, chains
the first pass refuses (with no leaf, with a syntax error, an indent,
`<>`, bytes beside str, a constant identifier, a lambda's constant
parameter, a flat line of NAME-led elements, a chain of `+ not`) at the
second pass's boundary pair (`band`), below it and where the first pass
overflows, 30
bracket stacks drawn by a fixed LCG around a `-` chain at their boundary
pair (`band`: the port answers as the reference or declines) and 150
calls either side (answered exactly), brackets
to the tokenizer's 200, and for a sum and an attribute chain the port's
last accepted, first declined and first refused depths of `ast2obj`
(the interpreter's own edge moves with its caller, so it is not pinned). Two sweep rows pin by count and SHA-256 the answers to
the 20,000 sources of `pysyntax_fstring.jsonl`'s sweep and to 20,000
expressions drawn by a fixed LCG from 51 templates three deep, in
parentheses, a third with one character inserted or deleted.
`golden_pysyntax_expr` and `golden_pysyntax_expr_posix` check every
row; `pysyntax_expr_kills` (each bracket's bounds by one, the stack
before the leaf, the second pass, spans, the entries for 5c) and
`pysyntax_expr_robustness` (each boundary on a 64 KiB thread, 100,000
lines and a 1,000,000-term sum within ten times the time of a tenth, a
million prefix operators within twice the time of ten thousand, token
soups and every truncation of a long line without a panic) hold the
rest.

### Left for later units

Unit 5d removes `LexError::NeedsIdentTable` and `NeedsNameTable`,
`LiteralError`'s and `ModuleError`'s variants passing them on, and the
branches of `module_lex` and `fstring_lex` that answer them: since unit
claims-6 nothing produces them. For `module_lex`: the statement grammar
(5c, which calls `module_expr`'s entries and owns the lines it
declines), and the reads of the parsed module by `check_claim` and
`symbols` (5d, which also decides what `Refused("stack")` becomes, since
the reference raises MemoryError out of `check_claim`).

What unit 5b2 must know of `pysyntax_fstring.jsonl`:

- A non-raw literal part that does not decode is the tokenizer's
  refusal (`lex` true, the port answers `Syntax("(unicode error)")`)
  even where `ast.parse` raises a grammar error first: for `f'{=}\x4'`
  `ast.parse` says "f-string: valid expression required before '='".
  The grammar must not take such a row's `parse` class as its own
  answer's order.
- `ast.parse`'s class on a row the tokenizer accepts may be
  UnicodeDecodeError, not the grammar's SyntaxError: the error pass
  decodes a raw f-string's specification (`Rf"""{x:\x4\}"""` followed
  by an indented line).
- A row with `"tok": "unjudged"` has no tokens to compare against.

## The store's row writers

`store::home` (`src/store/home.rs`) and `store::tables`
(`src/store/tables.rs`): a record's home, a standing answer, the episode
journal's writers and the verification, conflict, import and quarantine
writers. Reference read at faa1b32e; line numbers are that commit's.

### The design (what each reads, decides, appends, mints, returns)

Every refusal below is `WriteError::Refused { class, text }` with the
reference's class and `str(exc)`, raised before anything is appended (or,
inside a transaction, rolled back with it). `NotFoundError` is a
`KeyError`, so its text is the key's `repr` (`'x'`, or `('m', None)` for a
verification), reproduced with the crate's `repr`.

- `Store._home_row(record_id, kind, home)` (`store.py` 1459-1497) is
  `home::home_row(tx, record_id, kind, Option<&Home>) ->
  Result<Option<PyValue>, WriteError>`. No home: None, nothing read. A
  project that is not a non-empty `str`: `ValueError` "a home names a
  project (or global)"; then a rule likewise: "a home names the rule that
  decided it" (the project is checked first). Reads `SELECT project,
  checkout, rule FROM homes WHERE record_id = ?` through
  `tx.connection()`. A row equal as a Python tuple (column values against
  the caller's, `==`): None, nothing written. Any other row: `ValueError`
  "{id} already has a home; a home is written once". Else the row
  `{record_id, kind, project, checkout, rule, decided}`, `decided` the
  wall clock read once (`datetime.now` in `store`).
  `home::put_home(tx, &row, session)` appends `home_put {"home": row}`.
- `_standing_row(memory, answer)` (`store_records.py` 202-222) is
  `home::standing_row(tx, record_id, body, &Answer) -> Result<PyValue, _>`.
  A probability that is a `bool` or not an `int`/`float`, not finite or
  outside 0 to 1: `ValueError` "a standing answer is a probability from 0
  to 1" (an `int` too large for a float: `OverflowError` "int too large to
  convert to float", from `float()`); a falsy source or giver:
  `ValueError` "a standing answer names its source and who gave it". The
  row `{record_id, probability: float(p), body_sha256: sha256 of the
  stored body's UTF-8, source, answered_by, answered}`, `answered` the
  wall clock read once, after the checks. `home::put_standing_row` appends
  `standing_put {"standing": row}`.
- `put_standing(record_id, answer, session=)` (225-239) is
  `WritableStore::put_standing(&str, &Answer, session, provider) ->
  (row, Committed)`: one transaction; `get_memory` under the lock
  (`home::get_memory`: `_MEMORY_SELECT ... WHERE id = ?`, the row read by
  `records::rows::memory`; none: `NotFoundError(id)`, checked before the
  answer), the row, `standing_put`. Returns the row.
- `put_episode(episode, session=, home=)` (`store_journal.py` 44-59):
  `WritableStore::put_episode(&Episode, session, Option<&Home>, provider)
  -> (Episode, Committed)`: one transaction; `_home_row(id, "episode",
  home)`, then `episode_put {"episode": model_dump(mode="json")}`, then
  `home_put` when a row was decided. Returns the episode.
- `delete_episode(id, session=)` (87-90): `_require_row(episodes, id)`
  (`NotFoundError(id)`), then `episode_delete {"id"}`. Returns None.
- `write_episode(*, session_id, body, scopes, takeaway, swarm_id, origin,
  now, home)` (96-122): `EpisodeArgs` plus `now: Option<DateTime>` and
  the home. A falsy body, or a `str` body blank after `strip()`:
  `ValueError` "episode body must be a non-empty string"; a truthy body
  that is not a `str`: `AttributeError` "'int' object has no attribute
  'strip'" (nothing minted or read in either case). Then, in the
  constructor's argument order: the mint once (`generate_ulid`), the wall
  clock once unless `now` is given (`utcnow`), the body stripped plus a
  newline, `list(scopes or [])` (a `str` gives its characters, a dict its
  keys, any other truthy non-iterable `TypeError` "'int' object is not
  iterable"), the takeaway stripped when truthy (a truthy non-`str`:
  `AttributeError`), then `Episode(...)` (a ValidationError's first line,
  "1 validation error for Episode"). Then `put_episode` with
  `session=session_id`. Returns the episode.
- `write_floor(*, session_id, origin, now, home)` (125-146): the mint,
  the wall clock unless `now`, the floor episode (`is_floor`, its fixed
  body), `put_episode`.
- `put_verification(memory_id, *, verified_at, ...)` (`store_tables.py`
  36-72): `Verification`; the payload `{memory_id, machine_id,
  verified_at: verified_at.isoformat(), verified_head, the four lists}`
  plus each target map when given (`dict(targets)`); `verification_put`.
  No check of its own: the fold refuses what the payload cannot hold.
- `delete_verification(memory_id, *, machine_id=)` (111-133): a row whose
  `COALESCE(machine_id, '')` matches, else `NotFoundError((memory_id,
  machine_id))`; `verification_delete`.
- `put_conflict(record)` (137-145): the record's `_CONFLICT_COLUMNS`
  (`record.get`, None when absent; a record that is not a dict:
  `AttributeError` "'list' object has no attribute 'get'"); a falsy `id`,
  `a_id`, `b_id`, in that order: `ValueError` "a conflict needs {name}",
  before the transaction; `conflict_put`. `delete_conflict` (157-162).
- `put_import` / `delete_import` (165-196), `put_quarantine` /
  `delete_quarantine` (199-236): the payload as given, one mutation; the
  deletes `_require_row` first.

Every table writer and episode writer is one transaction on the
`WritableStore` and returns what the reference returns with the
`Committed` rows and head. No writer here names a record for the
`returned` settle (only memory kinds do).

The clocks and the mint, per call (what the fixture replays exactly):
`home` (a decided row) reads the wall clock once; `put_standing` once;
`write_episode` and `write_floor` mint one id and read the wall clock
once unless `now` is given, plus once more for a decided home; every
appended row reads the log clock once, and the head's move once more. The
provider's mint is `Provider::ulid` (`src/store/create.rs`): by default
`create::system_ulid()` (the system clock's seconds through
`create::ulid_millis`, which is `mint::millis`: wrapped at 48 bits, an
infinite time the reference's OverflowError and NaN its ValueError, as an
error naming the class; then ten OS bytes through `mint::ulid`, as `generate_ulid`
reads `time.time()` apart from both clocks); `Fixed` mints the constant
id of millisecond 0 and ten zero bytes (the create and open fixtures never
mint); `Clocks` passes to its inner provider. `utcnow` is the wall clock
(`wall_now`), the same read: it has no method of its own.

`home_put` and `standing_put` are written only through these functions
(`Transaction::mutate_home_or_standing`, crate-private); a direct
`Transaction::mutate("home_put", ...)` is still refused as not ported. In
the reference `_mutate` is private and its only callers with these kinds
are `put_memory`, `put_episode` and `put_standing`: no public caller
reaches it otherwise.

Another writer calls them inside its own transaction: `let row =
home::home_row(&mut tx, id, "memory", home)?;` before its record's rows,
then `home::put_home(&mut tx, &row, session)?` after them (as
`_put_memory` does), and `home::standing_row(&mut tx, &id, &body,
&answer)?` / `home::put_standing_row`. Run in a `tx.scope(..)`, a refusal
rolls back that scope only.

Not ported, refused with nothing written: `prune_episode_sessions`
(chunked, its own unit), and whatever a transaction refuses (membership
kinds, a native-path origin, a rekeyed store). Not expressible:
`write_episode` and `write_floor` take `now` as `Option<DateTime>`, so a
falsy or non-datetime `now`, which the reference passes through `now or
utcnow()` and then pydantic, cannot be given natively.

A refusal that quotes a type (`'int' object has no attribute 'strip'`,
`... 'get'`, `... is not iterable`) spells it as CPython's messages do
(`tp_name`): `NoneType`, `bool`, `int`, `float`, `str`, `list`, `tuple`,
`dict`, `PurePosixPath`, and `datetime.datetime` for a datetime (where
`type(x).__name__` is `datetime`), each checked against the reference.

Reference findings (pinned in the fixture, not changed): (1) a home whose
checkout is not a `str` (an int, say) is stored by the `TEXT` column as
text, so the same home written again compares unequal and is refused as
"already has a home" (`store.py` 1480-1491; case `homes`, steps 12-15).
(2) `put_verification` takes any item types in its lists
(`store_tables.py` 54-62; `verified_paths=[1, 2]` writes). (3) a standing
row's source and giver are not type-checked by `_standing_row`
(`store_records.py` 214); a `bool` or `int` giver is stored as given,
and a list, float or other giver is refused only by the fold
(`TypeError`), after the wall clock was read and the row appended (case
`type_names`).

Pinned natively only, since the fixture's JSON cannot carry them: a NaN
or infinite probability (`ValueError` "a standing answer is a probability
from 0 to 1", the reference's text, established by running it), and
arguments nested 9,998 and 100,000 deep. For those the reference was run
at both depths in a child process (it did not crash for any shape tried):
`session_id`, `scopes`, `swarm_id` and `origin` give pydantic's "1
validation error for Episode", `body` and `takeaway` `.strip()`'s
AttributeError, a probability the range ValueError, and every value that
reaches the payload's encoder (a home's checkout, a standing source or
giver, any quarantine, import, conflict or verification field) is
RecursionError, with nothing written. `PyValue`'s `Clone`, `PartialEq` and
`Debug` are iterative (`src/pyvalue.rs`), so no copy or comparison on the
way overflows the stack.

## The returned marks' backfill (`store::returned`)

`store::returned` (`src/store/returned.rs`): the half of
`store_returned.py` a writing open runs once an upgrade's step 2 left
meta's `returned_backfill` key. The other half is built elsewhere:
`_is_active` and `_targets` are `store::write::is_active` and
`targets`, `before` and `candidates` are `store::write`'s, `settle` is
`store::tx`'s, `linking_sources` is `store::writers`'. Reference read at
1e6fae21; line numbers are that commit's.

| function | reference | needs | status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `missing_links` | `store_returned.py` 236-267 | a connection | built |
| `returned_rows` | 270-298 | a connection | built |
| `backfill` | 301-368 | the writable store, its key ring, the clocks | built |
| `ensure_backfilled` | 371-398 | the same, `has_key` given | built |
| `_put_relinked` | `store_records.py` 706-741 | the transaction, the key ring | built (`store::writers::put_relinked`) |
| wiring into the writing open | `Store.open` | | later (unit store-3c) |

- `missing_links(conn)` reads every id (`str(id)`), every index row
  (`str()` of its source, type and target, the note as stored), then each
  record with a link list other than NULL and `'[]'` in id order. The
  list is `json.loads`'d (TypeError and ValueError pass the record over;
  a blob, which `json.loads` would decode, declines as
  `WriterNotPorted::Blob`) and iterated as Python iterates it: a list's
  items, a str's characters, a dict's keys, TypeError for a number, a
  bool or null. A link counts when it is an object whose `target_id`
  (the last of a repeated key) names an active record and no index row
  holds its source, type, target and note. The tuple test is reproduced
  as Python makes it: the target is hashed first (a list or object
  raises TypeError), then the type and the note; the source matches only
  a text id (an integer id is never the index's `str()`), the type only
  a str, the note by Python's `==` between a JSON value and a column
  (`1 == 1.0`, `True == 1`, a str never equal to a blob, an integer past
  64 bits compared exactly with a real). Each record maps to its least
  lost target. The index rows are held in a map by source, type and
  target, so the read is linear, as the reference's sets make it. A
  target or a type holding a lone surrogate equals no text the database
  holds: such a target is never active and such a type never indexed,
  even beside an id or a type that spells the escape out.
- `returned_rows(conn, ids)` answers a list of (record id, `via`,
  `returned`) in the order the reads return them, each column through
  `str()` (a NULL is `None`). The ids are taken once each in their first
  order and read 500 at a time with the reference's own statement; an
  empty list reads nothing. An error whose text holds "no such table"
  answers none; any other passes out.
- `WritableStore::backfill(provider, session, reads)` reads the named
  records before its transaction, on the store's connection: each
  `tombstone_delete` row's `json_extract` id that is text, each
  `supersedes` target (a str other than the record's own id) of a
  `memory_put` row's record, less each id a `returned_put` or
  `returned_delete` row names. A put whose payload does not parse, or is
  not an object, is passed over; one whose `memory` is a truthy value
  other than an object raises AttributeError, and one whose `links` is a
  truthy number or bool raises TypeError, as in the reference (neither is
  caught by `ensure_backfilled`). A `json_extract` over a payload that is
  not JSON raises SQLite's "malformed JSON". Inside the transaction:
  `missing_links` on its connection, `put_relinked` over them (the
  labels read once with the caller's `Relink`), the wall clock read once
  (always, as the reference reads it), then for each named record in id
  order that is active, superseded by no other active record and not
  marked, a `returned_put` row `{"returned": {"record_id", "via",
  "returned"}}` with `via` the record itself, appended through
  `Transaction::mutate_returned_put` (`Transaction::mutate` refuses the
  kind: it is outside `write.rs`'s `KINDS`). Then meta's key is deleted
  and the transaction commits, `settle` writing the marks the relinked
  puts leave due. A store whose file lacks the `returned` table raises
  "no such table: returned" at the first record that reaches the mark
  test. The named ids are held as code points and ordered as Python
  orders a str; a `supersedes` target holding a lone surrogate is kept
  as it is, and when the loop reaches it the backfill raises the
  UnicodeEncodeError sqlite3 raises binding it ("'utf-8' codec can't
  encode character '\ud800' in position 0: surrogates not allowed"),
  so the transaction rolls back and `ensure_backfilled` logs it and
  keeps the key.
- `WritableStore::ensure_backfilled(provider, has_key, reads)` answers
  nothing without the key or without meta's key (the value is read, so
  a text that is not UTF-8 raises), else runs `backfill` with no
  session. A failure of class `sqlite3.Error`, `OSError` or `ValueError`
  (pydantic's ValidationError and `UnknownFieldsError` among them) is
  logged at WARNING as "returned: the backfill failed and will run at
  the next open: " and `str(exc)`, and marks nothing; a success that
  marked records logs at INFO their count. The lines are returned as
  `LogLine { level, message }`, the message None where it carries an
  exception text this build does not word. What this build does not
  port, and a clock it could not read, pass out uncaught.
- `store::writers::put_relinked(tx, ring, reads, sources, session)` is
  the relink of a restore split in two: `relink` builds its sources from
  `linking_sources` and calls it, as `Store._relink` calls
  `_put_relinked`. Its behaviour is unchanged.

No pattern of `re` is involved.

Fixtures: `gen_store_returned.py`. `store_returned.jsonl` (45 cases,
14,745 bytes, ungated) pins `missing_links` and `returned_rows` over a
bare in-memory connection whose cells are typed (a lone surrogate in a link, a repeated mark); a raise is recorded by
its class only, since CPython 3.14 words an unhashable value's TypeError
otherwise. `store_returned_posix.jsonl` (12 cases, 109 steps, 164,608
bytes; POSIX only, gated as `store_records_e.jsonl` is) runs whole stores
through `gen_store_records_b.run_case`: a chain whose head an earlier
build deleted under the log, restores whose marks and rows were taken
away, index rows a restore left out, records this build marked, a link
into the record itself, a store without the table, a malformed
`tombstone_delete` payload, record puts that are passed over or
raise, a named record no longer active, a target holding a lone
surrogate, an unaccounted linking record and fold problems at seqs 2
and 10; each step's rows, clock reads, state and index compared.
Tests: `golden_store_returned.rs`, `golden_store_returned_posix.rs`,
`store_returned_not_posix.rs` (the Windows gap, class os),
`store_returned_kills.rs`, `store_returned_robustness.rs`. On Windows
the backfill runs as on POSIX; the crate's Windows flavour does not
resolve paths (ENG-124), which this unit does not need.

## The store's connection leaves and admitted reads (`store::reads`)

`src/store/reads.rs` ports the connection leaves of `store.py` and the
reads the index used to serve, each over a `rusqlite::Connection` with the
caller's admission a closure. Reference lines are those of `store.py` at
a9bfd8ce.

| function | reference | needs from the machine | status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `STORE_BUSY`, `STORE_FULL`, `_RETRYABLE_CODES` | 319-331 | nothing | built |
| `note_residue` | 342-353 | a process-wide latch (`AtomicBool`); the caller logs `residue_message` when it answers true | built |
| `error_code_name` | 356-360 | nothing: CPython 3.13's result-code name table is `ERROR_NAMES` | built |
| `retryable_code` | 363-372 | nothing | built |
| `Store.set_busy_timeout` | 1074-1083 | the connection | built |
| `Store.document_frequencies` (outside the memo) | 1681-1745 | the connection | built |
| `Store._term_masks` | 1832-1851 | the connection | built |
| `Store.scope_counts` | 1853-1874 | the connection | built |
| `Store.scopes_for` | 1876-1893 | the connection | built |
| `Store.category_rows` | 1895-1916 | the connection | built |
| `Store.brief_rows` | 1918-1961 | the connection | built |
| `StoreSource`, `DefaultStoreSource` | 2048-2072 | the binder of `principal_of`, as an argument | built |

What each reproduces, and the decisions:

- An exception is named by its class and its SQLite code. `failure_of`
  maps a `rusqlite` failure to the class sqlite3 raises for its primary
  code (`_pysqlite_seterror`'s table: InternalError, MemoryError without a
  code, OperationalError, DatabaseError, DataError, IntegrityError,
  InterfaceError) and the extended code it carries. `error_code_name`
  answers the code's name from `ERROR_NAMES`, the class name for a code
  the table lacks or none. The class mapping is private to this module;
  `store::fold`'s own is left as it is.
- `retryable_code` reads `code & 0xFF` as Python's `&` reads it on an
  int, so a negative code reads its two's complement low byte (-251 is
  SQLITE_BUSY). A code that is not an int is no code.
- `set_busy_timeout` takes an `f64`: the ValueError text is the float's
  `repr` (`float_repr`); the reference words an `int` argument without
  `.0`, which a Rust caller cannot pass. `int(seconds * 1000)` is spelled
  in full (`pyvalue::py_int`). SQLite 3.50.4, the reference's, reads a
  value past 32 bits as 0 (`sqlite3Atoi`) and so disables the timeout;
  the bundled SQLite 3.54.1 leaves the timeout as it was. The port sends
  0 for such a value, so it answers as the reference under its SQLite;
  those rows are in `store_reads_python.jsonl`, gated on the release and
  on SQLite. An infinite product is the reference's OverflowError.
- A scope list is `store_rows._load_json(text, None)` (`records::rows::
  load_json`), so `admit` sees every JSON value the list holds, as the
  reference hands it `list(scopes)`; the fixture's predicates compare
  texts. The home project is handed as the column's value, None as
  `SqlValue::Null`. The actor of `document_frequencies` is built when
  either column is not NULL; a column pydantic's `str | None` refuses
  (a number) raises ValidationError, a blob is decoded as UTF-8.
- `scope_counts` keys its counts as a Python dict does: 1, True and 1.0
  are one key and the first spelling stays; json's NaN is one object, so
  every NaN is one key; a list or object raises TypeError once its row is
  admitted. Keys are hashed by a canonical form, so the count is linear.
- `scopes_for` answers in the order the `IN` queries give rows, a later
  row of an id replacing the value in place; each scope is `str()` of the
  JSON value (`pyvalue::py_str`).
- `_term_masks` takes the row number to position map and the width that
  `PoolReader::read_inputs` builds, and answers each mask as a `Vec<bool>`
  over positions in place of the reference's int.
- `StoreSource<C>` is a trait over the request context type; the default
  source serves its one store. `principal_of` takes the binder
  (`identity.bind`) as an argument, since the binder reads the session
  registry, the environment and the working directory.
- Each row's selected columns are all decoded before any is used, as
  sqlite3 converts a whole row when it fetches it: a text that is not
  UTF-8 raises OperationalError in any selected column, on a row the read
  then skips or refuses too, and before the actor's ValidationError or a
  scope list's JSON error.

Fixtures: `tests/contract/gen_store_reads.py` builds small stores in
memory (untyped `memories` and `homes`, so a hostile row keeps its type,
and `memories_fts`), runs the reference's unbound `Store` methods on an
object holding the connection under the predicates all, none, by scope,
by project, without a home and by actor (stores with a text that is not
UTF-8 in an id, a home and a scope list, and two rows of one id among
them), and writes `store_reads.jsonl`
(the reads, the retryable codes, live SQLite failures, the busy timeouts
from -inf to NaN and past 2**31). A store of 1,200 rows is named by rule
and an answer whose compact JSON passes 1,500 characters is pinned as
its length and SHA-256. `store_reads_python.jsonl` holds the name of
every result code in the release's table and the busy timeouts past 32
bits, gated on the Python release and on SQLite; the generator stops
unless the names sqlite3 attaches to errors it raises for real agree with
that table.
Tests: `golden_store_reads`, `store_reads_kills`, `store_reads_robustness`.
No regular expression is involved.

Left for later units: the memoised branch of `document_frequencies` and
`ranking_statistics` (`_DOC_FREQS`) and `_read_doc_freq_inputs` beyond the
pool reader's. `store_orphans` is built in `store::create::store_orphans`
(store-1b).

## The rule a .git entry is followed by

`src/bettermemory/gitfile_rule.py` (1,537 lines, read at v9's 6000b993)
decides whether a folder's `.git` entry (a directory, a `gitdir:` file or
a link to either) is followed. A wrong follow keys a folder on another
checkout's git directory, so "native follows where the reference refuses"
is the most serious difference this port can have. It is ported unit by
unit, and all five units are built: the whole module answers on POSIX,
and from unit 2 on the Windows flavour is declined.

past kind and identity.
