## A transcript read from its end (`transcript.py`)

`transcript.py` reads a Claude Code transcript newest row first, for the
hooks. Its map, by function, against the reference at `origin/v9`:

| function | lines | needs from the machine | status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `CHUNK_BYTES`, `WALK_BYTES` | 46-56 | nothing | transcript-1a, built |
| `ReverseLines` | 58-130 | open, `fstat` size, seek, read | transcript-1a, built |
| `_row`, `_prompt_id` | 131-148 | nothing (`json.loads`) | transcript-1a, built |
| `StopTurn`, `_Pending`, `stop_turn` | 149-258 | through `ReverseLines` | transcript-1a, built |
| `InterruptedTurn`, `interrupted_turns` | 258-356 | as `stop_turn`, `parse_event_ts` | transcript-1b, built |
| `owner_words` | 359-396 | as `stop_turn`, and `Path.is_file` | transcript-1b, built |
| `CompactMarker`, `compact_marker` | 399-438 | as `stop_turn`, `parse_event_ts` | transcript-1b, built |

The module is cut in two: 1a (`src/transcript`) and 1b, which
reads `owner_prompt(row, cut=False)` (reference line 388) and
`datetime::parse_event_ts`.

What 1a reproduces:

- `ReverseLines` (`transcript::reverse`): the iterator opens the file at
  its first `next`, as the reference's generator does, takes the size
  once, and walks back chunk by chunk, each read with the byte before it.
  The carry of a line that runs across a chunk's start, the budget's floor
  (`max(0, end - budget)`, a negative budget reading nothing), the needle
  filter (a chunk whose complete lines lack the needle yields nothing,
  while a chunk that holds it yields every line, with or without it),
  `reached_start = (end == 0)` set only when the loop ends by itself, and
  the end of the walk on any OSError (the open, the size, a seek, a read)
  or on a read shorter than asked (a file truncated under the walk) are
  the reference's. `reached_start` stays False after any of those.
- The file is reached through the trait `transcript::Opener` (open, size,
  seek, read), not through `gitobjects::stream::Handle`, which has no
  size. `FsOpener` adapts any `fsdata::Fs`: `open_waiting` (Python's
  `open` sets no `O_NONBLOCK`), `fstat`'s size, `Fs::seek` and `Fs::read`
  (a buffered read: the count asked, fewer only at the end). A folder is
  refused after the open, as `io.FileIO` refuses it; a file system that
  does not offer `seek` declines, which ends the walk as an OSError would.
  No path is resolved, so the Windows flavour has no gap here.
- `_row` (`transcript::row`): blank by `bytes.strip()` (ASCII
  whitespace), decoded with `errors="replace"` (`String::from_utf8_lossy`
  replaces the same maximal subparts as CPython), `json::loads`, dicts
  only. RecursionError is no ValueError: the reference raises it out of
  `_row` and out of `stop_turn`, and the port answers `Err` from both.
  Where the decoder stops recursing follows the release and the system,
  so those rows are in `transcript_python.jsonl`.
- `_prompt_id`, `StopTurn`, `_Pending` and `stop_turn`
  (`transcript::stop`): the walk, the passing over of newer turns, the
  break on an older turn, the undecided answer when the budget ended
  inside the turn, and the turn without ids ended by its newest submitted
  row, as the reference's `for ... else`.
- The calls into `owner_prompt.py` (`is_submitted`, `owner_prompt` with
  `cut`, `submitted_text`, `text_blocks`) are the trait
  `transcript::OwnerPrompt`, with `INTERRUPT_OPENING` a constant here.
  The unit that ports `owner_prompt.py` implements it. The golden test
  gives back the answers the reference's own functions gave, in the order
  `stop_turn` asked, and fails on a call out of order or missing.

Decisions:

- `chunk_bytes` is a `NonZeroUsize`. With 0 the reference never ends: a
  chunk is then the one byte before `end`, `end` does not move, and the
  same line is yielded for ever (reference finding; reproduction:
  `list(ReverseLines(path, chunk_bytes=0))` over `b"a\n"` does not
  return). A negative chunk size is not representable here either: with
  -1 the reference never ends (`end` climbs by one each pass and no line
  is yielded), with -2 the first read asks for -1 bytes, reads to the
  end, comes back short and ends the walk with nothing yielded and
  `reached_start` false, and with -3 or less `handle.read` raises
  `ValueError`, which is not an `OSError` and leaves the iteration.
- The needle test is linear in the chunk (Knuth-Morris-Pratt), as the
  reference's `in` is.
- Two conditions carry equivalent mutants and so no kill: dropping
  `in_turn` from the undecided-walk check (without it `submitted` is
  false and the next check also answers None), and dropping 0x0b from the
  whitespace set of `_row` (a line of whitespace alone fails `json.loads`
  either way).
- No regular expression is used: transcript-1a has no pattern.

Golden files: `transcript.jsonl` (not gated: walks over small files with
every chunk size from 1 to 64 and budgets from -3 to 2^30, CRLF ends, no
trailing newline, invalid UTF-8, needles, a missing file, a folder, a size
larger than the file, a file truncated mid-walk, a line longer than
several chunks, four walks over a 2.4 MB file pinned as count and SHA-256,
`_row` over blank, broken and non-dict lines, `stop_turn` over 33
transcripts) and `transcript_python.jsonl` (gated on the Python release:
lines nested 20,000 deep). Tests: `golden_transcript`,
`transcript_kills`, `transcript_robustness`.

What 1b (`transcript::turns`) reproduces:

- `interrupted_turns`: the walk newest row first, grouping user rows by
  `promptId` (a row without one, or with an empty one, is its own turn),
  the end of the walk at the first user row stamped at or before `since`,
  the reply and model taken from the assistant rows read before the turn's
  newest user row (and, while still None, before older rows of the same
  turn), the interrupt line found by `submitted_text(row).lstrip()`
  (Python's `str.isspace`) starting with `INTERRUPT_OPENING`, `at` the
  stamp of the turn's newest submitted row that carries one, and a turn
  returned only when it holds the interrupt line, a stamp and a prompt.
  The turns come oldest first.
- The stamps are `parse_event_ts(row.get("timestamp"))`: an absent key,
  null and any value that is not a `str` (a number, an object, a list)
  are no stamp, as the reference's `isinstance(value, str)` declines them;
  a `str` goes to `datetime::parse_event_ts`. Stamps are ordered by
  instant, and `at` keeps the row's own offset (`isoformat` shows it).
- A naive `since` (or `near`) cannot be ordered against the aware stamps
  `parse_event_ts` answers: the reference raises TypeError at the first
  comparison, and the port answers `Err(PyError::TypeError)` at the same
  point, so a transcript with no stamped row answers without error.
- `owner_words`: "" for `chars` at or below zero or a path that is not a
  regular file (`Opener::is_file`, `Path.is_file`: links followed, False
  on any error; the default declines with False, and `FsOpener` asks
  `Fs::stat`); a line without the bytes `"user"` is not parsed (a user
  row spelled with an escape is skipped, as in the reference);
  `owner_prompt(row, cut=False)`, an empty text no piece; the count of
  code points held with two for each separator, the walk stopped once it
  reaches `chars`, the pieces joined by blank lines and cut from the
  front to `chars` code points.
- `compact_marker`: the reader's needle `compact_boundary`, rows of type
  `system` and subtype `compact_boundary` only, a row with no stamp
  passed over, `abs(stamp - near) > window` passed over (a negative
  window holds nothing), the key the `uuid` when it is a nonempty `str`,
  else the timestamp's own text (a parsed stamp is a `str`, so `str()` of
  it is itself). The window is an `i128` count of microseconds, a
  `timedelta`'s exact value; it also holds counts no `timedelta` can.
- RecursionError from `_row` is raised out of all three, as in 1a.

Decisions:

- `Opener` gained `is_file` at its end with no default, so an opener that
  forgets it fails to compile instead of answering no file. The two
  openers, `FsOpener` and the test double `MemTranscript`, implement it.
- `_Pending`, `get` and `is_str` of `transcript::stop` are shared with
  `transcript::turns` (`pub(super)`), not copied.
- No regular expression is used: transcript-1b has no pattern.
- No path is resolved, so the Windows flavour has no gap here.

Golden file: `transcript_turns.jsonl` (not gated: no path, errno or
system text; every stamp is the reference's `fromisoformat` of the row's
text). Each transcript is written once as a `file` row and named by index.
It holds 31 `interrupted_turns` cases over transcripts and `since` values
(boundaries at a stamp, offsets either side, a naive `since`, timestamps
missing, null, a number, a float, an object, a list, naive text and text
that does not parse, rows without ids, harness rows, chunk sizes and
budgets), `owner_words` over 23 cases (`chars` from -1 to 10^12 across
every cut point, chunk sizes, budgets, a missing file, a folder, lines
with `"user"` that are not user rows) and `compact_marker` over 19 cases
(inclusive and negative windows, keys from an empty and a numeric uuid,
non-str and unparsable stamps, offsets, a naive `near`). Tests:
`golden_transcript_turns`, `transcript_turns_kills`,
`transcript_turns_robustness`.

The module is complete.

## The owner's prompt and the override policy (`owner_prompt.py`, `policy.py`)

Two leaves the handlers and the hooks read. Each fits in one unit.

| function | reference lines | needs from the machine | status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `REFUSAL_STATUS`, `_FORCE_KEY`, `_ACKNOWLEDGE_KEY`, `_label` | policy.py 62-71 | nothing | built |
| `PolicyRefusal`, `event_fields` | policy.py 74-106 | nothing | built |
| `_message` | policy.py 109-146 | nothing | built |
| `check_overrides` | policy.py 149-188 | the config | built |
| `PROMPT_CUT_CHARS`, `ENVELOPE_TAGS`, `INTERRUPT_OPENING`, `HARNESS_OPENINGS`, `COMPOSED_OPENINGS`, `HUMAN_ORIGIN`, `QUEUED_COMMAND` | owner_prompt.py 47-96, 175 | nothing | built |
| `_ENVELOPES`, `probe_text` | owner_prompt.py 98-114 | the regular-expression engine | waits for pyre-6 |
| `owner_text` | owner_prompt.py 117-127 | `probe_text` as an argument | built |
| `text_blocks`, `is_submitted`, `submitted_text` | owner_prompt.py 130-170 | nothing | built |
| `_subagents`, `queued_text`, `owner_prompt` | owner_prompt.py 178-217 | `probe_text` as an argument (`owner_prompt`) | built |

`policy` reproduces the refusal of a write tool's override flags.
`check_overrides` reads `policy.forbid_force` and
`policy.forbid_acknowledge` off the `Config` and asks `Config::is_managed`;
`check_overrides_with` takes the two switches as values and the managed
test as a closure, which is what the golden test drives (a duck-typed
config). `acknowledge` is a closure answering `acknowledge.get(name,
False)` as a truth value. The names are read in `ACKNOWLEDGE_NAMES` order,
whatever order the call passed them in, and the check returns at once
when both switches are at their default. The refusal is an error value
(`PolicyRefusal`) whose `Display` is `str(refusal)`; at the handler
boundary its class is `ValueError`. `managed` is held sorted, as
`event_fields` spells the frozenset; `_message` asks membership only, so
the order does not reach the text.

`owner_prompt` reproduces the module but its envelope removal. Rows are
`PyValue`s as `json.loads` gives them, and a row is a dict: the
reference's `row.get` raises on anything else, and no caller hands one.
`PyValue::get` answers None off a dict, which is the reference's
`message.get("content") if isinstance(message, dict) else None`. The
marks (`isMeta`, `isCompactSummary`, `isSidechain`, `agentId`, and an
attachment's `isMeta`) are read through `machine::truthy`, so `"0"` is a
mark and `0`, `""` and `[]` are not. `turnOrigin` is compared by Python
equality against the str `"human"`: a null or absent origin is the
owner's, and any other value (`false`, `0`, a list) is not. `strip` and
`lstrip` are `str.isspace` (`unicode::is_space`), so U+0085 and U+3000
are whitespace and U+200B is not; the openings are compared by code
point, case and all.

Decisions:

- `probe_text` is the argument `probe: &dyn Fn(&[u32], bool) -> PyStr`
  (text, `cut`) of `owner_text` and `owner_prompt`. Its patterns
  (`<tag\b[^>]*?(?:/>|>.*?</tag\s*>)` under `DOTALL|IGNORECASE`, one per
  envelope tag) are lazy choices, which rule 4 of the regular-expression
  decision names as never written by hand ("the envelopes"); they wait
  for pyre-6, and the unit that builds them passes `pyre::Regex::sub`
  here. This unit ports no pattern, so it adds none to the engine's
  inventory.
- `COMPOSED_OPENINGS` is written out, the three envelope tags with `<`
  first, as the reference's tuple concatenation gives; a kill test holds
  each opening.
- `Reference` implements `transcript::OwnerPrompt` over the functions,
  with the probe it holds.

Golden files: `policy.jsonl` (not gated: 16 hand cases over one flag and
several, force present or not, `memory_write` against `memory_update`
and another tool, managed and unmanaged keys, a flag passed false, a flag
the policy does not name and a name outside `ACKNOWLEDGE_NAMES`; and a
sweep of 4,096 combinations of tool, force, acknowledge subset, both
switches and the managed keys, pinned as count and SHA-256) and
`owner_prompt.jsonl` (not gated: `text_blocks` over contents that are not
lists and blocks that are not dicts or carry no text; `is_submitted`,
`submitted_text`, `queued_text` and `owner_prompt` over 74 rows: every
mark, falsy marks `0`, `""` and `[]`, `turnOrigin` null, missing, of
other types and other case, contents a dict or a number, queued prompts
blank by Unicode whitespace; `owner_text` over each composed opening,
leading whitespace and a tag after the first word, with `probe_text` the
identity). Lone surrogates travel as code points (`text_field`). Tests:
`golden_policy`, `golden_owner_prompt`, `owner_prompt_policy_kills`,
`owner_prompt_policy_robustness`.

Left for later: `_ENVELOPES` and `probe_text` (owner_prompt.py 98-114),
after pyre-6.

## Signed-log verification output

`cli::log_report::Report::from_verify` takes the store's typed verification
result and the displayed path. The caller adds the replacement history,
merges any external anchor checks into the ordered document and closes the
store before requesting output. Text prints anchor checks before replacement
history. JSON retains field insertion order, ASCII escapes and two-space
indentation. A SQLite bytes key keeps its Python representation in text
and raises the corresponding serialization error in JSON. The returned
exit status is 0 for an `ok` report and 1 for either other verdict.

The committed cases include the complete text and JSON digests of an
intact, rekeyed, restored and accepted signed store. The command parser,
read-only opening and anchor-file loading are separate units.

## Records and their errors

`records` reproduces what pydantic does with the inputs the reference's
record models meet, not pydantic in general: `str` (bytes decoded as UTF-8,
else `string_unicode`), `int` (bools, integral floats inside +-2**63, text
of an integer optionally followed by `.0...`, trimmed of White_Space, at
most 4300 bytes), `bool` (0/1, 0.0/1.0, the twelve words in any ASCII
case), `datetime` (speedate's RFC 3339 grammar with `T`, `t`, space or `_`,
`.`/`,` fractions truncated past six digits, `Z`/`z`/`+-HH[:]MM` below 24
hours; unix timestamps as numbers or text, past 2e10 read as milliseconds,
including speedate's second division for text floats and pydantic-core's
rounding of a float's fraction; year 0 is `datetime_parsing`, any other text
failure `datetime_from_date_parsing`), the `str` enums (bytes accepted),
lists, dicts (a key holding a lone surrogate comes back with each surrogate
as three U+FFFD, in the record and in the error location, as pydantic-core
rebuilds it), nested models, and the validators `models` adds.

A refusal is `RecordError::Validation { title, errors }`: the model's class
name and each error's location and pydantic's `type`, in pydantic's order;
never pydantic's message text. Anything else the reference raises on the
way (a row reader's `AttributeError`, `JSONDecodeError`, `IndexError` for
a missing column ...) is `RecordError::Raised(class name)`.

Validation never recurses: a deep value is matched one level at a time
and never cloned (`tests/records_robustness.rs`).

Two reference findings the port copies (filed, not changed here): a
`links_json` column holding a JSON object or string fails the whole read
as MemoryLink `model_type` (it iterates the keys or characters), and
`_path_targets` lets a numeric `attestation_payload` raise TypeError out
of the read (it catches only ValueError and RecursionError).

five are built (`src/history.rs`, `src/history_rows.rs`,

### Unit 1: the rows that name a record

The functions take the store as its `rusqlite::Connection` (the read-only
one of `store::StoreFile`, or a writing open's): nothing else of a store
is read. Every statement is the reference's text and SQLite answers it,
so `instr`'s semantics (an empty id is in every payload, a blob payload
is searched as text against a text id, the test is case-sensitive, a
NUL is a character) are the engine's in both builds.

- `read_snapshot(conn, body)`: `BEGIN`, the body, `ROLLBACK`, unless the
  connection already holds a transaction (`!is_autocommit()`, which is
  `conn.in_transaction`), when the body runs in it and nothing is ended.
  A body that ends the transaction itself makes the closing `ROLLBACK`
  fail ("cannot rollback - no transaction is active"), and that error
  takes the place of the body's value, as the `finally` block's
  exception does. A panic in the body rolls back on the way out. The
  body is a closure, the context manager's `with` block.
- `rows_naming`: `_rows_naming`. Text bound in the order `sqlite3` binds
  a parameter tuple: an id or kind holding a lone surrogate is
  UnicodeEncodeError, at the first one. A row is decoded when it is
  fetched, column by column: a text column that is not UTF-8 is
  OperationalError naming the first such column in column order. To
  hold that, `store::log_row` now reads `ts` before `session` (it read
  `session` first, which named the wrong column when both are bad).
  Each cell is `str()` of the value: a blob is its `b'...'` spelling.
- `with_linking_versions`: `_with_linking_versions`. The rows are kept
  by seq as a dict keeps them: a seq given twice keeps its last row in
  the place of its first, every row's payload is parsed (so its
  RecursionError is raised), and the scan for linking records walks
  that order. A linking record is the subject of a `memory_put` or
  `tombstone_put` row that is not the record and carries a link to it;
  each is scanned for in sorted order (code point order, a
  `BTreeSet<PyStr>`) over the four kinds of `LINK_SCAN_KINDS`, and a
  seq already held is not read again. The sources come back as a set.
- `with_restores` and `replaced_rows`: the bound is the seq of the first
  item given, not the lowest; a seq held keeps its item, but the
  replaced row's payload is parsed all the same, as `setdefault`'s
  argument is evaluated. An empty `found` comes back unasked.
  `replaced_rows` hands each row to a visitor as it is read, the
  reference's generator.
- `payload`: `json.loads` through `json::loads`; a dict or None.
  JSONDecodeError and the ValueError of an integer past 4,300 digits
  are None; RecursionError past `json::MAX_DEPTH` is raised, as the
  reference does not catch it.
- `mapping`, `subject`, `names_as_event`: the reference's branches,
  kind by kind; a name that is not a `str` is None, and a standing list
  is matched by member equality.
- `link_types`: `str()` of each matching link's `type` (`None` when it
  is missing), in sorted order: a scalar through `pyvalue::py_str`, a
  container spelled at its top level with each item through
  `pyvalue::repr`, since `str()` of a container writes one level more
  than `repr()` does (9,998 lists around a scalar, where `repr` writes
  9,997; measured through `_link_types` under 3.13.13). `str()` of a
  value nested deeper is RecursionError and of an `int` past 4,300
  digits ValueError, found in the order `repr` writes. No payload
  `json.loads` reads can hold either, so only the robustness tests
  reach them.

No regular expression is used. No crate is added.

Pinned by `history_rows.jsonl` (class i: the log table's statements cut
out of `store_schema.SCHEMA`, in memory; every branch of the pure
functions; the joins, the bounds, blobs, text that is not UTF-8,
surrogates, NUL, the seq bounds, the snapshot's three modes) and
`history_rows_python.jsonl` (class ii, gated on the Python release:
payloads nested half the budget deep or ten levels past
`json.loads`'s budget, where RecursionError is the interpreter's; the
exact bound moves with the caller's own C stack, 9,988 levels raising
under pytest, so no case sits near it).
`history_rows_kills` and `history_rows_robustness` hold the rest; the
second shows a history read growing linearly with the log (40,000 rows
against 20,000, fastest of three).

A row of the linking scan is merged on its text alone: a row of another
record whose id merely contains the linking record's id comes too (the
`links` case of `history_rows.jsonl`, record D and the row of record
`xDy`). Whether a report shows it is `_link_change_rows`'s to decide, in
unit 3; the port reproduces the merge.

### Unit 2: a row's MAC under its segment's key, and `_set`

`history_replaced` and `replaced_detail` were already built as
`Store::history_replaced`, so this unit is `_RowVerifier` and `_set`
(`src/history.rs`, about 130 lines).

- `RowVerifier::new(conn, ring, store_fingerprint)`: the store's sides
  are arguments (its connection, its `KeyRing`, its `key_fingerprint`),
  so `record_history` (unit 4) passes the `Store`'s. The statement is the
  reference's, bound to `rekey`. Each payload is `str()` of the cell
  (`SqlValue::py_str`): a blob is its `b'...'` spelling and a number or
  NULL its spelling, none of them a JSON object, so the row is skipped;
  a text cell that is not UTF-8 is the fetch's OperationalError naming
  `payload`. The payload is read by `json::loads`; a value that is not a
  dict (a list or a str is TypeError, any scalar too), a missing name
  (KeyError), JSON that does not parse and an integer past 4,300 digits
  (ValueError) skip the row, the old name read before the new one so a
  row missing either is skipped whole. RecursionError is not caught and
  is raised. Each name is `str()` of the value (`text_of`, the module's
  own, which writes one level more than `repr` as `str` does). The
  first parsed row names the first segment's key; the store's
  fingerprint names it only when no rekey row parses.
- `verified(row)`: the segment is the last in list order whose first
  seq is at or below the row's. The list is `(1, first)` then the rekey
  rows in seq order, so a rekey at seq 1 wins over the first segment
  for row 1, a rekey at seq 0 or below follows `(1, first)` in the list
  and wins for every row at or past its seq, and a row below every
  segment takes the first. The key is looked up once per name
  (`KeyRing::key_for_fingerprint`); a name holding a lone surrogate is
  no fingerprint and names no key. A key not held is None, else the
  answer of `log::row_verifies`.
- `set(detail, values)`: `_set` over a detail held as ordered pairs; a
  value that is None is left out, a name already present keeps its place
  and takes the new value.

Pinned by `history_rows_mac.jsonl` (class i), written by
`gen_history_rows.generate_mac`: the log table cut out of
`store_schema.SCHEMA` in memory, rows MACed with `log.compute_mac` under
three keys (SHA-256 of `k1`, `k2`, `k3`), and a duck-typed store whose
key ring is `KeyRing.key_for_fingerprint` without files. It covers no
rekey row, one and several, the store's fingerprint ignored, a key held
only as retired, a key absent, a tampered MAC, the wrong key, rekeys at
seq 0 and at seq 1, bad JSON, a blob, a list, a str, an int, null,
missing names, an over-long integer, names that are not `str`, an
uppercase fingerprint, duplicate names, a payload that is not UTF-8 in
a rekey row and in another row, and `_set`. Two rekeys at one seq cannot
sit in the table (seq is its key). No RecursionError row is written;
`history_mac_robustness` raises one from a payload nested 100,000 deep.
`history_mac_kills` holds seven cases a plausible wrong port fails;
`history_mac_robustness` also shows the constructor growing linearly
with the rekey rows (20,000 against 2,000).

No regular expression is used (`is_fingerprint` is `log.rs`'s). No crate
is added.

### Unit 3: what one row of a record's history says

Built in `src/history_rows.rs` (one file beside `src/history.rs`, which
unit 2 edits). The reference's lines, confirmed against the source as it
is: the constants 121-144, `HistoryRow` and `to_dict` 165-197,
`_changed` 521-532, `_body_diff` 534-543, `_set` 545-550,
`_event_detail` 553-568, `_RecordWalk` 581-590, `_record_row` 592-738,
`_link_change_rows` 741-778. `HistoryRow` moved here from unit 4 and
`_RecordWalk` with it, since `_record_row` builds and carries them.

- What later units own comes in as arguments: `verified` is unit 2's
  `_RowVerifier.verified(row)`; `before` and `after` are unit 4's
  `adjacent(index, -1)` and `adjacent(index, 1)`, already looked up.
  `base` is the row's seq, ts, session and kind, read off the `LogRow`
  as `_read_history` builds it.
- `py_ne`: Python's `!=` over payload values. Bool, int and float
  compare as numbers, exactly (2**53 + 1 differs from the float it
  rounds to; -0.0 equals 0); a dict compares by keys and values, a list
  in order, a list never equals a str. `json.loads` hands every `NaN` as
  the one object `json.decoder.NaN`, and a container's comparison takes
  the identity shortcut (`PyObject_RichCompareBool`) where the top-level
  `!=` does not: a top-level `NaN` field reads as changed, a `NaN`
  inside a list or dict does not. The walk keeps a work list, so a value
  nested to `json::MAX_DEPTH` compares without recursion (the reference
  compares 9,900 levels without RecursionError).
- `changed`: the `str` keys both records carry, outside `_UNCOMPARED`,
  sorted by code point. A payload record's keys are `str`.
- `event_detail`: `value not in (None, "", [], {})` drops exactly those
  four values (0, `False`, `0.0` and `[[]]` are kept); `forced` only when
  it is `True` itself; `*_acknowledged` by truthiness (`machine::truthy`),
  the names stripped and sorted.
- `record_row`: the reference's branches kind by kind, the `detail` dict
  in insertion order. A body equal to the empty text against no
  previous body is still a change: the diff is the empty text, not None.
  `_set` is a private helper here (`set`).
- `link_change_rows`: `_link_types` from unit 1, its error carried.
- `IMPORTED` and `UNACCOUNTED` (`store.IMPORTED`, `store.UNACCOUNTED`)
  are private constants here; no crate constant held them.

No regular expression is used. No crate is added. Nothing is read from
the machine, so the file is ungated.

Pinned by `history_detail.jsonl` (`gen_history_detail.py`): `_changed`
and `_event_detail` over values that differ only across types and over
`NaN`, walks of scripted rows through every kind branch (with a stub
verifier and adjacency), and link sets added and dropped.
`history_detail_kills` and `history_detail_robustness` hold the rest;
the second compares values nested to the reader's limit and shows wide
records comparing in linear time.

Left for unit 4: `RecordHistory`, `record_history`, `_read_history`,
`_table_kind`, `_state`; for unit 5: `render_text`, `render_json`.

### Unit 4: one record's whole history

Built in `src/history_record.rs`, a file of its own beside units 1 to
3, which it does not edit. The reference's lines, confirmed against the
source at e5eb23e3: the constants `FORMAT`, `FORMAT_VERSION`, `EVENT`,
`STORE`, `ACTOR_FROM_EVENT` 98-110, `RecordHistory` 200-266,
`replaced_detail` 432-459, `record_history` 571-577, `_read_history`
with its `adjacent` 780-918, `_table_kind` 921-932, `_state` 935-960.

- The store's sides are arguments: `record_history(source, ring,
  provenance, record_id)` takes any `store::provenance::Source` (a
  read-only `StoreFile`, as the command opens it, or a writer's
  `ConnSource`), the in-memory `log::KeyRing` the row verifier reads,
  and a `Provenance` reader over that same source, which answers
  `provenance_for`, `episode_provenance` and `can_verify`. Every
  statement runs on the source's connection, inside
  `history::read_snapshot`; its closing ROLLBACK error replaces the
  body's answer, as the reference's `finally` does.
- The order of effects is the reference's, and so the order errors
  surface in: meta's `key_fingerprint` (KeyError when meta lacks it,
  `HistoryError::NoKeyFingerprint`), the rekey rows, `_rows_naming`
  (UnicodeEncodeError for an id holding a lone surrogate), the linking
  versions, the restores, the walk, `_state`, `_table_kind` only when
  the state is `active` or `tombstoned` and the walk named no kind,
  then `can_verify`. The id is valid text by the time `_state` binds it
  again and hands it to the provenance reader, which takes `&str`.
- `adjacent`: the item next in `found` only when its seq is exactly one
  apart in the log, its payload is a mapping and its subject is the one
  asked. A row whose payload is None is skipped by the walk but stays
  in `found`, so it still stands between two rows.
- The walk's branches go in the reference's order, first match wins: a
  `store_restored` or `history_accepted` row is a `store` row whatever
  it names; the record's own row is `record_row`; a change event or the
  standing guard is an `event` row, its actor only when the payload's
  actor mapping is non-empty; a delete of a linking record pops its
  links into `unlinked` rows, sorted, unless the next row in the log is
  the put that carries them (then nothing is written and the links
  stay); a version of a linking record is `link_change_rows`; a
  `conflict_put` naming the record as `a_id` or `b_id` is a `conflict`
  row whose `other` is `b_id` when `a_id` is the record, else `a_id`
  (a self conflict names itself). `verifier.verified(row)` is asked
  once per row written, as the reference asks it; the ring is in
  memory, so the answer is a pure function of the row.
- `state`: memories, then episodes, then tombstones. An active memory's
  label is `provenance_for([id]).get(id)`, an episode's
  `episode_provenance`'s; a tombstone reads `unaccounted` unless the
  walk's last record row is its `tombstone_put`, with no key needed;
  with no table row the last record kind gives `unknown` (none),
  `deleted` (`memory_delete`), `pruned` (`tombstone_delete`,
  `episode_delete`) or `missing`. `table_kind` asks memories,
  tombstones, episodes, in that order, so a record held as an episode
  and a tombstone reads `active` from the episode and `memory` as its
  kind.
- `replaced_detail(kind, payload)`: a function of its own here.
  `head_after`, else `log_end_before` for a kind other than
  `store_restored`; an empty mapping has no seq; `from_seq` is the
  largest of the seqs that are exactly an `int` (a bool is not),
  compared at any size by `pyvalue::cmp_int_text`. `Store::history_replaced`
  keeps its own copy (`store::replaced_entry`) until a later unit joins
  them.
- Errors stay typed (`HistoryError`): a SQLite error or a `PyError`
  (RecursionError from a payload, UnicodeEncodeError) as `StoreError`,
  the missing key fingerprint, and what the provenance reader raised
  (`ProvenanceError::Raised`) or declined (`NotPorted`, passed on as a
  decline). A reader that would verify with no current key in the ring
  is refused by `Provenance::new` (NotPorted) before this unit runs;
  the caller passes that on as a decline. The CLI decides what to print.

No regular expression is used. No crate is added.

Pinned by `history_record.jsonl` (`gen_history_record.py`), gated as
`store_provenance.jsonl` is (Unicode, pydantic-core, POSIX only). Each
line is one store made by the reference (`Store.create`, rows appended
with `log.append_row` and applied with `_apply_mutation`, plants by
SQL), its five tables recorded, and per opening the key ring, the
fingerprint the read-only open verifies under, `strict_provenance`, and
per id `to_dict(diff=True)` as `json.dumps` writes it (exact, key order
included, about a third of `_common.neutral`'s size, which kept the file
under 150 KB), `exit_code` and `known`, or the exception's class. The
stores hold every case the unit's brief names: a memory created,
updated, verified, corroborated, removed, restored, pruned, deleted,
deleted outside the store; an episode put and pruned; a planted
tombstone and one whose last record row is not its put; unknown ids,
an id inside another, the empty id, a NUL, lone surrogates; pairings
broken by an unrelated row, by rows without a payload and by a gap in
seq; a delete followed by another record's put; links added, retyped,
dropped, carried and pruned, a supersedes link, a link whose removal
is followed by a put rather than its carrier (unlinked, then linked
again); conflicts; telemetry
with and without an actor; replaced rows before and after the record's
first row; a rekey with the old key held, retired and absent, a tampered
row; a store whose meta names a key this host does not hold; strict
provenance on. A seeded sweep (writes, updates, removals, restores,
prunes, links, telemetry, tampering over five records) is pinned by
count and SHA-256. A store without `key_fingerprint` in meta cannot be
opened by the reference (`Store.open` refuses it), so that KeyError is
held by `history_record_kills` only. `golden_history_record_not_posix`
records the fixture's gap off POSIX. `history_record_kills` holds the
pairing, branch, state and order hazards; `history_record_robustness`
a log of 40,000 rows against 20,000, 20,000 versions, a payload nested
100,000 deep (RecursionError from the port's budget, no stack overflow;
the reference's answer there follows the Python release and the system:
CPython 3.13 and macOS raise RecursionError, CPython 3.14 on Linux reads
the payload and the history continues, so the row matches the reference
only where it raises and is in no golden file), a megabyte body changed
by one line and ids at the edges.

Left for unit 5: `render_text`, `render_json`, `_actor_text`,
`_value_text`, `_VERIFIED_TEXT`, which read `RecordHistory`.

### Unit 5: the text and the JSON `memory history` prints

Built in `src/history_render.rs`, a file of its own beside units 1 to
4, which it does not edit. The reference's lines, confirmed against the
source at 6330bd5f: `_actor_text` 963-969, `_value_text` 972-979,
`_VERIFIED_TEXT` 982, `render_text` 985-1024, `render_json` 1027-1028
(the rest of the file, to 1050, is `__all__`). The functions are pure:
nothing is read from the machine.

- `render_text(history, diff)`: the header (`row` for exactly one row,
  `rows` for any other count, 0 included; `record` when the kind is
  None or empty, the reference's `or`), the provenance line when there
  is a label, with `(unverified: no key)` only for an `active` record
  without the key (a tombstone's `unaccounted` rests on the log's shape),
  the key line when the key is not held, one line per row, the diff's
  pieces under a row when `diff` is set and the row's diff is not empty,
  and the findings block only when there are findings. Each line is
  built whole, then passed through `printable` on its own and followed
  by a line feed (`"\n".join(...) + "\n"`). So a line feed, an escape
  sequence or a bidirectional control inside a record id, a label, a
  row's ts, kind or action, an actor's value, a changed field or a
  detail name or value is written as its escape and cannot start a line
  or close one, while the diff's own line feeds, split before the
  escaping (`str.split("\n")`, so a diff ending in a line feed gives a
  last line of six spaces), each start one. Every category `printable`
  escapes includes the lone surrogates, so the text holds none.
- A row's line: seq, ts, kind, action and `_VERIFIED_TEXT` (`mac ok`,
  `MAC FAILS`, `mac unverifiable`); then, when the actor is not None (an
  empty mapping is not None and reads `undeclared`), `author` when its
  source is `record` and `actor` for any other source or None; then
  `changed` with the fields joined by commas; then each detail item in
  insertion order. The parts are spelled in the reference's order, so
  the first error raised is the reference's: the actor, then each
  detail name, then its value.
- `actor_text`: `client`, `model`, `principal`, in that order, each
  when its value is a non-empty `str` (the last of a name given twice,
  as `json.loads` keeps it); `undeclared` when none is. The pairs are
  read once, from the last, until all three names are met, not once per
  name. An actor that is not a mapping is the AttributeError of
  `actor.get` (`RenderError::ActorNotMapping`).
- A row's actor of `Some(PyValue::None)` is read as no actor. No
  reference row holds it (the actor is a mapping or None, and
  `record_history` keeps only mappings), and `HistoryRow::to_dict`
  already writes it as `null`, as it writes None; so `render_text`
  prints no actor part for it, as the reference does for None, and the
  two renderers agree. `actor_text(&PyValue::None)` itself stays the
  AttributeError `_actor_text(None)` raises.
- `value_text`: a `str` as itself; anything else through `json::dumps`
  with `DumpOptions::SORTED_UNICODE_SPACED` (sorted keys, non-ASCII
  kept, `, ` and `: `); then a text of more than 80 code points is its
  first 77 and `...`. The count is in code points, as Python's `len`:
  an astral code point is one, a lone surrogate is one. A `str` is cut
  from its own code points, as the reference slices it, so its length
  costs nothing. TypeError for
  a value `json.dumps` cannot spell (a datetime, a path, a dict whose
  keys do not sort), ValueError for an `int` past 4,300 digits.
- A detail name that is not a `str` (no payload makes one) is `str()`
  of it, as the f-string writes it: ValueError for an `int` past 4,300
  digits, RecursionError past the budget below.
- `render_json(history, diff)`: `json::dumps(history.to_dict(diff))`
  with `JSON_OPTIONS`, `DOCUMENT_INDENT2` without the sort (insertion
  order, ASCII escapes with astral code points as surrogate pairs and a
  lone surrogate as its own escape, `,` and `: `, an empty list and dict
  as `[]` and `{}`, `NaN` and `Infinity` by name), and a line feed. It
  is not passed through `printable`. A dict key `json.dumps` refuses (a
  tuple) is TypeError; mixed key types are written, since nothing sorts.
- Errors are typed: `render_text` returns `RenderError` (what was
  raised, or the actor's AttributeError, with `name()` the class),
  `render_json` the `PyError`. The CLI decides what to print.
- Nesting: `json::MAX_DEPTH`, the port's budget, equal to what CPython
  3.13.13 showed from a plain script on macOS: 9,998 lists around a
  value in `_value_text` and 9,994 in `render_json` (four containers
  hold the value there), and a detail name of 9,997 tuples around a
  scalar (the f-string's `format` takes a level `str()` does not). The
  reference's bound follows the release and the caller's stack (3.11 and
  3.12 encode an indented document in Python and stop near a thousand
  levels; CPython 3.14 on Linux reads deeper), so no golden file sits
  near it and `history_render_robustness` holds the port's. The budget
  is one for every value. For a value no store produces whose bottom
  raises (a datetime or a path, a dict whose keys do not sort or a
  tuple key, an `int` past 4,300 digits) CPython 3.13.13's bound sits
  one to five levels lower, since the raise spends stack of its own:
  within those levels the port answers the bottom's TypeError or
  ValueError, or a detail name's text, where the reference answers
  RecursionError. Measured: under `_value_text` and a `render_text`
  value, 9,996 to 9,998 lists or dicts around a datetime or a path,
  9,996 and 9,997 around mixed keys, 9,997 around a tuple key, 9,998
  around a long `int`; under `render_json` 9,992 to 9,994 around a
  datetime or a path, 9,993 around a tuple key and 9,994 around a long
  `int`; a detail name of 9,993 to 9,997 tuples around a path, and 9,997
  around a long `int`.

No regular expression is used. No crate is added.

Pinned by `history_render.jsonl` (`gen_history_render.py`, class i):
`_actor_text` over 15 actors (the three names in either order, values
that are not text or empty, extra names, non-ASCII, a lone surrogate,
three that are not mappings), `_value_text` over 47 values (every JSON
type, text of 77, 80 and 81 code points in ASCII, Latin-1 and astral,
a lone surrogate at the cut, floats at their edges, a nested dict whose
keys sort otherwise than they were inserted, keys that are not text,
an `int` of 4,300 digits, values `json.dumps` refuses), and 36 whole
histories rendered four ways (text and JSON, with and without the
diff), compared whole: 0, 1 and 2 rows, each state, the kind None and
empty, provenance None, `local`, `imported`, `unaccounted`, empty and a
hostile label with the key held and not on an active record and a
tombstone, every verdict, every actor and source, changed empty, one
and several, the diffs of the brief, every finding, a row with every
part, hostile text in every field, and the errors. The histories are
built directly, without a store, and written field by field
(`_common.neutral` for the values). A seeded sweep of 600 histories
drawn from pools the row holds (splitmix64, seed 20261124) is pinned by
count and SHA-256 of the four renders of each. The file holds ASCII,
Latin-1 and code points whose category has not moved since Unicode 14,
so it regenerates byte for byte under 3.11 to 3.14.
`history_render_unicode.jsonl` (class ii, gated on the Unicode data:
`printable` escapes by category) pins `render_text` over every code
point, in chunks of 64 placed in the record id, an actor, a changed
field, a detail name and value and the diff, by count and SHA-256 per
65,536 code points. Both files confirm the brief's open point: the
indented writer spells an empty list and dict and a lone surrogate as
`json.dumps` does.

`history_render_kills` (18) holds `row` against `rows` at 0, 1 and 2,
the unverified note on a tombstone, `author` against `actor`, the empty
actor mapping, the cut at 80 and 81 code points with astral text and a
lone surrogate, the sort in `_value_text` and not in `render_json`,
`ensure_ascii` the other way round in each, `printable` per line, the
diff's last empty piece, the findings block absent when there are none,
the order errors are raised in (the actor, a detail name before its
value, a tuple name's items first to last), a negative name of 4,300
digits written and of 4,301 refused, and an actor of `Some(PyValue::None)`
read as none in both renderers. `history_render_robustness` (10)
renders 100,000 rows and a diff of a megabyte whole (the JSON compared
by the SHA-256 of the reference's text), holds the nesting bounds with
the texts written at them, a deep tuple item before a long `int` at the
bound, raises RecursionError for a value nested 100,000 deep without
overflowing the stack, and shows both renderers linear in the rows
(50,000 against 5,000), `render_text` linear in the diff, a long `str`
value's cost flat in its length (10,000,000 code points against 1,000)
and an actor's names read in one pass.

Left for later: the `memory history` command (its parser, the store's
read-only open, printing and the exit code), a CLI unit.
